s: You remember, holy brethren, that the Gospel according to John, read in the regular course of lessons, is the subject on which we usually preach; but because of the solemnity of the holy days now intervening, on which certain lessons must be read in the Church—lessons which come round every year in such a way that they cannot be other than they are—the order which we had undertaken is of necessity interrupted for a little while, not wholly abandoned.

But when I was thinking what subject of discourse from the Scriptures, in keeping with the joy of these days, I might undertake with you during the present week, as the Lord shall be pleased to grant—one such as could be finished in these seven or eight days—the Epistle of blessed John came to my mind: so that, since we have for a while interrupted the reading of his Gospel, we may, in discoursing on his Epistle, not depart from his side; all the more because in this same Epistle, which is very sweet to all who have a healthy taste of the heart to relish the Bread of God, and very fit to be kept in remembrance in God’s holy Church, charity is commended above all.
He has spoken many words, and nearly all are about charity.
He who has in himself that which he is to hear cannot but rejoice at what he hears.
For this reading will be to that man like oil upon a flame: if there is something there that can be nourished, it is nourished, and grows, and endures.
Again, to some it ought to be like flame to fuel: so that if he was not burning, he may be set on fire by the added discourse.
For in some, what is there is nourished; in some, it is kindled, if it is not there: so that we may all rejoice in one charity.
But where there is charity, there is peace; and where there is humility, there is charity.
Now let us hear the man himself; and at his words, whatever the Lord suggests, let us speak that also to you, so that you may understand well.

“That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, and which we have seen with our eyes, and our hands have handled, concerning the Word of life: and the life was manifested, and we have seen, and bear witness, and show to you that eternal life which was with the Father and was manifested to us: the things which we have seen and heard we declare to you, that you also may have fellowship with us; and that our fellowship may be with the Father, and with His Son Jesus Christ.
And these things we write to you, that your joy may be full.
This, then, is the message which we have heard from Him and declare to you, that God is light, and in Him is no darkness at all.

If we say that we have fellowship with Him, and walk in darkness, we lie and do not do the truth; if we walk in the light, as He is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus Christ His Son shall cleanse us from all sin.
If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
If we say that we have not sinned, we make Him a liar, and His word is not in us.
My little children, these things I write to you, that you may not sin.
And if anyone sins, we have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world.
And by this we know Him, if we keep His commandments.
He who says he knows Him, and does not keep His commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him.
But whoever keeps His word, in him truly the love of God is perfected.
By this we know that we are in Him, if we are perfect in Him.
He who says he abides in Him ought himself also to walk just as He walked.
Beloved, I write no new commandment to you, but an old commandment which you have had from the beginning.
The old commandment is the word which you have heard.
Again, a new commandment I write to you, which thing is true in Him and in you, because the darkness is past, and the true light now shines.
He who says he is in the light, and hates his brother, is in darkness even until now.
He who loves his brother abides in the light, and there is no occasion of stumbling in him.
For he who hates his brother is in darkness, and walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.”
1. “That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, and our hands have handled, concerning the word of life.”
Who is it that handles the Word with hands, except because “The Word was made flesh, and dwelt in us”?
Now this Word, which was made flesh so that it might be handled, began to be flesh from the Virgin Mary; but the Word did not begin then, for the apostle says, “That which was from the beginning.”
See whether his epistle does not bear witness to his gospel, where you lately heard, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God.”
Perhaps someone may take “Concerning the word of life” as a kind of expression about Christ, and not as the very body of Christ which was handled with hands.
See what follows: “And the Life was manifested.”
Christ, therefore, is “the word of life.”
And how was it manifested? For it was “from the beginning,” only not manifested to men; but it was manifested to angels, who saw it and fed on it as their bread.
But what does the Scripture say?
“Man ate angels’ bread.”

So then, “the Life was manifested” in the flesh; because it was set forth in manifestation, so that what can be seen by the heart alone might be seen by the eyes also, in order that it might heal the hearts.
For the Word is seen only by the heart; but the flesh is seen by the bodily eyes also.
We had the means to see the flesh, but had not the means to see the Word: “the Word was made flesh,” which we could see, so that there might be healed in us that by which we might see the Word.
2. “And we have seen and are witnesses.”

Perhaps some of the brethren who are not acquainted with Greek do not know what the word “witnesses” is in Greek; and yet it is a term used much by all, and held in religious reverence: for what in our language we call “witnesses,” in Greek are “martyrs.”

Now where is the man who has not heard of martyrs, or where is the Christian in whose mouth the name of martyrs does not dwell every day—and would that it dwelt so in the heart also, that we would imitate the sufferings of the martyrs, and not persecute them with our drinking cups!
So then, “We have seen and are witnesses” is as much as to say, We have seen and are martyrs.

For it was for bearing witness to what they had seen, and bearing witness to what they had heard from those who had seen, that—while their very testimony displeased the men against whom it was delivered—the martyrs suffered all that they did suffer.
The martyrs are God’s witnesses.
It pleased God to have men as His witnesses, so that men also may have God as their witness.
“We have seen,” he says, “and are witnesses.”
Where have they seen?
In the manifestation. What does “in the manifestation” mean?
In the sun, that is, in this light of day.

And how could He who made the sun be seen in the sun, except as “in the sun He has set His tabernacle; and He Himself, as a bridegroom going forth out of his chamber, rejoiced as a giant to run His course”?

He who was before the sun, who made the sun, He who was before the morning star, before all the stars, before all angels, the true Creator (“for all things were made by Him, and without Him nothing was made”), in order that He might be seen by eyes of flesh which see the sun, set His very tabernacle in the sun, that is, showed His flesh in the manifestation of this light of day; and that Bridegroom’s chamber was the Virgin’s womb, because in that virginal womb the two were joined, the Bridegroom and the bride, the Bridegroom the Word, and the bride the flesh; because it is written, “And the two shall be one flesh;” and the Lord says in the Gospel, “Therefore they are no longer two but one flesh.
And Isaiah remembers very well that they are two: for speaking in the person of Christ he says, “He has set a mitre upon me as upon a bridegroom, and adorned me with an ornament as a bride.”
One seems to speak, yet He makes Himself at once Bridegroom and Bride; because “not two, but one flesh”; because “the Word was made flesh, and dwelt in us.”
To that flesh the Church is joined, and so the whole Christ is made, Head and body.
3. “And we are witnesses, and show to you that eternal life which was with the Father and was manifested to us”—that is, manifested among us; which might be more plainly expressed, manifested to us.
“The things,” therefore, “which we have seen and heard we declare to you.”
They saw the Lord Himself present in the flesh, and heard words from the mouth of the Lord, and told them to us.
Consequently we also have heard, but have not seen.
Are we then less happy than those who saw and heard?
And how is it that he adds, “That you also may have fellowship with us”?
They saw, we have not seen, and yet we are their fellows, because we hold the faith in common.

For there was one who did not believe even upon seeing, and insisted on handling, and so believing, and said, “I will not believe unless I thrust my fingers into the place of the nails, and touch His scars.”

And He who always gives Himself to be seen by the sight of the angels did give Himself for a time to be handled by the hands of men; and that disciple did handle Him, and exclaimed, “My Lord and my God!”
Because he touched the Man, he confessed the God.

And the Lord, to console us who, now that He sits in heaven, cannot touch Him with the hand but only reach Him by faith, said to him, “Because you have seen, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen, and yet believe.”
We are described here; we are the ones designated.
Then let the blessedness take place in us which the Lord foretold would take place; let us firmly hold what we do not see, because those who have seen tell us.
“That you also,” he says, “may have fellowship with us.”
And what great thing is it to have fellowship with men?
Do not despise it; see what he adds: “and that our fellowship may be with God the Father, and Jesus Christ His Son.
And these things,” he says, “we write to you, that your joy may be full.”
He means full joy in that fellowship, in that charity, in that unity.
4. “And this is the message which we have heard from Him, and declare to you.”
What is this? These same men have seen, have handled with their hands, the Word of life: He “was from the beginning,” and for a time was made visible and tangible, the Only-begotten Son of God.
For what did He come, or what new thing did He tell us?
What was it His will to teach?

Why did He do what He did—that the Word should be made flesh, that “God over all things” should suffer indignities from men, that He should endure being struck on the face by the hands which He Himself had made?
What would He teach?
What would He show?
What would He declare?
Let us hear: for without the fruit of the precept, the hearing of the story of how Christ was born and how Christ suffered is a mere pastime of the mind, not a strengthening of it.
What great thing are you hearing?
See to it with what fruit you hear.
What would He teach?
What would He declare? Hear. That “God is light,” he says, “and there is no darkness in Him at all.”
So far he has indeed named the light, but the words are dark: it is good for us that the very light which he has named should enlighten our hearts, and that we should see what he has said.
This is what we declare, that “God is light, and there is no darkness in Him at all.”
Who would dare to say that there is darkness in God?
Or what is the light?
Or what is the darkness? Lest perhaps he is speaking of such things as pertain to these eyes of ours.
“God is light.” Someone says, “The sun also is light, and the moon also is light, and a candle is light.”
It ought to be something far greater than these, far more excellent, and far more surpassing.
As far as God is distant from the creature, as far as the Maker from what He made, as far as Wisdom from that which is made by Wisdom, so far beyond all things must this light be.

And perhaps we shall be near to it, if we come to know what this light is, and apply ourselves to it, so that by it we may be enlightened; because in ourselves we are darkness, and only when enlightened by it can we become light, and not be put to shame by it, as we are put to shame by ourselves.
Who is he that is put to shame by himself?
He who knows himself to be a sinner.
Who is he that is not put to shame by it?
He who is enlightened by it.
What is it to be enlightened by it?

He who now sees himself to be darkened by sins, and desires to be enlightened by it, draws near to it; hence the Psalm says, “Draw near to Him, and be enlightened; and your faces shall not be ashamed.”
But you will not be shamed by it if, when it shows you to yourself as foul, your own foulness displeases you, so that you may perceive its beauty.
This is what He would teach.
5. And might it be that we are saying this over-hastily?
Let the apostle himself make this plain in what follows.
Remember what was said at the outset of our discourse, that this epistle commends charity: “God is light,” he says, “and in Him is no darkness at all.”
And what did he say above?
“That you may have fellowship with us, and our fellowship may be with God the Father, and with His Son Jesus Christ.”

But moreover, if “God is light, and in Him is no darkness at all, and we must have fellowship with Him,” then the darkness must also be driven away from us, so that light may be created in us; for darkness cannot have fellowship with light.
To this end, see what follows: “If we say that we have fellowship with Him, and walk in darkness, we lie.”
You also have the Apostle Paul saying, “Or what fellowship has light with darkness?”
You say you have fellowship with God, and you walk in darkness; “and God is light, and in Him is no darkness at all”: then how should there be fellowship between light and darkness?
At this point, therefore, a man may say to himself, What shall I do? How shall I be light?
I live in sins and iniquities.
There steals over him, as it were, a despair and sadness.
There is no salvation except in the fellowship of God.
“God is light, and in Him is no darkness at all.”
But sins are darkness, as the apostle says of the devil and his angels, that they are “rulers of this darkness.”
He would not call them rulers of darkness except as rulers of sins, having lordship over the wicked.
Then what are we to do, my brethren?

Fellowship with God must be had; there is no other hope of eternal life. Now “God is Light, and in Him is no darkness at all”; now iniquities are darkness; we are pressed down by iniquities, so that we cannot have fellowship with God: what hope do we have then?
Did I not promise to speak during these days about something that would cause gladness?
If I do not make that good, this is sadness.
“God is Light, and in Him is no darkness at all”; sins are darkness: what will become of us?
Let us hear whether perhaps He will console us, lift us up, give us hope, so that we do not faint along the way.
For we are running, and running to our own country; and if we despair of arriving, by that very despair we fail.
But He whose will it is that we arrive, so that He may keep us safe in our own land, feeds us along the way.
Let us hear, then: “If we say that we have fellowship with Him and walk in darkness, we lie, and do not do the truth.”
Let us not say that we have fellowship with Him, if we walk in darkness.
“If we walk in the light, as He is in the light, we have fellowship with one another.”
Let us walk in the light, as He is in the light, so that we may be able to have fellowship with Him.
And what are we to do about our sins?
Hear what follows: “And the blood of Jesus Christ His Son shall purge us from all sin.”
What great assurance God has given!
Well may we celebrate the Passover, in which the blood of the Lord was shed, by which we are cleansed “from all sin”!
Let us be assured: the devil held “the handwriting which was against us,” the bond of our slavery; but by the blood of Christ it is blotted out.
“The blood,” he says, “of His Son shall purge us from all sin.”
What does “from all sin” mean?
Mark this: see, even now, in the name of Christ whom these here have now confessed—those who are called infants—all their sins have been cleansed.
They came in old, they went out new.
How is it that they came in old and went out new?
Old men they came in; infants they went out.
For the old life is old age with all its dotage, but the new life is the infancy of regeneration.
But what are we to do?
The past sins are pardoned, not only to these but to us; and after the pardon and abolition of all sins, by living in this world in the midst of temptations, some perhaps have been contracted.
Therefore let man do what he can; let him confess himself to be what he is, so that he may be cured by Him who always is what He is: for He always was and is; we were not, and are.
6. For see what He says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”
Consequently, if you have confessed yourself a sinner, the truth is in you: for the Truth itself is light.
Your life has not yet shone in perfect brightness, because there are sins in you; but yet you have already begun to be enlightened, because the confession of sins is in you.
For see what follows: “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to purge us from all iniquity.”
Not only the past ones, but perhaps any we have contracted from this life; because a man, so long as he bears the flesh, cannot but have some sins, at any rate light ones.
But these which we call light, do not make light of.
If you make light of them when you weigh them, be afraid when you count them.
Many light sins make one huge sin: many drops fill the river; many grains make the lump.
And what hope is there?
Before all, confession: lest anyone think himself righteous, and man, who was not and is, lift up his neck before the eyes of God, who sees that which is.
Before all, then, confession; then, love: for what is said of charity?
“Charity covers a multitude of sins.”
Now let us see whether he commends charity with regard to the sins which afterward overtake us: because charity alone extinguishes sins.
Pride extinguishes charity: therefore humility strengthens charity; charity extinguishes sins.

Humility goes along with confession, the humility by which we confess ourselves sinners: this is humility—not to say it with the tongue, as if only to avoid arrogance, lest we should displease men if we should say that we are righteous.
This is what the ungodly and insane do: “I know indeed that I am righteous, but what shall I say before men?

If I call myself righteous, who will bear it, who will tolerate it? Let my righteousness be known to God: I, however, will say that I am a sinner, but only so that I may not be found odious for arrogance.”
Tell men what you are; tell God what you are. Because if you do not tell God what you are, God condemns what He shall find in you.
Would you not have Him condemn you?
Condemn yourself. Would you have Him forgive? Acknowledge, so that you may be able to say to God, “Turn Your face from my sins.”
Say to Him also those words in the same Psalm, “For I acknowledge my iniquity.”
“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to purge us from all iniquity.
If we say that we have not sinned, we make Him a liar, and His word is not in us.”
If you say, I have not sinned, you make Him a liar, while you wish to make yourself true.
How is it possible that God should be a liar and man true, when the Scripture says the contrary, “Every man a liar, God alone true”?
Consequently, God is true through Himself, you are true through God; because through yourself, you are a liar.

7. And lest perhaps he should seem to have granted impunity for sins, in that he said, “He is faithful and just to cleanse us from all iniquity,” and men should from then on say to themselves, Let us sin, let us do securely what we will, Christ purges us, He is faithful and just, He purges us from all iniquity—He takes from you an evil security, and puts in a useful fear.
To your own hurt you would be secure; you must be anxious.
For “He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins,” provided you always displease yourself, and keep changing until you are perfected.
Accordingly, what follows? “My little children, these things I write to you, that you may not sin.”
But perhaps sin overtakes us from our mortal life: what shall be done then?
What? Shall there now be despair?
Hear: “And if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous: and He is the propitiator for our sins.”

He, then, is the advocate; do your utmost not to sin: if from the infirmity of this life sin overtakes you, see to it immediately, immediately be displeased, immediately condemn it; and when you have condemned it, you will come with assurance to the Judge.
There you have the advocate: do not fear to lose your cause in your confession.
For if often in this life a man commits his cause to an eloquent tongue and is not lost, you commit yourself to the Word—and shall you be lost?
Cry out, “We have an advocate with the Father.”
8. See John himself observing humility.

Assuredly he was a righteous and a great man, who drank in the secrets of His mysteries from the Lord’s breast; he, the man who by drinking from the Lord’s breast wrote of His Godhead, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God”: he, being such a man as this, does not say, You have an advocate with the Father; but, “If anyone sins, an advocate,” he says, “we have.”
He does not say, you have; nor does he say, you have me; nor does he say, you have Christ Himself: but he puts forward Christ, not himself, and says also, “We have,” not, you have.

He chose rather to put himself among the number of sinners, so that he might have Christ for his advocate, than to put himself in Christ’s place as advocate and be found among the proud who shall be condemned.
Brethren, Jesus Christ the righteous, even Him we have as our advocate with the Father; “He,” even He, “is the propitiation for our sins.”
Whoever has held this fast has made no heresy; whoever has held this fast has made no schism.
For where did schisms come from?
When men say, “we” are righteous; when men say, “we” sanctify the unclean, “we” justify the ungodly; “we” ask, “we” obtain.
But what does John say?
“And if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.”
But someone will say: then do the saints not ask for us?
Then do bishops and rulers not ask for the people?
Yes, but mark the Scriptures, and see that rulers also commend themselves to the prayers of the people.
Thus the apostle says to the congregation, “Praying also for us.”
The apostle prays for the people; the people pray for the apostle.
We pray for you, brethren; but you also pray for us.
Let all the members pray for one another; let the Head intercede for all.
Therefore it is no wonder that he here goes on to shut the mouths of those who divide the Church of God.

For he who has said, “We have Jesus Christ the righteous, and He is the propitiation for our sins,” with an eye to those who would divide themselves, and would say, “Look, here is Christ, look, there,” and would show in a part Him who bought the whole and possesses the whole, immediately goes on to say, “Not our sins only, but also the sins of the whole world.”
What is this, brethren?
Certainly “we have found it in the fields of the woods”: we have found the Church in all nations.
Behold, Christ “is the propitiation for our sins; not ours only, but also the sins of the whole world.”
Behold, you have the Church throughout the whole world; do not follow false justifiers who in truth are cutters-off.
Be in that mountain which has filled the whole earth: because “Christ is the propitiation for our sins; not only ours, but also the sins of the whole world,” which He has bought with His blood.
9. “And by this,” he says, “we know Him, if we keep His commandments.”
What commandments? “He who says, I know Him, and does not keep His commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him.”
But still you ask, What commandments?
“But whoever,” he says, “keeps His word, in him truly the love of God is perfected.”
Let us see whether this same commandment is not called love.
For we were asking, what commandments? and he says, “But whoever keeps His word, in him truly the love of God is perfected.”
Mark the Gospel, whether this is not the commandment: “A new commandment,” says the Lord, “I give to you, that you love one another.—By this we know that we are in Him, if we are perfected in Him.”
He calls them perfected in love: what is the perfection of love?
To love even enemies, and to love them for this end, that they may be brethren.
For our love ought not to be a carnal love.
To wish a man temporal well-being is good; but even if that fails, let the soul be safe.
Do you wish life to anyone who is your friend?
You do well. Do you rejoice at the death of your enemy?
You do ill. But perhaps both the life you wish your friend is not for his good, and the death you rejoice at has been for your enemy’s good.
It is uncertain whether this present life is profitable or unprofitable to any man: but the life which is with God is without doubt profitable.
So love your enemies as to wish them to become your brethren; so love your enemies that they may be called into your fellowship.
For so He loved who, hanging on the cross, said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do.”
For He did not say, Father, let them live long; they are indeed killing me, but let them live.
He was casting out from them the death which is forever and ever, by His most merciful prayer, and by His most surpassing power.
Many of them believed, and the shedding of the blood of Christ was forgiven them.
At first they shed it while they raged; now they drank it while they believed.
“By this we know that we are in Him, if we are made perfect in Him.”
Concerning the very perfection of love of enemies, the Lord, admonishing us, says, “Therefore be perfect, as your Heavenly Father is perfect.
He,” therefore, “who says he abides in Him ought himself also to walk just as He walked.”
How, brethren? What does he advise us?
“He who says he abides in Him,” that is, in Christ, “ought himself also to walk just as He walked.”
Is the advice perhaps this, that we should walk on the sea?
Far be that from us!
It is this, then: that we walk in the way of righteousness.
In what way? I have already mentioned it.
He was fastened to the cross, and yet He was walking in this very way: this way is the way of charity, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do.”
If, therefore, you have learned to pray for your enemy, you are walking in the way of the Lord.
10. “Dearly beloved, I write to you no new commandment, but the old commandment which you had from the beginning.”
What commandment does he call “old?
Which you had,” he says, “from the beginning.
Old” then in this regard, that you have already heard it: otherwise he will contradict the Lord, where He says, “A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another.”
But why an “old” commandment?
Not as pertaining to the old man.
But why? “Which you had from the beginning.
The old commandment is the word which you have heard.”
Old, then, in this regard, that you have already heard it.
And he shows the very same to be new, saying, “Again, a new commandment I write to you.”
Not another, but the very same which he has called old is also new.
Why? “Which thing is true in Him and in you.”
Why old—you have already heard: that is, because you knew it already.
But why new? “Because the darkness is past, and the true light now shines.”
See, this is why it is new: because the darkness pertains to the old man, but the light to the new man.
What does the Apostle Paul say?
“Put off the old man, and put on the new.”
And again, what does he say?
“You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord.”
11. “He who says he is in the light”—now he is making clear all that he has been saying—“he who says he is in the light, and hates his brother, is in darkness even until now.”
What, my brethren! How long shall we say to you, “Love your enemies”?
See whether—what is worse—you do not hate your brethren.
If you loved only your brethren, you would not yet be perfect: but if you hate your brethren, what are you, where are you?
Let each look to his own heart: let him not keep hatred against his brother for any hard word; on account of earthly contention let him not become earth.
For whoever hates his brother, let him not say that he walks in the light.
“He who says he is in the light, and hates his brother, is in darkness even until now.”

Thus, some man who was a pagan has become a Christian; mark well: see, he was in darkness while he was a pagan; now he is made a Christian from here on; thanks be to God, all say joyfully; the apostle is read, where he says joyfully, “For you were once darkness, but now light in the Lord.”
Once he worshiped idols, now he worships God; once he worshiped the things he made, now he worships Him who made him.
He is changed: thanks be to God, all Christians say with joyful greeting.
Why? Because from now on he is one who adores the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit; one who detests demons and idols.
Yet John is still anxious about our convert: while many greet him with joy, he is still looked upon by John with apprehension.
Brethren, let us gladly welcome a mother’s anxious care.
Not without cause is the mother anxious about us when others rejoice: by the mother I mean charity; for she dwelt in the heart of John when he spoke these words.
Why, except that there is something he fears in us, even when men now hail us with joy?
What is it that he fears?
“He who says he is in the light”—What is this?
He who says he is now a Christian—“and hates his brother, is in darkness even until now.”
Which there is no need to expound, but only to be glad of it, if it is not so, or to bewail it, if it is.

12. “He who loves his brother abides (manet) in the light, and there is no occasion of stumbling in him.”—I beg you by Christ: God is feeding us; we are about to refresh our bodies in the name of Christ; both are in some good measure refreshed, and are yet to be refreshed: let the mind be fed.

I do not say this because I am going to speak for a long time; for see, the reading is now coming to an end: but lest perhaps out of weariness we should hear less attentively than we ought that which is most necessary.—“He who loves his brother abides in the light, and there is no scandal,” or “no occasion of stumbling, in him.”
Who are they that take scandal or make scandal?
Those who are offended in Christ, and in the Church.
Those who are offended in Christ are as if burned by the sun; those in the Church, as if by the moon.

But the Psalm says, “The sun shall not burn you by day, nor the moon by night”: that is, if you hold fast to charity, you will have no occasion of falling either in Christ or in the Church; you will forsake neither Christ nor the Church.
For he who forsakes the Church, how is he in Christ, when he is not in the members of Christ?
How is he in Christ who is not in the body of Christ?
Those therefore take scandal, or occasion of falling, who forsake Christ or the Church.
How do we understand that the Psalm, in saying, “By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night,” says it of this, that the burning means scandal, or occasion of stumbling?
In the first place, notice the comparison itself.

Just as the person whom something is burning says, I cannot bear it, I cannot endure it, and draws back; so those persons who cannot bear some things in the Church, and withdraw themselves either from the name of Christ or from the Church, are taking scandal.

For see how those took scandal as from the sun, those carnal ones to whom Christ preached of His flesh, saying, “He who does not eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink His blood shall have no life in him.”
Some seventy persons said, “This is a hard saying,” and went back from Him, and the twelve remained.
All those the sun burned, and they went back, not being able to bear the force of the Word.
So the twelve remained.

And lest perhaps men should imagine that they confer a benefit on Christ by believing in Christ, and not that the benefit is conferred by Him on them, when the twelve were left, the Lord said to them, “Will you also go?”
That you may know that I am necessary to you, not you to Me.
But those whom the sun had not burned answered by the voice of Peter: “Lord, You have the word of eternal life; where shall we go?”
But who are they whom the Church, as the moon, burns by night?
Those who have made schisms.
Hear the very word used in the apostle: “Who is offended, and I do not burn?”
In what sense then is it that there is no scandal or occasion of stumbling in him who loves his brother?
Because he who loves his brother bears all things for unity’s sake; because it is in the unity of charity that brotherly love exists.
Someone, I know not who, offends you: whether he is a bad man, or a bad man as you suppose, or a bad man as you pretend: and do you desert so many good men?
What sort of brotherly love is this that has appeared in these persons?
While they accuse the Africans, they have deserted the whole world!
What, were there no saints in the whole world?
Or was it possible that they should be condemned by you unheard?
But oh! if you loved your brethren, there would be no occasion of stumbling in you.
Hear the Psalm, what it says: “Great peace have those who love Your law, and to them there is no occasion of stumbling.”
Great peace, it says, there is for those who love the law of God, and that is why there is no occasion of stumbling for them.
Those then who take scandal, or occasion of stumbling, destroy peace.
And of whom does he say that they neither take nor make occasion of stumbling?
Those who love God’s law.
Consequently they are in charity.
But someone will say, “He said it of those who love God’s law, not of the brethren.”
Hear what the Lord says: “A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another.”
What is the Law but commandment?
Moreover, how is it that they do not take occasion of stumbling, except that they bear with one another?
As Paul says, “Bearing with one another in love, striving to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.”
And to show that this is the law of Christ, hear the same apostle commending this very law.
“Bear one another’s burdens,” he says, “and so you will fulfill the law of Christ.”
13. “For he who hates his brother is in darkness, and walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going.”
A great thing, my brethren: mark it, we beg you.
“He who hates his brother walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.”
What is so blind as those who hate their brethren?
For that you may know that they are blind, they have stumbled at a Mountain.
I say the same things often, so that they may not slip out of your memory.
The Stone which was “cut out of the Mountain without hands,” is it not Christ, who came from the kingdom of the Jews without the work of man?
Has not that Stone broken in pieces all the kingdoms of the earth, that is, all the dominions of idols and demons?
Has not that Stone grown, and become a great mountain, and filled the whole earth?
Do we point with the finger to this Mountain in the same way that the moon on its third day is pointed out to people?

For example, when they want people to see the new moon, they say, Look, the moon! Look, there it is! And if there are some there who are not sharp-sighted, and say, Where? then the finger is put out so that they may see it.
Sometimes, when they are ashamed to be thought blind, they say they have seen what they have not seen.
Do we point out the Church in this way, my brethren?
Is it not open?
Is it not manifest?
Has it not taken possession of all nations?
Is not that fulfilled which was promised to Abraham so many years before, that in his seed all nations should be blessed?
It was promised to one believer, and the world is filled with thousands of believers.
Behold here the mountain filling the whole face of the earth!
Behold the city of which it is said, “A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden!”
But those men stumble at the mountain, and when it is said to them, Go up, “There is no mountain,” they say, and they would sooner dash their heads against it than seek a dwelling there.

Isaiah was read yesterday; whoever of you was awake, not with his eyes only but with his ear, and not the ear of the body but the ear of the heart, noted this: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be manifest, prepared on the top of the mountains.”
What is so manifest as a mountain?
But there are even mountains that are unknown, because they are situated in one part of the earth.
Which of you knows Mount Olympus?
Just as the people who live there do not know our Giddaba.
These mountains are in different parts of the earth.
But not so that Mountain, for it has filled the whole face of the earth, and of it is said, “Prepared on the top of the mountains.”
It is a Mountain above the tops of all mountains.
“And,” he says, “to it all nations shall be gathered.”
Who can fail to be aware of this Mountain?
Who breaks his head by stumbling against it?
Who is ignorant of the city set on a mountain?
But do not marvel that it is unknown to those who hate the brethren, because they walk in darkness and do not know where they are going, because the darkness has blinded their eyes.
They do not see the Mountain: I would not have you marvel; they have no eyes.
How is it that they have no eyes?
Because the darkness has blinded them.
How do we prove this?

Because they hate the brethren, in that, while they are offended at Africans, they separate themselves from the whole earth: in that they do not tolerate, for the peace of Christ, those whom they defame, and yet do tolerate, for the sake of Donatus, those whom they condemn.
“I write to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven through His name.
I write to you, fathers, because you have known Him who is from the beginning.
I write to you, young men, because you have overcome the wicked one.
I write to you, children, because you have known the Father.
I write to you, fathers, because you have known Him who is from the beginning.
I write to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you have overcome the wicked one.
Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world.
If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.
For all that is in the world is the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, which is not of the Father, but is of the world.
And the world passes away, and the lust of it: but he who does the will of God abides forever (even as God also abides forever).”
1. All things that are read from the Holy Scriptures for our instruction and salvation, we ought to hear with earnest attention.
Yet most of all those things must be committed to our memory which have the most force against heretics, whose treacherous designs never cease to ensnare all who are weaker and more negligent.
Remember that our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ both died for us and rose again: died, namely, for our offenses, and rose again for our justification.

Even as you have just heard concerning the two disciples whom He met on the way, how “their eyes were restrained, so that they should not know Him”: and He found them despairing of the redemption that was in Christ, and supposing that He had now suffered and was dead as a man, not reckoning that as Son of God He lives forever; and supposing too that He was so dead in the flesh as not to come to life again, but just as one of the prophets: as those of you who were attentive have just now heard their own words.

Then “He opened to them the Scriptures, beginning at Moses,” and going through all the prophets, showing them that all He had suffered had been foretold, lest they should be more staggered if the Lord should rise again, and fail all the more to believe Him, if these things had not been told beforehand concerning Him.
For the firmness of faith lies in this, that all things which came to pass in Christ were foretold.
The disciples, then, did not know Him, except “in the breaking of bread.”
And truly, he who does not eat and drink judgment to himself in the breaking of bread does know Christ.
Afterward also those eleven “thought they saw a spirit.”

He gave Himself to be handled by them, He who also gave Himself to be crucified; to be crucified by enemies, to be handled by friends: yet the Physician of all, both of the ungodliness of the former and of the unbelief of the latter.
For you heard, when the Acts of the Apostles were read, how many thousands of Christ’s slayers believed.
If those who had killed believed afterward, should not those believe who doubted for a little while?

And yet even in regard to them (a thing which you ought especially to observe and to commit to your memory, because God has been pleased to put in the Scriptures that which shall make us strong against treacherous errors, Scriptures against which no one dares to speak who in any way wishes to seem a Christian), when He had given Himself to be handled by them, that did not suffice Him, but He would also confirm by means of the Scriptures the heart of those who believe: for He looked forward to us who would come afterward; seeing that in Him we have nothing that we can handle, but have that which we may read.
For if those believed only because they held and handled Him, what shall we do?
Now, Christ has ascended into heaven; He is not to come except at the end, to judge the living and the dead.
By what shall we believe, but by that by which it was His will that even those who handled Him should be confirmed?

For He opened to them the Scriptures and showed them that it was needful for Christ to suffer, and that all things must be fulfilled which were written of Him in the Law of Moses, and the Prophets, and the Psalms.
He embraced in His discourse the whole ancient text of the Scriptures.
All that there is of those former Scriptures tells of Christ; but only if it finds ears.
He also “opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures.”
Therefore we also must pray for this, that He would open our understanding.
2. But what did the Lord show to be written of Him in the Law of Moses, and the Prophets, and the Psalms?
What did He show?
Let Him say it Himself. The evangelist has put this briefly, that we might know what, in all that great compass of the Scriptures, we ought to believe and to understand.
Certainly there are many pages, and many books; the content of them all is this which the Lord spoke briefly to His disciples.
What is this? That “it was needful for Christ to suffer, and to rise again the third day.”
You have it now concerning the Bridegroom, that “it was needful for Christ to suffer, and to rise again”: the Bridegroom has been set before us.
Concerning the Bride, let us see what He says; so that you, when you know the Bridegroom and the Bride, may not come to the marriage without reason.
For every celebration is a celebration of marriage: the Church’s nuptials are being celebrated.
The King’s Son is about to take a wife, and that King’s Son is Himself a King: and the guests who throng to the marriage are themselves the Bride.
It is not as in a carnal marriage, where some are guests and another is the one who is married; in the Church, those who come as guests, if they come to good purpose, become the Bride.
For the whole Church is Christ’s Bride, of which the beginning and firstfruits is the flesh of Christ: there the Bride was joined to the Bridegroom in the flesh.
With good reason, when He would signify that same flesh, He broke bread; and with good reason “in the breaking of bread” the eyes “of the disciples were opened, and they knew Him.”
Well then, what did the Lord say was written of Him in the Law and the Prophets and the Psalms?
That “it was needful for Christ to suffer.”
Had He not added, “and to rise again,” those whose eyes were restrained might well mourn; but “to rise again” is also foretold.
And why this? Why was it needful for Christ to suffer and to rise again?
Because of that Psalm which we especially commended to your attention on the fourth day, the first station, of last week.
Why was it needful for Christ to suffer and to rise again?
For this reason: “All the ends of the earth shall be reminded and turned to the Lord, and all the kindreds of the nations shall worship before Him.”

For, so that you may know that it was needful for Christ to suffer and to rise again, what has He added in this place also, so that after setting forth the Bridegroom He might also set forth the Bride?
“And that there be preached,” He says, “in His name, repentance and remission of sins throughout all nations, beginning at Jerusalem.”
You have heard, brethren; hold it fast.
Let no one doubt concerning the Church, that it is “throughout all nations”: let no one doubt that it began at Jerusalem and has filled all nations.
We know the field where the Vine is planted: but when it has grown we do not know it, because it has taken up the whole.
Where did it begin?
“At Jerusalem.” How far has it come?
To “all nations.” A few remain: it shall possess all.
In the meantime, while it is taking possession of all, it has seemed good to the Vinedresser to cut off some unprofitable branches, and they have made heresies and schisms.
Do not let the branches that are cut off induce you to be cut off: rather urge those who are cut off to be grafted in again.

It is manifest that Christ has suffered, has risen again, and has ascended into heaven: manifest also is the Church, because “repentance and remission of sins is preached in His name throughout all nations.”
Where did it begin?

“Beginning at Jerusalem.” The man hears this; foolish and vain, and (how shall I express it?) worse than blind! So great a mountain, and he does not see it; a lamp set on a lampstand, and he shuts his eyes against it!

3. When we say to them, If you are Catholic Christians, be in communion with that Church from which the Gospel is spread abroad over the whole earth: be in communion with that Jerusalem; when we say this to them, they answer us, We do not hold communion with that city where our King was slain, where our Lord was slain: as though they hate the city where our Lord was slain.
The Jews slew Him whom they found on earth; these scorn Him who sits in heaven!
Which are the worse: those who despised Him because they thought Him a man, or those who scorn the sacraments of Him whom they now confess to be God?
But they hate, so they say, the city in which their Lord was slain!
Pious men, and merciful! They grieve greatly that Christ was slain, and in men they slay Christ!
But He loved that city and pitied it: from it He commanded the preaching of Him to begin, “beginning at Jerusalem.”
He made there the beginning of the preaching of His name: and you shrink back in horror from having communion with that city!
No wonder that, being cut off, you hate the root.
What did He say to His disciples?
“Sit still in the city, because I send My promise upon you.”
Behold what the city is that they hate!
Perhaps they would love it, if Christ’s murderers lived in it.
For it is manifest that all Christ’s murderers, that is, the Jews, are expelled from that city.
That which once had in it those who were fierce against Christ, now has those who adore Christ.
Therefore these men hate it, because Christians are in it.
There it was His will that His disciples should remain, and there that He should send the Holy Spirit to them.
Where did the Church have its beginning, but where the Holy Spirit came from heaven and filled the hundred and twenty sitting in one place?
That number twelve was made tenfold.

They sat, a hundred and twenty persons, and the Holy Spirit came, “and filled the whole place, and there came a sound, as it were the rushing of a mighty wind, and there were cloven tongues like fire.”
You have heard the Acts of the Apostles: this was the reading today: “They began to speak with tongues, as the Spirit gave them to speak.”

And all who were on the spot, Jews who had come from various nations, each recognized his own tongue, and marveled that those unlearned and ignorant men had suddenly learned not one or two tongues, but the tongues of all nations whatever.
There, then, where all tongues sounded, it was signified that all tongues should believe.

But these men, who love Christ so much, and therefore refuse to hold communion with the city which killed Christ, so honor Christ as to affirm that He is left with two tongues, the Latin and the Punic, that is,
African. Christ possessing only two tongues!
For there are but these two tongues on the side of Donatus; more they do not have.

Let us awake, my brethren; let us rather see the gift of the Spirit of God, and let us believe the things spoken beforehand concerning Him, and let us see fulfilled the things foretold in the Psalm: “There are neither speeches nor discourses, but their voices are heard among them.”

And lest perhaps the case be that the tongues themselves came to one place, and not rather that the gift of Christ came to all tongues, hear what follows: “Into all the earth their sound has gone out, and to the ends of the world their words.”
Why this? Because “in the sun He has set His tabernacle,” that is, in the open light.
His tabernacle, His flesh: His tabernacle, His Church: it is set “in the sun”; not in the night, but in the day.
But why do those men not acknowledge it?

Return to the reading at the place where it ended yesterday, and see why they do not acknowledge it: “He who hates his brother walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.”
As for us, then, let us see what follows, and not be in darkness.
How shall we not be in darkness?
If we love the brethren.
How is it proved that we love the brotherhood?
By this, that we do not tear apart unity, that we hold fast to charity.
4. “I write to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven you through His name.”
Therefore, “little children,” because in the forgiveness of sins you have your birth.
But through whose name are sins forgiven?
Through Augustine’s? No; therefore neither through the name of Donatus.
Let it be your concern to see who Augustine is, or who Donatus is: no, not through the name of Paul, not through the name of Peter.

For to those who divided the Church among themselves, and out of unity tried to make parties, mother charity in the apostle, laboring in birth with her little ones, lays bare her own inmost being, with words as it were tears open her breasts, bewails her children whom she sees carried out dead, calls back to the one Name those who insisted on making for themselves many names, repels them from love of herself so that Christ may be loved, and says, “Was Paul crucified for you?
Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?”

What does he say? “I would not have you be mine, so that you may be with me: be with me; we all are His who died for us, who was crucified for us”: hence here also it is said, “Your sins are forgiven you through His name,” not through the name of any man.
5. “I write to you, fathers.”
Why sons first? “Because your sins are forgiven you through His name,” and you are regenerated into a new life; therefore sons.
Why fathers? “Because you have known Him who is from the beginning”: for the beginning has relation to fatherhood.
Christ is new in the flesh, but ancient in Godhead.
How ancient, do we think? How many years old?
Of greater age, do we think, than His mother?
Assuredly of greater age than His mother, for “all things were made by Him.”
If all things, then the Ancient made the very mother of whom the New was to be born.
Was He, do we think, before His mother only?
Yes, and His antiquity is before His mother’s ancestors.
The ancestor of His mother was Abraham; and the Lord says, “Before Abraham I am.”
Before Abraham, do we say?
Heaven and earth were made before man was.
Before these was the Lord, or rather also is.
For rightly He says, not, Before Abraham I was, but, “Before Abraham I Am.”
For that of which one says “was,” is not; and that of which one says “will be,” is not yet: He knows nothing other than to be.
As God, He knows “to be”: “was” and “will be” He does not know.
It is one day there, but a day that is forever and ever.
That day is not set in the midst between a yesterday and a tomorrow: for when the “yesterday” is ended, the “today” begins, to be finished by the coming “tomorrow.”
That one day there is a day without darkness, without night, without spaces, without measure, without hours.
Call it what you will: if you will, it is a day; if you will, a year; if you will, years.
For it is said of this same, “And Your years shall not fail.”
But when is it called a day?
When it is said to the Lord, “Today I have begotten You.”
Begotten of the eternal Father, begotten from eternity, begotten in eternity: with no beginning, no bound, no space of breadth; because He is what is, because He Himself is “He who Is.”
This name of His He told to Moses: “You shall say to them, He who Is has sent me to you.”
Why speak then of “before Abraham”? Why, before Noah? Why, before Adam?
Hear the Scripture: “Before the day-star I have begotten You.”
In short, before heaven and earth.
Why? Because “all things were made by Him, and without Him nothing was made.”
By this know the “fathers”: for they become fathers by acknowledging “That which is from the beginning.”
6. “I write to you, young men.”
There are sons, there are fathers, there are young men: sons, because begotten; fathers, because they acknowledge the Beginning; why young men?
“Because you have overcome the wicked one.”
In the sons, birth; in the fathers, antiquity; in the young men, strength.
If the wicked one is “overcome” by the young men, he fights with us.
He fights, but does not conquer.
Why? Because we are strong, or because He is strong in us who in the hands of the persecutors was found weak?
He who did not resist His persecutors has made us strong.
“For He was crucified out of weakness, but He lives by the power of God.”
7. “I write to you, children.”
Why children? “Because you have known the Father.
I write to you, fathers”: he presses this home and repeats, “Because you have known Him who is from the beginning.”
Remember that you are fathers: if you forget “Him who is from the beginning,” you have lost your fatherhood.
“I write to you, young men.”
Consider again and again that you are young men: fight, that you may overcome; overcome, that you may be crowned; be humble, that you may not fall in the fight.
“I write to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you have overcome the wicked one.”

8. All these things, my brethren (“because we have known That which is from the beginning, because we are strong, because we have known the Father”), do they not all, while in a manner they commend knowledge, commend charity?
If we have known, let us love: for knowledge without charity does not save.
“Knowledge puffs up, charity builds up.”
If you have a mind to confess and not to love, you begin to be like the demons.
The demons confessed the Son of God, and said, “What have we to do with You?” and were driven back.
Confess and embrace. For those feared because of their iniquities; you, love Him who forgives your iniquities.
But how can we love God, if we love the world?
He prepares us, therefore, to be inhabited by charity.

There are two loves: of the world, and of God: if the love of the world dwells within, there is no way for the love of God to enter: let the love of the world make way, and the love of God dwell within; let the better have place.

You loved the world: do not love the world: when you have emptied your heart of earthly love, you will drink in love divine: and from then on charity begins to dwell in you, from which nothing of evil can proceed.
Hear therefore his words, how he goes to work in the manner of one who makes a clearing.
He comes upon the hearts of men as upon a field that he would occupy: but in what state does he find it?
If he finds a wood, he roots it up; if he finds the field cleared, he plants it.
He would plant a tree there: charity.
And what is the wood he would root up?
Love of the world.
Hear him, the uprooter of the wood!
“Do not love the world,” (for this comes next,) “nor the things that are in the world; if anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.”
9. You have heard that “if anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.”

Let no one say in his heart that this is false, brethren: God says it; the Holy Spirit has spoken by the Apostle; nothing is more true: “If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.”
Would you have the Father’s love, so that you may be a joint heir with the Son?
Do not love the world.
Shut out the evil love of the world, that you may be filled with the love of God.
You are a vessel; but as yet you are full.
Pour out what you have, that you may receive what you do not have.
Certainly our brethren are now born again of water and of the Spirit: we also, some years ago, were born again of water and of the Spirit.
It is good for us that we do not love the world, lest the sacraments remain in us to our damnation, rather than as means of strengthening to salvation.
That which strengthens to salvation is to have the root of charity, to have the “power of godliness,” not “the form” only.
Good is the form, holy the form: but what does the form avail, if it does not hold the root?
The branch that is cut off, is it not cast into the fire?
Have the form, but in the root.
But in what way are you rooted so that you may not be rooted up?
By holding charity, as the Apostle Paul says, “rooted and grounded in charity.”
How shall charity be rooted there, amid the overgrown wilderness of the love of the world?
Make a clean clearing of the woods.
A mighty seed you are about to put in: let there be nothing in the field that will choke the seed.
These are the uprooting words which he has spoken: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world.
If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.”
10. “For all that is in the world is the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life”: three things he has named, which are not of the Father, but are of the world.
“And the world passes away, and the lust of it: but he who does the will of God abides forever, even as He abides forever.”
Why am I not to love what God made?
What will you have? Will you love the things of time, and pass away with time; or not love the world, and live to eternity with God?
The river of temporal things sweeps one along: but like a tree sprung up beside the river is our Lord Jesus Christ.
He took on flesh, died, rose again, ascended into heaven.
It was His will, in a manner, to plant Himself beside the river of the things of time.
Are you rushing down the stream to the headlong deep?
Hold fast to the tree.
Is love of the world whirling you along?
Hold fast to Christ. For you He became temporal, that you might become eternal; because He also became temporal in such a way that He still remained eternal.
Something was added to Him from time; nothing went from His eternity.
But you were born temporal, and by sin were made temporal: you were made temporal by sin; He was made temporal by mercy, in remitting sins.
How great the difference, when two are in a prison, between the criminal and the one who visits him!
For at times a person comes to his friend and goes in to visit him, and both seem to be in prison; but they differ by a wide distinction.
The one, his case presses down; the other, humanity has brought there.
So in this our mortal state, we were held fast by our guilt; He came down in mercy: He came in to the captive, a Redeemer, not an oppressor.
The Lord shed His blood for us, redeemed us, changed our hope.
As yet we bear the mortality of the flesh, and take the future immortality on trust: and on the sea we are tossed by the waves, but we have the anchor of hope already fixed on the land.
11. But let us “not love the world, nor the things that are in the world.
For the things that are in the world are the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life.”
These are the three: lest perhaps someone say, “The things that are in the world God made: that is, heaven and earth, the sea; the sun, the moon, the stars, all the adornment of the heavens.
What is the adornment of the sea? All creeping things.
What of the earth? Animals, trees, flying creatures.
These are ‘in the world’; God made them.
Why then am I not to love what God has made?”
Let the Spirit of God be in you, that you may see that all these things are good: but woe to you if you love the things made and forsake their Maker!
Fair are they to you: but how much fairer is He who formed them!

Mark this well, beloved. For by comparisons you may be instructed: lest Satan steal upon you, saying what he is accustomed to say, Take your enjoyment in the creature of God; why did He make those things except for your enjoyment?
And men drink themselves drunk, and perish, and forget their own Creator: while they use the things created not temperately but lustfully, the Creator is despised.
Of such the apostle says: “They worshiped and served the creature in place of the Creator, who is blessed forever.”
God does not forbid you to love these things, yet not to set your affections on them for blessedness, but to approve and praise them to this end, that you may love your Creator.

In the same way, my brethren, as if a bridegroom should make a ring for his bride, and she, having received the ring, should love it more than she loves the bridegroom who made the ring for her: would not her soul be found guilty of adultery in the very gift of the bridegroom, even though she loved only what the bridegroom gave her?
By all means let her love what the bridegroom gave: yet if she should say, “This ring is enough for me; I do not wish to see his face now,” what sort of woman would she be?
Who would not detest such folly? Who would not pronounce her guilty of an adulterous mind?

You love gold in place of the man, you love a ring in place of the bridegroom: if this is in you, that you love a ring in place of your bridegroom and have no wish to see your bridegroom, then the pledge he has given you serves not to bind you to him, but to turn your heart away from him!
For this is why the bridegroom gives a pledge: that in his pledge he himself may be loved.
Well then, God gave you all these things: love Him who made them.
There is more that He would gladly give you, that is, His very Self who made these things.
But if you love these (even though God made them) and neglect the Creator and love the world, shall not your love be counted adulterous?

12. For “the world” is the name given not only to this fabric which God made—heaven and earth, the sea, things visible and invisible—but the inhabitants of the world are also called the world, just as we call a “house” both the walls and those who dwell in it.
And sometimes we praise a house, and find fault with those who live in it.

For we say, “A good house,” because it is laid with marble and has beautiful paneled ceilings; and in another sense we say, “A good house”: no one there suffers wrong, no acts of plunder, no acts of oppression are done there.
Now we are praising not the building, but those who dwell within the building; yet we call both the one and the other a “house.”

For all lovers of the world—because by love they inhabit the world, just as those inhabit heaven whose heart is on high while in the flesh they walk on earth—all lovers of the world, I say, are called the world.
These have only these three things: “lust of the flesh, lust of the eyes, vainglory of life.”
For they lust to eat, to drink, to lie together: to use these pleasures.
Surely it is not that there is no permitted measure in these things, or that when it is said, “Do not love these things,” it means that you are not to eat, or not to drink, or not to beget children?
This is not what is being said.
Only let there be measure, for the Creator’s sake, so that these things may not bind you through your love of them; lest you love for enjoyment what you ought to have for use.
But you are not put to the test except when two things are set before you, this or that: “Will you have righteousness, or gain?”
“I have nothing to live on, nothing to eat, nothing to drink.”
But what if you cannot have these except by wickedness?
Is it not better to love what you cannot lose than to lose yourself by wickedness?
You see the gain of gold; the loss of faith you do not see.
This, then, he tells us, is “the lust of the flesh,” that is, the lusting after those things which pertain to the flesh, such as food and bodily union, and all other things of that kind.
13. “And the lust of the eyes”: by “the lust of the eyes” he means all curiosity.
Now how wide is the scope of curiosity!
It is this that is at work in spectacles, in theaters, in the sacraments of the devil, in magical arts, in dealings with darkness: none other than curiosity.

Sometimes it tempts even the servants of God, so that they wish, as it were, to work a miracle, to test God whether He will hear their prayers by the working of miracles; it is curiosity: this is “the lust of the eyes”; it “is not of the Father.”
If God has given the power, do the miracle, for He has put it in your way to do it; for do not think that those who have not done miracles will not belong to the kingdom of God.
When the apostles were rejoicing that the demons were subject to them, what did the Lord say to them?
“Do not rejoice in this, but rejoice because your names are written in heaven.”
He wanted the apostles to rejoice in that very thing in which you also rejoice.
Woe to you indeed if your name is not written in heaven!
Is it woe to you if you do not raise the dead? Is it woe to you if you do not walk on the sea? Is it woe to you if you do not cast out demons?
If you have received power to do them, use it humbly, not proudly.
For even of certain false prophets the Lord has said that “they shall do signs and wonders.”
Therefore let there be no “ambition of the world”: ambitio saeculi is pride.
A man wishes to make much of himself in his honors; he thinks himself great, whether because of riches or because of some power.
14. These three there are, and you can find nothing by which human craving can be tempted except either by the lust of the flesh, or the lust of the eyes, or the pride of life.
By these three the Lord was tempted by the devil.
By the lust of the flesh He was tempted when it was said to Him, “If You are the Son of God, speak to these stones that they may become bread,” when He was hungry after His fast.
But in what way did He repel the tempter, and teach His soldier how to fight?
Notice what He said to him: “Not by bread alone does man live, but by every word of God.”

He was tempted also by the lust of the eyes concerning a miracle, when he said to Him, “Throw Yourself down; for it is written, He shall give His angels charge concerning You, and in their hands they shall bear You up, lest at any time You dash Your foot against a stone.”

He resisted the tempter, for to do the miracle would only have been to seem either to have yielded or to have done it out of curiosity; for He worked miracles when He willed, as God, yet as healing the weak.
For if He had done it then, He might have been thought to wish only to do a miracle.

But lest men should think this, notice what He answered; and when a similar temptation happens to you, you also say the same: “Get behind Me, Satan; for it is written, You shall not tempt the Lord your God”: that is, if I do this I shall tempt God.
He said what He would have you say.
When the enemy suggests to you, “What sort of man, what sort of Christian, are you?

Have you yet done a single miracle, or by your prayers have the dead been raised, or have you healed the feverish? If you were truly of any account, you would do some miracle”—answer and say: “It is written, You shall not tempt the Lord your God”; therefore I will not tempt God, as if I should belong to God if I do a miracle, and not belong to Him if I do none: and what then becomes of His words, “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven”?
By “the pride of life,” how was the Lord tempted?
When he carried Him up to a high place and said to Him, “All these I will give You, if You will fall down and worship me.”
By the loftiness of an earthly kingdom he wished to tempt the King of all worlds; but the Lord who made heaven and earth trod the devil underfoot.
What great thing is it for the devil to be conquered by the Lord?
Then what did He do in the answer He made to the devil but teach you the answer He would have you make?
“It is written, You shall worship the Lord your God, and Him only shall you serve.”

Holding these things fast, you will not have the lust of the world; and by not having the lust of the world, neither the lust of the flesh, nor the lust of the eyes, nor the pride of life will subdue you; and you will make room for Charity when she comes, that you may love God.
Because if love of the world is there, love of God will not be there.
Rather hold fast the love of God, that as God is forever and ever, so you also may remain forever and ever: because each one is such as his love is.
Do you love earth? You will be earth.
Do you love God? What shall I say? You will be a god?
I dare not say it on my own authority; let us hear the Scriptures: “I have said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High.”
If then you would be gods and sons of the Most High, “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world.
If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.
For all that is in the world is the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, which is not of the Father, but is of the world”: that is, of men, the lovers of the world.
“And the world passes away, and its lusts; but he who does the will of God abides forever, even as God also abides forever.”
“Children, it is the last hour; and as you have heard that antichrist shall come, even now there are many antichrists; by which we know that it is the last hour.
They went out from us, but they were not of us; if they had been of us, they would no doubt have continued with us; but they went out, that they might be made manifest that they were not all of us.
But you have an anointing from the Holy One, and you know all things.
I write to you, not because you do not know the truth, but because you know it, and that no lie is of the truth.
Who is a liar but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ?
[He is antichrist who denies the Father and the Son.]
Whoever denies the Son, the same has neither the Father nor the Son; and he who acknowledges the Son has both the Father and the Son.
Therefore let that abide in you which you have heard from the beginning.
If what you have heard from the beginning remains in you, you also will continue in the Son and in the Father.
And this is the promise that He has promised us, even eternal life.
These things I have written to you concerning those who lead you astray; that you may know that you have an anointing, and that the anointing which you have received from Him may abide in you.
And you do not need anyone to teach you, because His anointing teaches you concerning all things.”
1. “Children, it is the last hour.”
In this reading he addresses the children, that they may make haste to grow, because “it is the last hour.”
The age or stature of the body is not at one’s own will.
A man does not grow in respect of the flesh when he wills, any more than he is born when he wills; but where being born rests with the will, growth also rests with the will.
No one is “born of water and the Spirit” unless he is willing.
Consequently, if he wills, he grows or increases; if he wills, he decreases.
What is it to grow?
To go forward by making progress.
What is it to decrease?
To go backward by falling away.
Whoever knows that he is born, let him hear that he is an infant; let him cling eagerly to his mother’s breasts, and he grows quickly.
Now his mother is the Church, and her breasts are the two Testaments of the Divine Scriptures.

From these, then, let him suck the milk of all the things that were done in time as signs of spiritual truths for our eternal salvation, so that, being nourished and strengthened, he may attain to the eating of solid food, which is, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”
Our milk is Christ in His humility; our solid food, the very same Christ equal with the Father.
With milk He nourishes you, that He may feed you with bread; for to touch Christ spiritually with the heart is to know that He is equal with the Father.
2. That is why He forbade Mary to touch Him, and said to her, “Do not touch Me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father.”
What is this? He gave Himself to be handled by the disciples, and did He shun Mary’s touch?
Is He not the same who said to the doubting disciple, “Reach here your fingers, and feel the scars”?
Had He at that time ascended to the Father?
Then why does He forbid Mary, and say, “Do not touch Me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father”?
Or are we to say that He was not afraid to be touched by men, but was afraid to be touched by women?
The touch of Him cleanses all flesh.
Those to whom He willed first to be made manifest—was He afraid to be handled by them?
Was not His resurrection announced by women to the men, so that the serpent might be overcome by a kind of counterplot?
For because he first announced death to man through the woman, therefore life also was announced to men through a woman.
Then why was He unwilling to be touched, unless it was because He wanted that spiritual touch to be understood?
The spiritual touch takes place from a pure heart.
That person reaches Christ with his touch from a pure heart who understands Him as coequal with the Father.
But whoever does not yet understand Christ’s Godhead reaches only as far as the flesh; he does not reach the Godhead.
Now what great thing is it to reach only as far as the persecutors reached, who crucified Him?

But this is the great thing: to understand the Word, God with God, in the beginning, by whom all things were made—as He wanted Himself to be known when He said to Philip, “Have I been with you so long a time, and have you not known Me, Philip?
He who sees Me sees also the Father.”
3. But lest anyone be sluggish in going forward, let him hear: “Children, it is the last hour.”
Go forward, run, grow; “it is the last hour.”
This same last hour is long; yet it is the last.
For he has put “hour” for “the last time,” because it is in the last times that our Lord Jesus Christ is to come.
But some will say, How the last times? How the last hour?
Certainly antichrist will come first, and then the day of judgment will come.

John perceived these thoughts: lest people should in some way become secure, and think it was not the last hour because antichrist was still to come, he said to them, “And as you have heard that antichrist is to come, now many antichrists have come.”
Could it have many antichrists unless it were “the last hour”?
4. Whom has he called antichrists?
He goes on and explains.
“By which we know that it is the last hour.”
By what? Because “many antichrists have come.
They went out from us”; see the antichrists!
“They went out from us”: therefore we mourn the loss.
Hear the consolation: “But they were not of us.”
All heretics, all schismatics went out from us, that is, they go out from the Church; but they would not go out if they were of us.
Therefore, before they went out they were not of us.
If before they went out they were not of us, many are within, have not gone out, and yet are antichrists.
We dare to say this: and why, except so that no one, while he is within, may be an antichrist?
For he is about to describe and mark out the antichrists, and we shall see them now.
And each person ought to question his own conscience, whether he is an antichrist.
For antichrist in our language means “contrary to Christ.”
Not, as some take it, that antichrist is to be so called because he is to come ante Christum, before Christ, that is,
with Christ to come after him: it does not mean this, nor is it so written, but Antichristus, that is, contrary to Christ.

Now who is contrary to Christ you already perceive from the apostle’s own explanation, and you understand that none can go out except antichrists; whereas those who are not contrary to Christ can in no way go out.
For he who is not contrary to Christ holds fast in His body, and is counted with it as a member.
The members are never contrary to one another.
The entire body consists of all the members.
And what does the apostle say concerning the harmony of the members?
“If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; and if one member is glorified, all the members rejoice with it.”
If, then, when a member is glorified the other members rejoice with it, and when it suffers all the members suffer, the harmony of the members has no antichrist.

And there are those who are inwardly in the body of our Lord Jesus Christ in such a way—seeing that His body is still under treatment, and its soundness will not be perfect except in the resurrection of the dead—they are in the body of Christ in such a way as bad humors are.
When these are vomited up, the body is relieved; so too when bad men go out, then the Church is relieved.
And when the body vomits and casts them out, one says, “These humors went out of me, but they were not of me.”
How were they not of me?
They were not cut out of my flesh, but they oppressed my chest while they were in me.
5. “They went out from us; but”—do not be sad—“they were not of us.”
How do you prove this?
If they had been of us, they would no doubt have continued with us.

From this, therefore, you may see that many who are not of us receive the Sacraments with us, receive baptism with us, receive with us what the faithful know they receive—the Blessing, the Eucharist, and whatever there is in the Holy Sacraments: the communion of the very altar they receive with us, and yet they are not of us.
Temptation proves that they are not of us.
When temptation comes to them, as if blown by a wind they fly off, because they were not grain.
But all of them will fly off, as we must often tell you, once the winnowing of the Lord’s threshing floor begins on the day of judgment.
“They went out from us, but they were not of us; if they had been of us, they would no doubt have continued with us.”
For would you know, beloved, how very certain this saying is—that those who perhaps have gone out and return are not antichrists, are not contrary to Christ?
Those who are not antichrists cannot possibly continue outside.
