But it is by his own will that each one is either an antichrist or in Christ.
Either we are among the members, or among the bad humors.
He who changes himself for the better is in the body, a member; but he who continues in his badness is a bad humor; and when he has gone out, then those who were oppressed will be relieved.

“They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would no doubt have continued with us; but (they went out) that they might be made manifest that they were not all of us.”
He has added, “that they might be made manifest,” because even when they are within they are not of us; yet they are not manifest, but by going out they are made manifest.
“And you have an anointing from the Holy One, that you may be manifest to your own selves.”
The spiritual anointing is the Holy Spirit Himself, of whom the Sacrament is in the visible anointing.
Of this anointing of Christ he says that all who have it know the bad and the good; and they do not need to be taught, because the anointing itself teaches them.
6. “I write to you not because you do not know the truth, but because you know it, and that no lie is of the truth.”
Behold, we are admonished how we may know antichrist.
What is Christ? Truth.
He Himself has said, “I am the Truth.”
But “no lie is of the truth.”
Consequently, all who lie are not yet of Christ.
He has not said that some lie is of the truth and some lie is not of the truth.
Mark the sentence. Do not pamper yourselves, do not flatter yourselves, do not deceive yourselves, do not cheat yourselves: “No lie is of the truth.”
Let us see, then, how antichrists lie, because there is more than one kind of lying.
“Who is a liar, but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ?”
The meaning of the word “Jesus” is one thing, the meaning of the word “Christ” another: though it is one Jesus Christ our Savior, yet “Jesus” is His proper name.
Just as Moses was so called by his proper name, as Elijah, as Abraham, so our Lord has the name “Jesus” as His proper name; but “Christ” is the name of His sacred office.
As when we say “Prophet,” as when we say “Priest,” so by the name Christ we are given to understand the Anointed, in whom the redemption of the whole people was to be.
The coming of this Christ was hoped for by the people of the Jews; and because He came in lowliness, He was not acknowledged; because the stone was small, they stumbled at it and were broken.
But “the stone grew and became a great mountain”; and what does the Scripture say?
“Whoever stumbles at this stone shall be broken; and on whomever this stone comes, it will grind him to powder.”
We must note the difference in the words: it says, he who stumbles shall be broken; but he on whom it comes shall be ground to powder.
At first, because He came lowly, men stumbled at Him; because He shall come lofty to judgment, on whomever He comes, He will grind him to powder.
But He will not grind to powder at His future coming that man whom He did not break when He came.
He who did not stumble at the lowly One shall not dread the lofty One.
You have heard it briefly, brethren: he who did not stumble at the lowly One shall not dread the lofty One.
For to all bad men Christ is a stone of stumbling; whatever Christ says is bitter to them.
7. For hear and see.

Certainly all who go out from the Church and are cut off from the unity of the Church are antichrists; let no one doubt it; for the apostle himself has marked them: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would no doubt have continued with us.”
Therefore, whoever do not continue with us but go out from us, it is manifest that they are antichrists.
And how are they proved to be antichrists?
By lying. “And who is a liar, but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ?”
Let us ask the heretics: where do you find a heretic who denies that Jesus is the Christ?
See now, my beloved, a great mystery.
Notice what the Lord God may have inspired us with, and what I would gladly work into your minds.
Behold, they went out from us and became Donatists; we ask them whether Jesus is the Christ; they at once confess that Jesus is the Christ.
If, then, the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ is an antichrist, neither can they call us antichrists, nor we them; therefore neither did they go out from us, nor we from them.

If, then, we have not gone out from one another, we are in unity; if we are in unity, what does it mean that there are two altars in this city? What does it mean that there are divided houses, divided marriages? That there is a common bed, and a divided Christ?
He admonishes us; he would have us confess what the truth is: either they went out from us, or we from them.
But let it not be imagined that we have gone out from them.
For we have the testament of the Lord’s inheritance; we recite it, and there we find, “I will give You the nations for Your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for Your possession.”
We hold fast Christ’s inheritance; they do not hold it, for they are not in communion with the whole earth, are not in communion with the universal body redeemed by the blood of the Lord.

We have the Lord Himself rising from the dead, who presented Himself to be felt by the hands of the doubting disciples; and while they still doubted, He said to them, “It was necessary for Christ to suffer, and to rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in His name”—Where? In what direction? To what persons?—“among all nations, beginning at Jerusalem.”
Our minds are set at rest concerning the unity of the inheritance!
Whoever is not in communion with this inheritance has gone out.
8. But let us not be made sad: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would no doubt have continued with us.”
If, then, they went out from us, they are antichrists; if they are antichrists, they are liars; if they are liars, they deny that Jesus is the Christ.
Once more we come back to the difficulty of the question.
Ask them one by one: they confess that Jesus is the Christ.
The difficulty that hampers us comes from our taking what is said in the Epistle in too narrow a sense.
At any rate you see the question; this question brings both us and them to a standstill, if it is not understood.
Either we are antichrists, or they are antichrists; they call us antichrists and say that we went out from them; we say the same of them.
But now this epistle has marked out the antichrists by this badge: “Whoever denies that Jesus is the Christ,” that same one “is an antichrist.”
Now therefore let us inquire who denies; and let us observe not the tongue, but the deeds.
For if all are asked, all with one mouth confess that Jesus is the Christ.
Let the tongue keep still for a little while; question the life.

If we find this—if the Scripture itself tells us that denial is a thing done not only with the tongue but also with deeds—then assuredly we find many antichrists, who with the mouth profess Christ and in their conduct dissent from Christ.
Where do we find this in Scripture?
Hear Paul the Apostle; speaking of such people, he says, “For they confess that they know God, but in their deeds they deny Him.”
We find these also to be antichrists: whoever denies Christ in his deeds is an antichrist.
I do not listen to what he says, but I look at what life he leads.
Works speak, and do we require words?
For where is the bad man who does not wish to talk well?
But what does the Lord say to such people?
“You hypocrites, how can you speak good things, while you are evil?”
Your voices you bring to My ears; I look into your thoughts.
I see an evil will there, and you make a show of false fruits.
I know what I must gather, and from where; I do not “gather figs from thistles,” I do not gather “grapes from thorns”; for “every tree is known by its fruit.”
A more lying antichrist is he who with his mouth professes that Jesus is the Christ and with his deeds denies Him.
A liar in this, that he says one thing and does another.
9. Now therefore, brethren, if deeds are to be questioned, we find not only many antichrists who have gone out, but many not yet manifest, who have not gone out at all.

For as many as the Church has within it who are perjurers, defrauders, given to black arts, consulters of fortune-tellers, adulterers, drunkards, usurers, kidnappers of boys, and all the other vices that we are not able to list—these things are contrary to the teaching of Christ, are contrary to the word of God.
Now the Word of God is Christ: whatever is contrary to the Word of God is in Antichrist.
For Antichrist means “contrary to Christ.”
And would you know how openly these people resist Christ?

Sometimes it happens that they do some evil, and someone begins to rebuke them; because they dare not blaspheme Christ, they blaspheme His ministers by whom they are rebuked; but if you show them that you are speaking Christ’s words, not your own, they try all they can to convict you of speaking your own words, not Christ’s; if, however, it is manifest that you are speaking Christ’s words, they go even against Christ, they begin to find fault with Christ: “How,” they say, “and why did He make us such as we are?”
Do not people say this every day, when they are convicted of their deeds?
Perverted by a depraved will, they accuse their Maker.
Their Maker cries to them from heaven (for the One who made us is the same who made us new): What did I make you?
I made man, not avarice; I made man, not robbery; I made man, not adultery.
You have heard that My works praise Me.
Out of the mouth of the Three Children—it was the hymn itself that kept them from the fires.

The works of the Lord praise the Lord; the heaven, the earth, the sea praise Him; all things that are in the heaven praise Him; the angels praise Him, the stars praise Him, the lights praise Him; whatever swims, whatever flies, whatever walks, whatever creeps praises Him; all these praise the Lord.
Have you heard there that avarice praises the Lord?
Have you heard that drunkenness praises the Lord?
That self-indulgence praises Him, that frivolity praises Him?
Whatever you do not hear giving praise to the Lord in that hymn, the Lord did not make that thing.
Correct what you have made, that what God made in you may be saved.
But if you will not, and you love and embrace your sins, you are contrary to Christ.
Whether you are within or without, you are an antichrist; whether you are within or without, you are chaff.
But why are you not without?
Because you have not met with a wind to carry you away.
10. These things are now manifest, my brethren.
Let no one say, “I do not worship Christ, but I worship God His Father.”
“Everyone who denies the Son has neither the Son nor the Father; and he who confesses the Son has both the Son and the Father.”
He speaks to you who are grain; and let those who were chaff hear, and become grain.
Let each one, looking well to his own conscience, if he is a lover of the world, be changed; let him become a lover of Christ, that he may not be an antichrist.
If someone tells him that he is an antichrist, he is angry, he thinks it a wrong done to him; perhaps, if he is told by one who quarrels with him that he is an antichrist, he threatens a lawsuit.

Christ says to him: Be patient; if you have been falsely spoken of, rejoice with Me, because I also am falsely spoken of by the antichrists; but if you are truly spoken of, come to terms with your own conscience; and if you fear to be called this, fear more to be it.
11. “Therefore let that abide in you which you have heard from the beginning.
If what you have heard from the beginning abides in you, you also will abide in the Son and in the Father.
And this is the promise that He has promised us.”

For perhaps you might ask about the wages, and say, Behold, “What I have heard from the beginning I keep safe in me, I comply with it; perils, labors, temptations, for the sake of this continuing, I bear up against them all: with what fruit? What wages? What will He give me hereafter, since in this world I see that I labor among temptations?

I see no rest here: mere mortality weighs down the soul, and the corruptible body presses it down to lower things; but I bear all things, that ‘what I have heard from the beginning’ may ‘remain’ in me, and that I may say to my God, ‘Because of the words of Your lips I have kept hard ways.’”
To what wages, then?
Hear, and do not faint.
If you were fainting in the labors, be strong upon the promised wages.
Where is the man who will work in a vineyard and let slip from his heart the reward he is to receive?
Suppose him to have forgotten it: his hands fail.
The remembrance of the promised wages makes him persevere in the work; and yet the one who promised it is a man who can disappoint your expectation.
How much stronger ought you to be in God’s field, when He who promised is the Truth, who can neither have any successor, nor die, nor deceive the one to whom the promise was made!
And what is the promise?
Let us see what He has promised.
Is it gold, which men here love so much, or silver?
Or possessions, on which men lavish gold, however much they love gold?
Or pleasant lands, spacious houses, many slaves, numerous cattle?
These are not the wages, so to speak, for which he exhorts us to endure in labor.
What are these wages called? “Eternal life.”
You have heard, and in your joy you have cried out: love what you have heard, and you are delivered from your labors into the rest of eternal life.
Behold, this is what God promises: “eternal life.”
Behold, this is what God threatens: eternal fire.
What to those set on the right hand?
“Come, you blessed of My Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the beginning of the world.”
To those on the left, what?
“Go into eternal fire, prepared for the devil and his angels.”
You do not yet love that: at least fear this.
12. Remember, then, my brethren, that Christ has promised us eternal life: “This,” he says, “is the promise which He has promised us, even eternal life.
These things I have written to you concerning those who lead you astray.”
Let no one lead you astray to death: desire the promise of eternal life.
What can the world promise?
Let it promise what you will, it makes the promise perhaps to one who will die tomorrow.
And with what face will you go from here to Him who abides forever?
“But a powerful man threatens me, so that I must do some evil.”
What does he threaten?
Prisons, chains, fires, torments, wild beasts: yes, but not eternal fire?
Dread what the One Almighty threatens; love what the One Almighty promises; and the whole world becomes worthless in our eyes, whether it promises or terrifies.
“These things I have written to you concerning those who lead you astray; that you may know that you have an anointing, and that the anointing which we have received from Him may abide in you.”

In the anointing we have the sacramental sign [of a thing unseen]; the power itself is invisible; the invisible anointing is the Holy Spirit; the invisible anointing is that charity which, in whomever it is, shall be like a root to him: however burning the sun, he cannot wither.
All that is rooted is nourished by the sun’s warmth, not withered.
13. “And you have no need that anyone teach you, because His anointing teaches you concerning all things.”
Then to what purpose is it that “we,” my brethren, teach you?
If “His anointing teaches you concerning all things,” it seems we labor without cause.
And what do we mean by crying out as we do?
Let us leave you to His anointing, and let His anointing teach you.

But this is putting the question only to myself: I put it also to that same apostle: let him deign to hear a little child who asks of him: to John himself I say, Did those to whom you were speaking have the anointing?
You have said, “His anointing teaches you concerning all things.”
To what purpose have you written an epistle like this? What teaching did “you” give them? What instruction? What edification?
See here now, brethren, see a mighty mystery.
The sound of our words strikes the ears; the Master is within.
Do not suppose that any man learns anything from man.
We can admonish by the sound of our voice; if there is not One within who teaches, the noise we make is in vain.
Yes, brethren, do you wish to know it?
Have you not all heard this present discourse? And yet how many will go from this place untaught!
I, for my part, have spoken to all; but those to whom that Anointing within does not speak, those whom the Holy Spirit within does not teach, go back untaught.
The teachings of the master from without are a kind of aids and admonitions.
He who teaches the hearts has His chair in heaven.
Therefore He also says Himself in the Gospel: “Call no man your master upon earth; One is your Master, even Christ.”
Let Him therefore Himself speak to you within, when no one of mankind is there: for though there may be someone at your side, there is no one in your heart.

Yet let there not be no one in your heart: let Christ be in your heart: let His anointing be in the heart, lest it be a heart thirsting in the wilderness, and having no fountains with which to be watered.
There is then, I say, a Master within who teaches: Christ teaches; His inspiration teaches.
Where His inspiration and His anointing are not, words make a noise from without in vain.

So are the words, brethren, which we speak from without, as the farmer is to the tree: he works from without, applies water and diligent cultivation; let him apply from without whatever he will, does he form the apples? Does he clothe the nakedness of the wood with a shady covering of leaves? Does he do anything like this from within?
But whose doing is this?

Hear the farmer, the apostle: both see what we are, and hear the Master within: “I planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase: neither is he who plants anything, nor he who waters, but He who gives the increase, even God.”

This then we say to you: whether we plant, or whether we water, by speaking we are not anything; but He who gives the increase, even God: that is, “His anointing which teaches you concerning all things.”
“And it is true, and does not lie.
Even as it has taught you, abide in it.
And now, little children, abide in Him; that, when He appears, we may have confidence, and not be put to shame by Him at His coming.
If you know that He is righteous, know that everyone who does righteousness is born of Him.

Behold, what manner of love the Father has bestowed upon us, that we should be called and should be the sons of God: therefore the world does not know us, because it did not know Him; us also the world does not know.
Beloved, now we are the sons of God, and it has not yet been revealed what we shall be.
We know that, when He appears, we shall be like Him; for we shall see Him as He is.
And every man who has this hope in Him purifies himself, even as He is pure.
Whoever commits sin also commits iniquity.
Sin is iniquity. And you know that He was revealed to take away sin; and in Him there is no sin.
Whoever abides in Him does not sin: whoever sins has not seen Him, nor known Him.
Little children, let no one lead you astray.
He who does righteousness is righteous, even as He is righteous.
He who commits sin is of the devil; for the devil has sinned from the beginning.
For this purpose the Son of God was revealed, that He might destroy the works of the devil.”
1. You remember, brethren, that yesterday’s reading was brought to a close at this point, that “you have no need that anyone teach you, but the anointing itself teaches you concerning all things.”

Now this, as I am sure you remember, we so expounded to you, that we who speak to your ears from without are like workmen applying cultivation to a tree from without, but we cannot give the increase nor form the fruits: only He who created and redeemed and called you, He, dwelling in you by faith and the Spirit, must speak to you within, or else all our noise of words is in vain.
From what does this appear?
From this: that while many hear, not all are persuaded of what is said, but only those to whom God speaks within.
Now those to whom He speaks within are those who give place to Him: and those give place to God who “do not give place to the devil.”
For the devil wishes to inhabit the hearts of men, and to speak there the things that are able to lead astray.
But what does the Lord Jesus say?
“The ruler of this world is cast out.”
Cast out from where? Out of heaven and earth? Out of the fabric of the world?
No, but out of the hearts of those who believe.
The invader being cast out, let the Redeemer dwell within: because the same One who created has redeemed.
And the devil now assaults from without; he does not conquer Him who has possession within.
And he assaults from without, by casting in various temptations: but that person does not consent to them to whom God speaks within, and the anointing of which you have heard.
2. “And it is true,” namely, this same anointing; that is, the very Spirit of the Lord who teaches men cannot lie: “and is not false.
Even as it has taught you, abide in the same.
And now, little children, abide in Him, that when He is revealed, we may have boldness in His sight, that we may not be put to shame by Him at His coming.”

You see, brethren: we believe in Jesus whom we have not seen: those announced Him who saw, who handled, who heard the word from His own mouth; and that they might persuade all mankind of its truth, they were sent by Him; they did not dare to go of themselves.
And where were they sent?
You heard when the Gospel was read, “Go, preach the Gospel to the whole creation which is under heaven.”
Consequently, the disciples were sent “everywhere,” with signs and wonders to attest that what they spoke, they had seen.
And we believe in Him whom we have not seen, and we look for Him to come.
Those who look for Him by faith shall rejoice when He comes: those who are without faith, when that which they do not now see has come, shall be ashamed.
And that confusion of face shall not be for a single day and so pass away, in the way that those are usually confounded who are found out in some fault and are scoffed at by their fellow men.
That confusion shall carry those who are confounded to the left hand, so that it may be said to them, “Go into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels.”
Let us abide then in His words, that we may not be confounded when He comes.
For He Himself says in the Gospel to those who had believed in Him: “If you abide in My word, then you are truly My disciples.”
And, as if they had asked, With what fruit?
“And,” He says, “you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.”
For as yet our salvation is in hope, not in fact: for we do not already possess what is promised, but we hope for it to come.
And “He who promised is faithful”; He does not deceive you: only do not faint, but wait for the promise.
For He, the Truth, cannot deceive.
Do not be a liar, professing one thing and doing another; keep the faith, and He keeps His promise.
But if you do not keep the faith, it is your own self, not He who promised, who has defrauded you.
3. “If you know that He is righteous, know that everyone who does righteousness is born of Him.”
The righteousness which is ours at present is of faith.

Perfect righteousness does not exist, except only in the angels: and scarcely in angels, if they are compared with God: yet if there is any perfect righteousness of souls and spirits which God has created, it is in the angels, holy, just, good, turned aside by no lapse, falling by no pride, but remaining ever in the contemplation of the Word of God, and having nothing else sweet to them except Him by whom they were created; in them is perfect righteousness: but in us it has begun to be, of faith, by the Spirit.
You heard when the Psalm was read, “Begin to the Lord in confession.”
“Begin,” it says; the beginning of our righteousness is the confession of sins.

You have begun not to defend your sin; now you have made a beginning of righteousness: but it shall be perfected in you when to do nothing else shall delight you, when “death shall be swallowed up in victory,” when there shall be no itching of lust, when there shall be no struggling with flesh and blood, when there shall be the palm of victory, the triumph over the enemy; then there shall be perfect righteousness.
At present we are still fighting: if we fight, we are in the arena; we strike and are struck; but who shall conquer remains to be seen.
And that man conquers who, even when he strikes, does not presume on his own strength, but relies upon God who cheers him on.
The devil is alone when he fights against us.
If we are with God, we overcome the devil: for if you fight alone with the devil, you will be overcome.
He is a skillful enemy: how many palms he has won!
Consider to what he has cast us down!
That we are born mortal comes from this, that he in the first place cast our very origin down from Paradise.
What then is to be done, seeing he is so well practiced?
Let the Almighty be called upon to your aid against the devices of the devil.
Let Him dwell in you who cannot be overcome, and you shall securely overcome him who is accustomed to overcome.
But to overcome whom?
Those in whom God does not dwell.

For, that you may know it, brethren: Adam, being in Paradise, despised the commandment of God, and lifted up his neck, as if he desired to be his own master and were unwilling to be subject to the will of God: so he fell from that immortality, from that blessedness.

But there was a certain man, a man now well skilled, though born a mortal, who even as he sat on the dunghill, putrefying with worms, overcame the devil: yes, Adam himself then overcame: even he, in Job; because Job was of his race.
So then Adam, overcome in Paradise, overcame on the dunghill.
Being in Paradise, he listened to the persuasion of the woman which the devil had put into her: but being on the dunghill he said to Eve, “You have spoken as one of the foolish women.”
There he lent an ear, here he gave an answer: when he was glad, he listened; when he was scourged, he overcame.
Therefore see what follows, my brethren, in the Epistle: because this is what it would have us take to heart, that we may overcome the devil indeed, but not of ourselves.
“If you know that He is righteous,” it says, “know that everyone who does righteousness is born of Him”: of God, of Christ.
And in saying, “Is born of Him,” he cheers us on.
Already therefore, in that we are born of Him, we are perfect.
4. Hear. “Behold what manner of love the Father has given us, that we should be called sons of God, and be (such).”
For those who are called sons and are not sons, what does the name profit them where the thing is not?
How many are called physicians who do not know how to heal! How many are called watchmen who sleep all night long!
So many are called Christians, and yet in deeds are not found to be such; because they are not what they are called, that is, in life, in conduct, in faith, in hope, in charity.
But what have you heard here, brethren?

“Behold, what manner of love the Father has bestowed upon us, that we should be called, and should be, the sons of God: therefore the world does not know us, because it has not known Him; us also the world does not know.”
There is a whole world Christian, and a whole world ungodly; because throughout the whole world there are ungodly, and throughout the whole world there are godly: those do not know these.
In what sense, do we think, do they not know them?
They deride those who live good lives.
Mark well and see: for perhaps there are such also among you.

Each one of you who now lives godly, who despises worldly things, who does not choose to go to the shows, who does not choose to make himself drunk as if by solemn custom, yes, what is worse, to make himself unclean under the cover of holy days: the man who does not choose to do these things, how he is derided by those who do them!
Would he be scoffed at if he were known?
But why is he not known?
“The world does not know Him.”
Who is “the world”?
Those inhabitants of the world.
Just as we say, “a house,” meaning its inhabitants.
These things have been said to you again and again, and we refrain from repeating them, lest they weary you.

By this time, when you hear the word “world” in a bad sense, you know that you must understand it to mean only lovers of the world, because through love they inhabit it, and by inhabiting have come to be entitled to the name.
Therefore the world has not known us, because it has not known Him.
He walked here Himself, the Lord Jesus Christ in the flesh; He was God, He was hidden in weakness.
And why was He not known?
Because He reproved all sins in men.
They, through loving the delights of sins, did not acknowledge the God: through loving what the fever prompted, they did wrong to the Physician.
5. For us then, what are we?
Already we are begotten of Him; but because we are such in hope, he says, “Beloved, now we are sons of God.”
Now already? Then what is it we look for, if already we are sons of God?
“And not yet,” he says, “has it been revealed what we shall be.”
But what else shall we be than sons of God?
Hear what follows: “We know that, when He appears, we shall be like Him, because we shall see Him as He is.”
Understand, my beloved. It is a great matter: “We know that, when He appears, we shall be like Him; for we shall see Him as He is.”
In the first place mark what is called “Is.”
You know what it is that is so called.

That which is called “Is,” and is not only called so but is so, is unchangeable: It ever remains, It cannot be changed, It is in no part corruptible: It has neither progress, for It is perfect; nor decline, for It is eternal.
And what is this?
“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”
And what is this?
“Who, being in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God.”
To see Christ in this way, Christ in the form of God, the Word of God, the Only-Begotten of the Father, equal with the Father, is impossible for the wicked.
But inasmuch as the Word was made flesh, the wicked also shall be able to see Him: because in the day of judgment the wicked also will see Him; for He shall so come to judge, as He came to be judged.
In the selfsame form, a man, but yet God: for “cursed is everyone who puts his trust in man.”
As a man He came to be judged; as a man He will come to judge.
And if He shall not be seen, what is this that is written, “They shall look on Him whom they pierced”?
For of the ungodly it is said that they shall see and be confounded.
How shall the ungodly not see, when He shall set some on the right hand, others on the left?
To those on the right hand He will say, “Come, you blessed of My Father, receive the kingdom”: to those on the left He will say, “Go into everlasting fire.”
They will see only the form of a servant; the form of God they will not see.
Why? Because they were ungodly; and the Lord Himself says, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.”

Therefore we are to see a certain vision, my brethren, “which neither eye has seen, nor ear has heard, nor has entered into the heart of man”: a certain vision, a vision surpassing all earthly beauty, of gold, of silver, of groves and fields; the beauty of sea and air, the beauty of sun and moon, the beauty of the stars, the beauty of angels: surpassing all things, because from it all things are beautiful.
6. What then shall “we” be, when we see this?
What is promised to us?
“We shall be like Him, for we shall see Him as He is.”
The tongue has done what it could, it has sounded the words: let the rest be thought out by the heart.
For what has even John himself said in comparison with That which Is, or what can be said by us men, who are so far from being equal to his merits?

Let us return therefore to that anointing of His, let us return to that anointing which inwardly teaches what we cannot speak: and because you cannot see at present, let your part and duty be in desire.
The whole life of a good Christian is a holy desire.
Now what you long for, you do not yet see: however, by longing you are made capable, so that when that has come which you may see, you shall be filled.

For just as, if you would fill a bag, and know how great the thing is that shall be given, you stretch the opening of the sack or the skin, or whatever else it may be; you know how much you would put in, and see that the bag is narrow; by stretching you make it capable of holding more: so God, by deferring our hope, stretches our desire; by the desiring, stretches the mind; by stretching, makes it more capacious.
Let us desire therefore, my brethren, for we shall be filled.
See Paul widening, as it were, his bosom, that it may be able to receive what is to come.
He says, namely, “Not that I have already received, or am already perfect: brethren, I do not consider myself to have apprehended.”
Then what are you doing in this life, if you have not yet apprehended?
“But this one thing [I do]: forgetting the things that are behind, reaching forth to the things that are before, under strain I follow on toward the prize of the high calling.”
He says he reaches forth, or stretches himself, and says that he follows “under strain.”
He felt himself too small to take in that “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man.”
This is our life, that we should be exercised by longing.
But holy longing exercises us just so much as we prune off our longings from the love of the world.
We have already said, “Empty out what is to be filled.”
You are to be filled with good: pour out the bad.
Suppose that God would fill you with honey: if you are full of vinegar, where will you put the honey?

What the vessel bore in it must be poured out: the vessel itself must be cleansed; it must be cleansed, even with labor, even with hard rubbing, that it may become fit for that thing, whatever it may be.
Let us say honey, say gold, say wine; whatever we say it is, being that which cannot be said, whatever we would gladly say, It is called—God.
And when we say “God,” what have we said?
Is that one syllable the whole of what we look for?
So then, whatever we have been able to say is beneath Him: let us stretch ourselves toward Him, that when He comes, He may fill us.
For “we shall be like Him, because we shall see Him as He is.”
7. “And everyone who has this hope in Him.”
You see how he has set our place for us, in “hope.”
You see how the Apostle Paul agrees with his fellow apostle: “By hope we are saved.
But hope that is seen is not hope: for what a man sees, why does he hope for it?
For if we hope for what we do not see, by patience we wait for it.”
This very patience exercises desire.
Continue, for He continues: and persevere in walking, that you may reach the goal: for that toward which you are heading will not move away.
See: “And everyone who has this hope in Him purifies himself, even as He is pure.”
See how he has not taken away free will, in that he says, “purifies himself.”
Who purifies us but God?
Yes, but God does not purify you if you are unwilling.
Therefore, in that you join your will to God, in that you purify yourself.
You purify yourself, not by yourself, but by Him who comes to dwell in you.
Still, because you do something in it by the will, therefore something is attributed to you.
But it is attributed to you only to the end that you should say, as in the Psalm, “Be my helper; do not forsake me.”
If you say, “Be my helper,” you are doing something: for if you are doing nothing, how could He be said to “help” you?
8. “Everyone who does sin also does iniquity.”
Let no one say, Sin is one thing, iniquity another: let no one say, I am a sinful man, but not a doer of iniquity.
For, “Everyone who does sin also does iniquity.
Sin is iniquity.” Well then, what are we to do concerning sins and iniquities?
Hear what He says: “And you know that He was revealed to take away sin; and sin is not in Him.”
He in whom sin is not, the same has come to take away sin.
For if there were sin in Him, it would have to be taken away from Him, not He take it away Himself.
“Whoever abides in Him does not sin.”
Insofar as he abides in Him, so far he does not sin.
“Whoever sins has not seen Him, nor known Him.”
A great question this: “Whoever sins has not seen Him, nor known Him.”
No wonder. We have not seen Him, but are going to see; we have not known Him, but are going to know: we believe in One we have not known.
Or perhaps by faith we have known, and by actual beholding have not yet known?
But then in faith we have both seen and known.
For if faith does not yet see, why are we said to have been enlightened?
There is an enlightening by faith, and an enlightening by sight.
At present, while we are on pilgrimage, “we walk by faith, not by sight,” or actual beholding.
Therefore our righteousness also is “by faith, not by sight.”
Our righteousness shall be perfect when we see by actual beholding.
Only, in the meantime, let us not forsake that righteousness which is of faith, since “the just lives by faith,” as the apostle says.
“Whoever abides in Him does not sin.”
For, “whoever sins has not seen Him, nor known Him.”
That man who sins does not believe: but if a man believes, so far as pertains to his faith, he does not sin.
9. “Little children, let no one lead you astray.
He who does righteousness is righteous, as He is righteous.”
What, on hearing that we are “righteous as He is righteous,” are we to think ourselves equal with God?
You must know what that “as” means: thus he said a while ago, “Purifies himself even as He is pure.”
Then is our purity like and equal to the purity of God, and our righteousness to God’s righteousness?
Who can say this?
But the word “as” is not always used in the sense of equality.

As, for example, if, having seen this large church, a person should wish to build a smaller church, but with the same proportions: as, for example, if this is one measure in width and two measures in length, he too should build his church one measure in width and two measures in length: in that case one sees that he has built it “as” this is built.
But this church has, say, a hundred cubits in length, the other thirty: it is at once “as” this, and yet unequal.
You see that this “as” does not always refer to parity and equality.
For example, see what a difference there is between the face of a man and its image in a mirror: there is a face in the image, a face in the body: the image exists in imitation, the body in reality.
And what do we say?
Why, “as” there are eyes here, so also there; “as” ears here, so ears also there.
The thing is different, but the “as” is said of the resemblance.

Well then, we also have in us the image of God; but not that which the Son, equal with the Father, has: yet unless we also, according to our measure, were “as” He, we should in no respect be said to be like Him.
“He purifies us,” then, “even as He is pure”: but He is pure from eternity, we pure by faith.
We are “righteous even as He is righteous”; but He is so in His unchangeable perpetuity, we righteous by believing in One we do not see, so that we may one day see Him.
Even when our righteousness is perfect, when we are equal to the angels, not even then shall it be made equal to Him.
How far then is it from Him now, when not even then shall it be equal!
10. “He who does sin is of the devil, because the devil sins from the beginning.”
“Is of the devil”: you know what he means: by imitating the devil.

For the devil made no man, begot no man, created no man: but whoever imitates the devil, that person, as if begotten of him, becomes a child of the devil; by imitating him, not literally by being begotten of him.
In what sense are you a child of Abraham, since Abraham did not beget you?

In the same sense as the Jews, the children of Abraham, by not imitating the faith of Abraham, have become children of the devil: of the flesh of Abraham they were begotten, and the faith of Abraham they have not imitated.

If then those who were begotten from him were put out of the inheritance because they did not imitate, you, who are not begotten of him, are made a child, and in this way shall be a child of his by imitating him.
And if you imitate the devil, in the way that he became proud and impious against God, you will be a child of the devil: by imitating, not because he created you or begot you.
11. “For this end the Son of God was revealed.”
Now then, brethren, mark!
All sinners are begotten of the devil, as sinners.
Adam was made by God: but when he consented to the devil, he was begotten of the devil; and he begot all men such as he was himself.
With lust itself we were born; even before we add our own sins, we have our birth from that condemnation.
For if we are born without any sin, why this running with infants to baptism that they may be released?
Then mark well, brethren, the two birth-stocks, Adam and Christ: two men there are; but one of them a man who is man, the other a Man who is God.
By the man who is man we are sinners; by the Man who is God we are justified.
That birth has cast down to death; this birth has raised up to life: that birth brings sin with it; this birth sets free from sin.
For to this end Christ came as Man, to undo the sins of men.
“For this end the Son of God was revealed, that He might undo the works of the devil.”
12. The rest I commend to your thoughts, my beloved, that I may not burden you.
For the question we labor to solve is this—that we call ourselves sinners: for if any man shall say that he is without sin, he is a liar.
And in the Epistle of this same John we have found it written, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves.”
For you should remember what went before: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”

And yet, on the other hand, in what follows you are told, “He who is begotten of God does not sin: he who does sin has not seen Him, nor known Him.—Everyone who does sin is of the devil”: sin is not of God: this frightens us again.
In what sense are we begotten of God, and in what sense do we confess ourselves sinners?
Shall we say it is because we are not begotten of God?
And what then do these Sacraments do in regard to infants?
What has John said?
“He who is begotten of God does not sin.”
And yet again the same John has said, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us!”
A great question it is, and a perplexing one; and may I have made you intent upon having it solved, my beloved.
Tomorrow, in the name of the Lord, we will discourse on it, according to what He will give.
“Whoever is born of God does not commit sin; for his seed remains in him: and he cannot sin, because he is born of God.
In this the children of God are revealed, and the children of the devil: whoever is not righteous is not of God, nor is he who does not love his brother.
For this is the message that you heard from the beginning, that we should love one another.
Not as Cain, who was of the wicked one, and killed his brother.
And why did he kill him?
Because his own works were evil, and his brother’s righteous.
Do not marvel, my brethren, if the world hates us.
We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love the brethren.
He who does not love abides in death.
Whoever hates his brother is a murderer: and you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him.
By this we know love, that He laid down His life for us: and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren.
But whoever has this world’s goods, and sees his brother in need, and shuts up his heart of compassion from him, how can the love of God dwell in him?
My little children, let us not love only in word and in tongue, but in deed and in truth.”

1. Listen intently, I beg you, because it is no small matter that we have to deal with: and I do not doubt, because you were intent upon it yesterday, that you have come together today with even greater intentness of purpose.

For it is no slight question, how he says in this Epistle, “Whoever is born of God does not sin,” and how in the same Epistle he has said above, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”
What shall the man do who is pressed by both sayings from the same Epistle?
If he confesses himself a sinner, he fears lest it be said to him, Then you are not born of God; because it is written, “Whoever is born of God does not sin.”

But if he says that he is righteous and that he has no sin, he receives on the other side a blow from the same Epistle, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”
Placed then as he is in the middle, he cannot find what he can say and what confess, or what profess.

To profess himself to be without sin is full of peril; and not only full of peril, but also full of error: “We deceive ourselves,” he says, “and the truth is not in us, if we say that we have no sin.”
But oh, that you had none, and said this! For then you would speak truly, and in uttering the truth would have not so much as a trace of wrong to be afraid of.
But the reason you do wrong if you say so is that what you say is a lie.
“The truth,” he says, “is not in us, if we say that we have no sin.”
He does not say, “Have not had,” lest perhaps it should seem to be spoken of the past life.
For the man here has had sins: but from the time that he was born of God, he has begun not to have sins.
If it were so, there would be no question to perplex us.
For we should say, We have been sinners, but now we are justified: we have had sin, but now we have none.
He does not say this: but what does he say?
“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”
And then after a while he says on the other hand, “Whoever is born of God does not sin.”
Was John himself not born of God?

If John was not born of God—John, of whom you have heard that he lay in the Lord’s bosom—does any man dare to vouch for himself that in him has taken place that regeneration which it was not granted to that man to have, to whom it was granted to lie in the bosom of the Lord?
The man whom the Lord loved more than the rest, him alone had He not begotten of the Spirit?
2. Mark these words now.

Still, I am pressing it upon you: see what straits we are put to, so that by the straining of your minds—that is, by your praying for us and for yourselves—God may make room and give us an outlet: lest some man find in His word an occasion of his own ruin, that word which was preached and put in writing only for healing and salvation.
“Everyone,” he says, “who does sin also does iniquity.”
Lest perhaps you make a distinction: “Sin is iniquity.”
Lest you say, I am a sinner, but not a doer of iniquity: “Sin is iniquity.
And you know that He was revealed for this purpose, that He should take away sin; and in Him there is no sin.”
And what does it profit us that He came without sin?
“Everyone who does not sin abides in Him; and everyone who sins has not seen Him, nor known Him.
Little children, let no one lead you astray.
He who does righteousness is righteous, just as He is righteous.”
This we have already said, that the word “as” is commonly used of a certain likeness, not of equality.
“He who does sin is of the devil, because the devil sins from the beginning.”
This too we have already said, that the devil created no man, nor begot any, but his imitators are, as it were, born of him.
“For this purpose the Son of God was revealed, that He might undo the works of the devil.”
Consequently, it is He who has no sin who comes to undo (or loose) sins.

And then follows: “Everyone who is born of God does not commit sin; for his seed remains in him; and he cannot sin, because he is born of God.” He has drawn the cord tight! Perhaps it is with regard to some one sin that he has said, “Does not sin,” not with regard to all sin: so that in his saying, “Whoever is born of God does not sin,” you may understand some one particular sin which the man who is born of God cannot commit; and that sin is such that, if one commits it, it confirms the rest.
What is this sin?
To act contrary to the commandment.
What is the commandment?
“A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another.”
Mark well! This commandment of Christ is called “love.”
By this love sins are loosed.
If this love is not kept, the failure to hold it is at once a grievous sin and the root of all sins.
3. Mark well, brethren; we have brought forward something by which, for those who understand well, the question is solved.
But do we walk the way only with those who run more swiftly?
Those who walk more slowly must not be left behind.
Let us turn the matter every way, in such words as we can, so that it may be brought within reach of all.

For I suppose, brethren, that every man is concerned for his own soul who does not come to church without cause, who does not seek temporal things in the Church, who does not come here to transact worldly business, but comes here in order to lay hold of some eternal thing promised to him, which he may attain: he must consider how he shall walk in the way, lest he be left behind, lest he go back, lest he go astray, lest by limping he fail to arrive.
Whoever, therefore, is in earnest, whether he be slow or swift, let him not leave the way.

This, then, I have said: that in saying, “Whoever is born of God does not sin,” it is probable he meant it of some particular sin; for otherwise it will contradict that passage: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”
In this way, then, the question may be solved.
There is a certain sin which he who is born of God cannot commit; a sin which, when it is not committed, other sins are loosed, and when it is committed, other sins are confirmed.
What is this sin?
To act contrary to the commandment of Christ, contrary to the New Testament.
What is the new commandment?
“A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another.”

Whoever acts contrary to charity and contrary to brotherly love, let him not dare to boast and say that he is born of God; but whoever is in brotherly love, there are certain sins which he cannot commit, and above all this one, that he should hate his brother.
And how does it stand with him concerning his other sins, of which it is said, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us”?
Let him hear from another place of Scripture that which will set his mind at rest: “Charity covers a multitude of sins.”
4. Charity, therefore, is what we commend; charity is what this Epistle commends.
The Lord, after His resurrection, what question did He put to Peter, but, “Do you love Me?”
And it was not enough to ask it once; a second time also He put no other question, and a third time also none other.

Although, when it came to the third time, Peter, as one who did not know the purpose of this, was grieved because it seemed as if the Lord did not believe him; nevertheless, a first time and a second and a third He put this question.
Three times fear denied; three times love confessed.
See, Peter loves the Lord.
What is he to do for the Lord?
For do not think that the one in the Psalm did not feel at a loss what to do: “What shall I render to the Lord for all the benefits He has done for me?”
He who said this in the Psalm noted what great things had been done for him by God; and he sought what he should render to God, and could find nothing.
For whatever you would render, you received from Him in order to render it.
And what did he find to offer in return?
That which, as we said, my brethren, he had received from Him—that alone he found to offer in return.
“I will receive the cup of salvation, and will call upon the name of the Lord.”
For who had given him the cup of salvation, but He to whom he wished to offer something in return?

Now to receive the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord is to be filled with charity; and so filled that not only will you not hate your brother, but you will be prepared to die for your brother.
This is perfect charity, that you be prepared to die for your brother.
This the Lord displayed in Himself, who died for all, praying for those by whom He was crucified, and saying, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do.”
But if He alone had done this, He was not a Master, if He had no disciples.
Disciples who came after Him have done this.
Men were stoning Stephen, and he knelt down and said, “Lord, do not lay this sin to their charge.”
He loved those who were killing him, since for them also he was dying.
Hear also the Apostle Paul: “And I myself,” he says, “will be spent for your souls.”
For he was among those for whom Stephen, when he was dying at their hands, begged forgiveness.
This, then, is perfect charity.
If any man has such great charity that he is prepared even to die for his brethren, in that man charity is perfect.
But as soon as it is born, is it already quite perfect?
It is born that it may be made perfect; when born, it is nourished; when nourished, it is strengthened; when strengthened, it is perfected; when it has come to perfection, what does it say?
“For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.
I wished to be dissolved and to be with Christ, which is far better; nevertheless, to remain in the flesh is needful for you.”
For their sakes he was willing to live, for whose sakes he was prepared to die.

5. And that you may know that it is this perfect charity which the man who is born of God does not violate, and against which he does not sin, this is what the Lord says to Peter: “Peter, do you love Me?”
And he answers, “I love.”
He does not say, If you love Me, show kindness to Me.

For when the Lord was in mortal flesh, He hungered and He thirsted; at that time, when He hungered and thirsted, He was received as a guest; those who had the means ministered to Him from their substance, as we read in the Gospel.
Zacchaeus received Him as his guest; he was saved from his disease by receiving the Physician.
From what disease? The disease of avarice.
For he was very rich, and the chief of the tax collectors.
Mark the man made whole from the disease of avarice: “Half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken anything from any man, I will restore him fourfold.”
That he kept the other half was not in order to enjoy it, but to pay his debts.

Well, he at that time received the Physician as his guest, because there was weakness of the flesh in the Lord, to which men might show this kindness; and this because it was His will to grant this very thing to those who did Him kind service; for the benefit was for those who did the service, not for Him.
For could He to whom angels ministered require these men’s kindness?

Not even His servant Elijah, to whom on a certain occasion He sent bread and meat by the ravens, had need of this; and yet, that a devout widow might be blessed, the servant of God is sent, and he whom God fed in secret is fed by the widow.

But still, although by means of these servants of God those who consider their need do good to themselves, in respect of that reward most plainly set forth by the Lord in the Gospel—“He who receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man shall receive a righteous man’s reward; and he who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward; and whoever gives one of these little ones only a cup of cold water to drink in the name of a disciple, truly I say to you, he shall by no means lose his reward”—although, then, those who do this do it for their own good, yet this kind service could not be done to Him when He was about to ascend into heaven.
What could Peter, who loved Him, render to Him?
Hear what. “Feed My sheep”: that is, do for the brethren what I have done for you.
I redeemed all with My blood: do not hesitate to die for the confession of the truth, so that the rest may imitate you.
6. But this, as we have said, brethren, is perfect charity.
He who is born of God has it.
Mark, my beloved, see what I say.
See, a man has received the Sacrament of that birth by being baptized; he has the Sacrament, and a great Sacrament—divine, holy, inexpressible.
Consider what a Sacrament!
To make him a new man by the remission of all sins!
Nevertheless, let him look well to the heart, whether that which is done in the body is thoroughly done there; let him see whether he has charity, and then say, I am born of God.
If, however, he does not have it, he indeed bears the soldier’s mark upon him, but he roams as a deserter.
Let him have charity; otherwise let him not say that he is born of God.
But he says, I have the Sacrament.
Hear the Apostle: “If I know all mysteries, and have all faith, so that I can remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.”
7. This, if you remember, we gave you to understand when we began to read this Epistle: that nothing in it is so commended as charity.
Even if it seems to speak of various other things, it makes its way back to this; and whatever it says, it will bring all of it to bear upon charity.
Let us see whether it does so here.
Mark: “Whoever is born of God does not commit sin.”
We ask, what sin? Because if you understand it of all sin, it will contradict that passage, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”

Then let him say what sin; let him teach us; lest perhaps I have rashly said that the sin here is the violation of charity, because he said above, “He who hates his brother is in darkness, and walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.”
But perhaps he has said something in what comes afterward, and has mentioned charity by name?
See that this circuit of words has this end, has this outcome.
“Whoever is born of God does not sin, because His seed remains in him.”
The “seed” of God, that is, the word of God; hence the apostle says, “I have begotten you through the Gospel.
And he cannot sin, because he is born of God.”
Let him tell us this; let us see in what we cannot sin.
“In this the children of God and the children of the devil are made manifest.
Whoever is not righteous is not of God, nor is he who does not love his brother.”
Yes, now indeed it is manifest what he speaks of: “Nor he who does not love his brother.”
Therefore love alone makes the difference between the children of God and the children of the devil.

Let them all sign themselves with the sign of the cross of Christ; let them all respond, Amen; let all sing Alleluia; let all be baptized, let all come to church, let all build the walls of churches: there is no telling the children of God from the children of the devil except by charity.
Those who have charity are born of God; those who do not have it are not born of God.
A mighty sign, a mighty distinction!
Have what you will; if this alone you do not have, it profits you nothing; if you do not have other things, have this, and you have fulfilled the law.
“For he who loves another has fulfilled the law,” says the apostle; and, “Charity is the fulfilling of the law.”
I take this to be the pearl which the merchant in the Gospel is described as seeking, who “found one pearl, and sold all that he had, and bought it.”
This is the precious pearl, Charity, without which whatever you may have profits you nothing; and if you have it alone, it is enough for you.
Now you see with faith; then you shall see with actual sight.
For if we love when we do not see, how shall we embrace it when we see!
But in what must we exercise ourselves?
In brotherly love. You may say to me, I have not seen God; can you say to me, I have not seen man?
Love your brother. For if you love your brother whom you see, at the same time you shall see God also; because you shall see Charity itself, and within dwells God.
8. “Whoever is not righteous is not of God, nor he who does not love his brother.”
“For this is the message”: mark how he confirms it: “For this is the message which we heard from the beginning, that we should love one another.”
He has made it plain to us that it is of this he speaks; whoever acts against this commandment is in that accursed sin into which those fall who are not born of God.
“Not as Cain, who was of that wicked one, and killed his brother.
And why did he kill him?
Because his own works were evil, and his brother’s righteous.”
Therefore, where envy is, brotherly love cannot be.
Mark, my beloved. He who envies does not love.
The sin of the devil is in that man, because the devil through envy cast man down.
For he fell, and envied him who stood.
He did not wish to cast man down so that he himself might stand, but only so that he might not fall alone.
Hold fast in your mind, from what he has added here, that envy cannot exist in charity.
You have it openly where charity was praised: “Charity does not envy.”
There was no charity in Cain; and had there been no charity in Abel, God would not have accepted his sacrifice.

For when they had both offered, the one of the fruits of the earth, the other of the young of the flock, what do you think, brethren—that God slighted the fruits of the earth, and loved the young of the flock?

God did not regard the hands, but saw into the heart; and whom He saw offering with charity, to his sacrifice He had respect; whom He saw offering with envy, from his sacrifice He turned away His eyes.
By the good works of Abel, then, he means only charity; by the evil works of Cain he means only his hatred of his brother.
It was not enough that he hated his brother and envied his good works; because he would not imitate him, he would kill him.
And by this it appeared that he was a child of the devil, and by this also that the other was God’s righteous one.
By this, then, men are discerned, my brethren.
Let no one mark the tongue, but the deeds and the heart.
If anyone does not do good for his brethren, he shows what he has in him.
By temptations men are proved.
9. “Do not marvel, brethren, if the world hates us.”
Must one keep telling you what “the world” means?
Not the heaven, not the earth, nor these visible works which God made, but lovers of the world.
By saying these things often, I am burdensome to some; but I am so far from saying it without cause that some may be asked whether I said it, and they cannot answer.
Let something, then, even by pressing it upon them, stick fast in the hearts of those who hear.
What is “the world”?

The world, when taken in a bad sense, is the lovers of the world; the world, when the word is used in praise, is heaven and earth and the works of God that are in them; hence it is said, “And the world was made by Him.”

Also, the world is the fullness of the earth, as John himself has said, “Not only for our sins is He the propitiator, but (for the sins) of the whole world”: by “the world” he means all the faithful scattered throughout the whole earth.
But the world in a bad sense is the lovers of the world.
Those who love the world cannot love their brother.
10. “If the world hates us, we know”—what do we know?—“that we have passed from death to life”—how do we know?
“Because we love the brethren.”
Let no one ask man; let each return to his own heart: if he finds brotherly love there, let him set his mind at rest, because he has “passed from death to life.”
Already he is on the right hand; let him not mind that for the present his glory is hidden; when the Lord comes, then he shall appear in glory.

For he has life in him, but as yet in winter; the root is alive, but the branches, so to speak, are dry; within is the substance that has life in it, within are the leaves of the trees, within are the fruits; but they wait for the summer.
Well then, “we know that we have passed from death to life, because we love the brethren.
He who does not love abides in death.”
Lest you should think it a light matter, brethren, to hate, or not to love, hear what follows: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer.”
What now—if anyone made light of hating his brother, will he also in his heart make light of murder?
He does not stir his hands to kill a man, yet he is already held by God to be a murderer; the other lives, and yet this man is already judged as his killer!
“Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer; and you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him.”

11. “In this we know love”: he means the perfection of love, that perfection which we have urged you to take to heart: “In this we know love, that He laid down His life for us; and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren.”
See here where that came from: “Peter, do you love Me?

Feed My sheep.” For, that you may know that He wished His sheep to be fed by him in such a way that he would lay down his life for the sheep, He immediately said this to him: “When you were young, you girded yourself and walked where you wished; but when you are old, you shall stretch out your hands, and another shall gird you and carry you where you do not wish.
This He spoke,” says the evangelist, “signifying by what death he would glorify God”; so that the one to whom He had said, “Feed My sheep,” He might teach to lay down his life for His sheep.
12. Where does charity begin, brethren?

Attend a little: to what point it is perfected you have heard; its very end and its very measure is what the Lord has set before us in the Gospel: “Greater love has no man,” He says, “than that one lay down his life for his friends.”

Its perfection, therefore, He has set before us in the Gospel, and here also it is its perfection that is set before us; but you ask yourselves and say to yourselves, When will it be possible for us to have “this” charity?
Do not despair of yourself too soon.
Perhaps it is born and is not yet perfect; nourish it, so that it is not choked.
But you will say to me, And by what am I to know it?
For we have heard to what point it is perfected; let us hear where it begins.
He goes on to say: “But whoever has this world’s goods, and sees his brother hungry, and shuts up his heart of compassion from him, how can the love of God dwell in him?”
See, this is where charity begins!
If you are not yet equal to dying for your brother, be even now equal to giving your means to your brother.
Even now let charity strike your inmost heart, so that you do it not from vainglory but from the innermost marrow of mercy; that you consider him, now in want.
For if you cannot give your surplus to your brother, can you lay down your life for your brother?

There lies your money in your bosom, which thieves may take from you; and even if thieves do not take it, by dying you will leave it, even if it does not leave you while you live: what will you do with it?

Your brother is hungry, he is in need; perhaps he is in anxiety, distressed by his creditor; he is your brother, you are bought alike, one price was paid for you, you are both redeemed by the blood of Christ: see whether you have mercy, if you have this world’s means.
Perhaps you say, “What does it concern me?
Am I to give my money so that he may not suffer trouble?”
If this is the answer your heart gives you, the love of the Father does not abide in you.
If the love of the Father does not abide in you, you are not born of God.
How do you boast of being a Christian?
You have the name, and do not have the deeds.
But if the work follows the name, let anyone call you a pagan; show by deeds that you are a Christian.
For if by deeds you do not show yourself a Christian, all men may still call you a Christian; what does the name profit you where the thing itself is not to be found?
“But whoever has this world’s goods, and sees his brother in need, and shuts up his heart of compassion from him, how can the love of God dwell in him?”
And then he goes on: “My little children, let us not love in word, nor in tongue, but in deed and in truth.”
13. I suppose the thing is now made plain to you, my brethren: this great and most weighty secret and mystery.
What the power of charity is, all Scripture sets forth; but I do not know whether anywhere it is set forth more fully than in this Epistle.

We pray and beseech you in the Lord that you will both keep in memory what you have heard, and come with earnestness to what is yet to be said until the Epistle is finished, and hear it with earnestness.

But open your heart to the good seed; root out the thorns, so that what we are sowing in you is not choked, but rather that the harvest may grow, and that the Husbandman may rejoice and make ready the barn for you as for grain, not the fire as for chaff.
“And by this we know that we are of the truth, and assure our hearts before Him.
For if our heart thinks ill of us, God is greater than our heart, and knows all things.
Beloved, if our heart does not think ill of us, then we have confidence toward God.
And whatever we ask, we shall receive from Him, because we keep His commandments and do in His sight the things that please Him.
And this is His commandment: that we should believe on the name of His Son Jesus Christ, and love one another, as He gave us commandment.
And he who keeps His commandments shall dwell in Him, and He in him.
And by this we know that He abides in us, by the Holy Spirit whom He has given us.
Dearly beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits whether they are of God, because many false prophets have gone out into this world.

By this the Spirit of God is known: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is of God; and every spirit that does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is not of God; and this is the antichrist, of whom you have heard that he would come; and even now he is already in this world.”
1. If you remember, brethren, yesterday we closed our sermon at this sentence, which without doubt should have remained, and should still remain, in your heart, since it was the last you heard.
“My little children, let us not love only in word and in tongue, but in deed and in truth.”
Then he goes on: “And by this we know that we are of the truth, and assure our hearts before Him.”
“For if our heart thinks ill of us, God is greater than our heart, and knows all things.”
He had said, “Let us not love only in word and in tongue, but in work and in truth”; we are asked, In what work, or in what truth, is he known who loves God, or loves his brother?

Above he had said up to what point charity is perfected: what the Lord says in the Gospel, “Greater love than this has no man, that one lay down his life for his friends,” this same the apostle had also said: “As He laid down His life for us, we also ought to lay down our lives for the brethren.”
This is the perfection of charity, and a greater cannot be found at all.

But because it is not perfect in all, and the man in whom it is not perfect ought not to despair, if that which may be perfected is already born—and of course, if born, it must be nourished, and by certain nourishments of its own must be brought to its proper perfection—therefore we have asked concerning the beginning of charity, where it begins, and have immediately found there: “But whoever has this world’s goods, and sees his brother in need, and shuts up his heart of compassion from him, how does the love of the Father dwell in him?”

Here then, my brethren, this charity has its beginning: to give of one’s surplus to him who has need, to him who is in any distress; out of one’s temporal abundance to deliver one’s brother from temporal trouble.
Here is the first rising of charity.

If you nourish this, once it has thus begun, with the word of God and the hope of the life to come, you will come at last to that perfection, that you will be ready to lay down your life for your brethren.
2. But because many such things are done by men who seek other ends, and who do not love the brethren, let us come back to the testimony of conscience.
How do we prove that many such things are done by men who do not love the brethren?
How many in heresies and schisms call themselves martyrs!
They seem to themselves to lay down their lives for their brethren.
If they laid down their lives for the brethren, they would not separate themselves from the whole brotherhood.
Again, how many there are who for the sake of vainglory bestow much, give much, and seek in it only the praise of men and popular glory, which is full of wind and has no stability!
Since, then, there are such people, where shall the proof of brotherly charity be?
Since he wished it to be proved, and has said by way of admonition, “My little children, let us not love only in word and in tongue, but in deed and in truth,” we ask, in what work, in what truth?
Can there be a more evident work than to give to the poor?
Many do this from vainglory, not from love.
Can there be a greater work than to die for the brethren?
This also many would like to be thought to do, who do it from vainglory to get a name, not from the depths of love.

It remains that that man loves his brother who, before God, where God alone sees, assures his own heart, and questions his heart whether he does this truly for love of the brethren; and his witness is that eye which penetrates the heart, where man cannot look.

Therefore Paul the Apostle, because he was ready to die for the brethren, and said, “I will myself be spent for your souls,” yet, because God alone saw this in his heart, not the mortal men to whom he spoke, he says to them, “But to me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you, or by man’s court.”

And the same apostle also shows in a certain place that these things are often done from empty vainglory, not upon the solid ground of love; for, speaking of the praises of charity, he says, “If I distribute all my goods to the poor, and if I deliver up my body to be burned, but have not charity, it profits me nothing.”
Is it possible for a man to do this without charity?
It is. For those who have divided unity are persons who do not have charity.

Look there, and you will see many giving much to the poor; you will see others prepared to welcome death, so much so that where there is no persecutor they cast themselves down headlong: these, doubtless, do this without charity.
Let us come back, then, to conscience, of which the apostle says: “For our boasting is this, the testimony of our conscience.”
Let us come back to conscience, of which the same apostle says, “But let each one prove his own work, and then he shall have boasting in himself, and not in another.”
Therefore let each one of us “prove his own work,” whether it flows forth from the vein of charity, whether it is from charity as the root that his good works sprout forth as branches.
“But let each one prove his own work, and then he shall have boasting in himself, and not in another”—not when another’s tongue bears witness to him, but when his own conscience bears it.
3. This, then, is what he enforces here.
“By this we know that we are of the truth, when in deed and in truth” we love, “not only in word and in tongue: and assure our heart before Him.”
What does “before Him” mean?

Where He sees. Hence the Lord Himself says in the Gospel: “Take heed that you do not do your righteousness before men, to be seen by them; otherwise you have no reward with your Father who is in heaven.”
And what does “Do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing” mean, except that the right hand means a pure conscience, and the left hand the lust of the world?
Many through lust of the world do many wonderful things: the left hand works, not the right.
The right hand ought to work, and without the knowledge of the left hand, so that lust of the world may not even mix itself in when by love we do anything that is good.
And where do we come to know this?
You are before God: question your heart, see what you have done, and what your aim was in it—your salvation, or the windy praise of men.
Look within, for man cannot judge whom he cannot see.
If “we assure our heart,” let it be “before Him.”
Because “if our heart thinks ill of us”—that is, accuses us within, that we do not do the thing with the mind with which it ought to be done—“God is greater than our heart, and knows all things.”
You hide your heart from man: hide it from God if you can!
How will you hide it from Him, to whom a sinner, fearing and confessing, says, “Where shall I go from Your Spirit? And from Your face where shall I flee?”
He sought a way to flee, to escape the judgment of God, and found none.
For where is God not?
“If I ascend,” he says, “into heaven, You are there; if I descend into hell, You are there.”
Where will you go? Where will you flee?
Will you hear counsel?
If you would flee from Him, flee to Him.
Flee to Him by confessing, not from Him by hiding: hide you cannot, but confess you can.
Say to Him, “You are my place of refuge”; and let love be nourished in you, which alone leads to life.
Let your conscience bear you witness that your love is of God.
If it is of God, do not wish to display it before men; because neither men’s praises lift you up to heaven, nor their censures put you down from there.
Let Him see, who crowns you: let Him be your witness, by whom as judge you are crowned.
“God is greater than our heart, and knows all things.”
4. “Beloved, if our heart does not think ill of us, we have confidence toward God.” What does “If our heart does not think ill” mean?

If it answers us truly that we love and that there is genuine love in us—not feigned but sincere, seeking a brother’s salvation, expecting no gain from a brother, but only his salvation—“we have confidence toward God; and whatever we ask, we shall receive from Him, because we keep His commandments.” Therefore, not in the sight of men, but where God Himself sees, in the heart—“we have confidence,” then, “toward God; and whatever we ask, we shall receive from Him”—but only because we keep His commandments.
What are “His commandments”?
Must we always be repeating?
“A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another.”
It is charity itself that he speaks of; it is this that he enforces.

Whoever, then, has brotherly charity, and has it before God, where God sees, and whose heart, when questioned under righteous examination, gives him no other answer than that the genuine root of charity is there for good fruits to come from—that man has confidence with God, and whatever he asks, he shall receive from Him, because he keeps His commandments.

5. Here a question meets us: for it is not this or that man, or you or I, who come into question—for if I have asked anything of God and do not receive it, anyone may easily say of me, “He does not have charity”; and of any man whatever of this present time this may easily be said; and let anyone think what he will, a man of a man—not we, but rather those come into question, those men of whom it is known on all sides that they were saints when they wrote, and that they are now with God.

Where is the man who has charity, if Paul did not have it, who said, “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians, our heart is enlarged; you are not restricted by us”; who said, “I will myself be spent for your souls”; and so great was the grace in him that it was made plain that he had charity.
And yet we find that he asked and did not receive.
What do we say, brethren?
It is a question: look attentively to God; this too is a great question.
