Just as, where it was said of sin, “He who is born of God does not sin,” we found this sin to be the violation of charity, and that this was the thing strictly meant in that place, so too we now ask what it is that he means to say.
For if you look only at the words, it seems plain; if you take the examples into account, it is obscure.
Nothing can be plainer than the words here.
“And whatever we ask, we shall receive from Him, because we keep His commandments and do those things that are pleasing in His sight.”
“Whatever we ask,” he says, “we shall receive from Him.”
He has pressed us sorely.

In the other place also he would have pressed us hard, if he meant all sin; but there we found room to explain it in this way, that he meant it of a certain sin, not of all sin; yet of a sin which “whoever is born of God does not commit”; and we found that this same sin is none other than the violation of charity.
We also have a clear example from the Gospel, when the Lord says, “If I had not come, they would not have had sin.”
How? Were the Jews innocent when He came to them, because He speaks this way?
Then if He had not come, would they have had no sin?
Then did the Physician’s presence make a man sick, and not take away the fever?
What madman would even say this?
He came for no other purpose than to cure and heal the sick.
Therefore when He said, “If I had not come, they would not have had sin,” what would He have us understand, but a certain sin in particular?
For there was a sin which the Jews would not have had.
What sin? That they did not believe in Him, that when He had come they despised Him.

As then He said “sin” there, and it does not follow that we are to understand all sin, but a certain sin, so here also not all sin, lest it contradict that place where he says, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us”; but a certain sin in particular, that is, the violation of charity.

But in this place he has bound us more tightly: “If we ask,” he has said, “if our heart does not accuse us, and answers us in the sight of God that true love is in us”; “Whatever we ask, we shall receive from Him.”
6. Well now: I have already told you, my beloved brethren, let no one turn toward us.
For what are we? Or what are you?
What, but the Church of God, which is known to all?
And, if it pleases Him, we are in that Church; and those of us who abide in it by love, let us persevere there, if we would show the love we have.
But then the apostle Paul—what evil are we to think of him?
He not love the brethren!
He not have within himself the testimony of his conscience in the sight of God!
Paul not have within him that root of charity from which all good fruits proceeded!
What madman would say this?
Well then: where do we find that the apostle asked and did not receive?
He says himself: “Lest I should be lifted up beyond measure through the abundance of the revelations, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, an angel of Satan to strike me.
For this thing I pleaded with the Lord three times, that He would take it from me.
And He said to me, My grace is sufficient for you: for strength is made perfect in weakness.”
See, he was not heard in his prayer that the “angel of Satan” should be taken from him.
But why? Because it was not good for him.
He was heard, then, for salvation, when he was not heard according to his wish.
Know, my beloved, a great mystery, which we urge on your consideration on purpose that it may not slip away from you in your temptations.

The saints are in all things heard for salvation: they are always heard in what concerns their eternal salvation; it is this that they desire, because in regard to this their prayers are always heard.
7. But let us distinguish God’s different ways of hearing prayer.
For we find some not heard for their wish, but heard for salvation; and again we find some heard for their wish, but not heard for salvation.
Mark this difference; hold fast this example of a man not heard for his wish but heard for salvation.
Hear the apostle Paul; for God Himself showed him what the hearing of prayer for salvation is: “Sufficient for you,” He says, “is My grace; for strength is perfected in weakness.”

You have pleaded, have cried out, have cried out three times: the very cry you raised I heard once for all; I did not turn My ears away from you; I know what I should do: you would have it taken away, the healing thing by which you are burned; I know the infirmity by which you are burdened.
Well then: here is a man who was heard for salvation, while as to his will he was not heard.
Where do we find persons heard for their will, but not heard for salvation?
Do we find, do you think, some wicked, some ungodly man, heard by God for his will, but not heard for salvation?

If I put before you the instance of some man, perhaps you will say to me, “It is you who call him wicked, for he was righteous; had he not been righteous, his prayer would not have been heard by God.”
The instance I am about to bring forward is of one whose iniquity and ungodliness no one can doubt.
The devil himself: he asked for Job, and received.
Have you not also heard here concerning the devil, that “he who commits sin is of the devil”?
Not that the devil created him, but that the sinner imitates him.
Is it not said of him, “He did not stand in the truth”?
Is not he even “that old serpent,” who through the woman offered the first man the drink of poison?
Who even in the case of Job kept his wife for him, so that by her the husband might be, not comforted, but tempted?
The devil asked for a holy man, to tempt him, and he received; the apostle asked that the thorn in the flesh might be taken from him, and he did not receive.
But the apostle was heard more than the devil.
For the apostle was heard for salvation, though not for his wish; the devil was heard for his wish, but for damnation.
For Job was yielded up to him to be tempted in order that, by Job’s standing the test, the devil should be tormented.
But this, my brethren, we find not only in the books of the Old Testament, but also in the Gospel.
The demons begged the Lord, when He drove them out of the man, that they might be permitted to go into the swine.
Did the Lord not have power to tell them not to approach even those creatures?
For had it not been His will to permit this, they were not going to rebel against the King of heaven and earth.
But with a view to a certain mystery, with a certain deeper meaning, He let the demons go into the swine: to show that the devil has dominion in those who lead the life of swine.
The demons, then, were heard in their request; was the apostle not heard?
Or rather (what is truer) shall we say, The apostle was heard, the demons were not heard?
Their will was carried out; his welfare was perfected.
8. In keeping with this, we ought to understand that God, though He does not give to our will, does give for our salvation.
For suppose the thing you have asked for is to your hurt, and the Physician knows that it is to your hurt; what then?
It is not to be said that the physician does not listen to you when, perhaps, you ask for cold water, and if it is good for you, he gives it immediately; if it is not good, he does not give it.
Had he no ears for your request, or rather, did he listen for your welfare, even when he opposed your will?
Then let there be charity in you, my brethren; let it be in you, and then set your minds at rest: even when the thing you ask for is not given you, your prayer is granted—only you do not know it.
Many have been given over into their own hands, to their own hurt; of whom the apostle says, “God gave them up to the lusts of their own hearts.”
Some man has asked for a great sum of money; he has received it, to his hurt.
When he did not have it, he had little to fear; no sooner had he come to have it than he became a prey to the more powerful.
Was not that man’s request granted to his own hurt, who insisted on having that for which he would be hunted by the robber, whereas, being poor, no one hunted him?
Learn to plead with God in such a way that you commit it to the Physician to do what He knows best.
You confess the disease; let Him apply the means of healing.
Only hold fast to charity.
For He must cut, He must burn; what if you cry out, and are not spared for your crying under the cutting, under the burning and the tribulation? Yet He knows how far the rottenness reaches.
You would have Him take off His hands even now, and He considers only the depth of the sore; He knows how far to go.
He does not attend to you for your will, but He does attend to you for your healing.

Be sure, then, my brethren, that what the apostle says is true: “For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself intercedes for us with groanings that cannot be uttered: for He intercedes for the saints.”
How is it said, “The Spirit itself intercedes for the saints,” except as meaning the charity which is worked in you by the Spirit?
For this is why the same apostle says: “The charity of God is poured out in our hearts by the Holy Spirit who is given to us.”
It is charity that groans, it is charity that prays: against it He who gave it cannot shut His ears.
Set your minds at rest: let charity ask, and the ears of God are there.
Not what you wish is done, but what is advantageous is done.

Therefore, “whatever we ask,” he says, “we shall receive from Him.” I have already said: if you understand it to mean “for salvation,” there is no question; if not for salvation, there is a question, and a great one—a question that makes you an accuser of the apostle Paul.
“Whatever we ask, we receive from Him, because we keep His commandments and do these things that are pleasing in His sight”: within, where He sees.
9. And what are those commandments?
“This,” he says, “is His commandment, that we should believe on the name of His Son Jesus Christ, and love one another.”
You see that this is the commandment; you see that whoever does anything against this commandment commits the sin from which “everyone who is born of God” is free.
“As He gave us commandment”: that we love one another.
“And he who keeps His commandment”—you see that nothing else is commanded us than that we love one another—“and he who keeps His commandment shall abide in Him, and He in him.”
“And by this we know that He abides in us, by the Spirit whom He has given us.
Is it not plain that this is what the Holy Spirit works in a man, that there should be love and charity in him?
Is it not plain, as the apostle Paul says, that “the love of God is poured out in our hearts by the Holy Spirit who is given to us”?
For [our apostle] was speaking of charity, and was saying that we ought to question our own heart in the sight of God.
“But if our heart does not think ill of us”: that is, if it confesses that whatever is done in us in any good work is done from the love of our brother.
And then besides, in speaking of the commandment, he says this: “This is His commandment, that we should believe on the name of His Son Jesus Christ, and love one another, as He gave us commandment.”
“And he who does His commandment abides in Him, and He in him.
By this we know that He abides in us, by the Spirit whom He has given us.”
If in truth you find that you have charity, you have the Spirit of God in order to understand: for it is a very necessary thing.
10. In the earliest times, “the Holy Spirit fell upon those who believed, and they spoke with tongues,” which they had not learned, “as the Spirit gave them utterance.”
These were signs suited to the time.
For there had to be that sign of the Holy Spirit in all tongues, to show that the Gospel of God was to run through all tongues over the whole earth.
That thing was done as a sign, and it passed away.
In the laying on of hands now, that persons may receive the Holy Spirit, do we expect them to speak with tongues?

Or when we laid our hands on these infants, did each one of you watch to see whether they would speak with tongues, and, when he saw that they did not speak with tongues, was any of you so wrong-minded as to say, These have not received the Holy Spirit; for had they received Him, they would speak with tongues, as was the case in those times?
If then the witness of the presence of the Holy Spirit is not now given through these miracles, by what is it given? By what does one come to know that he has received the Holy Spirit?
Let him question his own heart.
If he loves his brother, the Spirit of God dwells in him.
Let him look, let him test himself before the eyes of God; let him see whether there is in him the love of peace and unity, the love of the Church that is spread over the whole earth.
Let him not rest only in loving the brother whom he has before his eyes, for we have many brethren whom we do not see, and in the unity of the Spirit we are joined to them.
What wonder that they are not with us?
We are in one body; we have one Head, in heaven.
Brethren, our two eyes do not see each other; as one might say, they do not know each other.
But in the charity of the bodily frame do they not know each other?
For, to show you that in the charity which knits them together they do know each other: when both eyes are open, the right cannot rest on any object on which the left will not rest likewise.
Direct the glance of the right eye without the other, if you can.
Together they meet in one object, together they are directed to one object: their aim is one, their places are different.
If then all who love God with you have one aim with you, do not heed that in the body you are separated in place; you have alike fixed the eyesight of the heart on the light of truth.
Then if you would know that you have received the Spirit, question your heart, lest perhaps you have the sacrament and do not have the virtue of the sacrament.
Question your heart. If love of your brethren is there, set your mind at rest.
There cannot be love without the Spirit of God, since Paul cries, “The love of God is poured out in your hearts by the Holy Spirit who is given to us.”
11. “Beloved, do not believe every spirit.”
Because he had said, “By this we know that He abides in us, by the Spirit whom He has given us.”
But how this same Spirit is known, mark this: “Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are from God.”
And who is he who tests the spirits?
A hard matter he has put before us, my brethren!
It is well for us that he should tell us himself how we are to discern them.
He is about to tell us; do not fear; but first see—mark—see that here is expressed the very thing that vain heretics taunt us with.
Mark, see what he says: “Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are from God.”
The Holy Spirit is spoken of in the Gospel by the name of water, where the Lord “cried out and said, If anyone thirsts, let him come to Me and drink.
He who believes in Me, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.”
But the evangelist has explained what He said this about; for he goes on to say, “But this He spoke of the Spirit, whom those who believed in Him would receive.”
Why did the Lord not baptize many?
But what does he say?
“For the Holy Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus was not yet glorified.”

Then, seeing that those had baptism, and had not yet received the Holy Spirit, whom the Lord sent from heaven on the day of Pentecost, the glorifying of the Lord was first waited for, so that the Spirit might be given.

Even before He was glorified, and before He sent the Spirit, He still invited men to prepare themselves to receive the water of which He said, “Whoever thirsts, let him come and drink”; and, “He who believes in Me, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.”
What does “Rivers of living water” mean?
What is that water?
Let no one ask me; ask the Gospel.
“But this,” it says, “He said of the Spirit, whom those who should believe in Him would receive.”
Consequently, the water of the sacrament is one thing; the water which signifies the Spirit of God is another.
The water of the sacrament is visible; the water of the Spirit is invisible.
That washes the body, and signifies what is done in the soul.
By this Spirit the soul itself is cleansed and fed.
This is the Spirit of God, which heretics and all who cut themselves off from the Church cannot have.
And whoever do not openly cut themselves off, but are cut off by iniquity, and, being within, whirl about as chaff and are not grain—these do not have this Spirit.

This Spirit is denoted by the Lord under the name of water; and we have heard from this epistle, “Do not believe every spirit”; and those words of Solomon bear witness, “Keep yourself far from strange water.”
What does “water” mean? Spirit.
Does water always signify spirit?

Not always: but in some places it signifies the Spirit, in some places it signifies baptism, in some places it signifies peoples, in some places it signifies counsel; thus you find it said in a certain place, “Counsel is a fountain of life to those who possess it.”
So then, in different places of the Scriptures, the term “water” signifies different things.

Now, however, you have heard the Holy Spirit spoken of by the term water, not by an interpretation of ours but by the witness of the Gospel, where it says, “But this He said of the Spirit, whom those who should believe in Him would receive.”

If then the Holy Spirit is signified by the name of water, and this epistle says to us, “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are of God,” let us understand that it is of this that it is said, “Keep yourself far from strange water, and do not drink from a strange fountain.”
What does “Do not drink from a strange fountain” mean?
Do not believe a strange spirit.
12. There remains, then, the test by which it is to be proved to be the Spirit of God.
He has indeed set down a sign, and this, perhaps, a difficult one; let us see, however.
We are to return to that charity; it is that which teaches us, because it is the anointing.
However, what does he say here?
“Test the spirits, whether they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out into this world.”
Here now are all the heretics and all the schismatics.
How then am I to test the spirit?
He goes on: “By this the Spirit of God is known.”
Wake up the ears of your heart.
We were at a loss; we were saying, Who knows? Who discerns?
Behold, he is about to tell the sign.

“By this the Spirit of God is known: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is of God; and every spirit that does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is not of God; and this is the antichrist, of whom you have heard that he would come; and even now he is already in this world.”
Our ears, so to speak, are on the alert for discerning the spirits; and we have been told something by which we discern not a bit the more.
For what does he say?
“Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ came in the flesh is of God.”
Then is the spirit that is among the heretics of God, seeing they “confess that Jesus Christ came in the flesh”?

Yes, here perhaps they rise up against us and say: You do not have the Spirit from God; but we confess “that Jesus Christ came in the flesh”; and the apostle here has said that those do not have the Spirit of God who do not confess “that Jesus Christ came in the flesh.”

Ask the Arians: they confess “that Jesus Christ came in the flesh”; ask the Eunomians: they confess “that Jesus Christ came in the flesh”; ask the Macedonians: they confess “that Jesus Christ came in the flesh”; put the question to the Cataphryges: they confess “that Jesus Christ came in the flesh”; put it to the Novatians: they confess “that Jesus Christ came in the flesh.”
Then do all these heresies have the Spirit of God?
Are they then no false prophets?
Is there then no deception there, no seduction there?
Assuredly they are antichrists; for “they went out from us, but they were not of us.”
13. What are we to do then?
By what are we to discern them?
Be very attentive; let us go together in heart, and knock.
Charity herself keeps watch; for it is none other than she who shall knock, and she also who shall open: soon you shall understand, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
You have already heard that it was said above, “Whoever denies that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, the same is an antichrist.”
There also we asked, Who denies? For neither do we deny, nor do they deny.
And we found that some deny in their deeds; and we brought testimony from the apostle, who says, “For they profess that they know God, but in their deeds they deny Him.”
So then let us now also make the inquiry in the deeds, not in the tongue.
What is the spirit that is not from God?
That “which denies that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.”
And what is the spirit that is from God?
That “which confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.”
Who is he who confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh?
Now, brethren, to the point! Let us look to the works, and not stop at the noise of the tongue.
Let us ask why Christ came in the flesh; so we shall get at the persons who deny that He has come in the flesh.
If you stop at tongues, why, you will hear many a heresy confessing that Christ has come in the flesh; but the truth convicts those men.
Why did Christ come in the flesh?
Was He not God?
Is it not written of Him, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”?
Was it not He who fed the angels? Is it not He who feeds the angels?
Did He not come here in such a way that He did not depart from there?
Did He not ascend in such a way that He did not forsake us?
Why then did He come in the flesh?
Because it was necessary for us to have the hope of resurrection shown to us.
He was God, and He came in flesh; for God could not die, flesh could die; He came then in the flesh, that He might die for us.
But how did He die for us?
“Greater charity than this no man has, that a man lay down his life for his friends.”
Charity therefore brought Him to the flesh.
Whoever therefore does not have charity denies that Christ has come in the flesh.
Here, then, question all heretics now.
Did Christ come in the flesh?
“He did come; this I believe, this I confess.”
No, this you deny.
“How do I deny it?
You hear me say it!”
No, I convict you of denying it.
You say it with the voice, deny it with the heart; say it in words, deny it in deeds.
“How,” you say, “do I deny it in deeds?”
Because the end for which Christ came in the flesh was that He might die for us.
He died for us, because in this He taught much charity.
“Greater charity than this no man has, that a man lay down his life for his friends.”
You do not have charity, seeing that for your own honor you divide unity.
Therefore by this understand the spirit that is from God.
Give the earthen vessels a tap; put them to the test, whether perhaps they are cracked and give a dull sound; see whether they ring full and clear, see whether charity is there.
You take yourself away from the unity of the whole earth, you divide the Church by schisms, you tear apart the Body of Christ.
He came in the flesh to gather into one; you raise an outcry to scatter abroad.
This, then, is the Spirit of God, which says that Jesus has come in the flesh; which says it, not in tongue but in deeds; which says it, not by making a noise but by loving.
And that spirit is not of God which denies that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh; denies, here also, not in tongue but in life; not in words but in deeds.
It is plain therefore by what we may know the brethren.
Many who are inside are inside only in a sense; but no one is outside unless he is truly outside.
14. Indeed, and so that you may know that he has referred the matter to deeds, he says, “And every spirit, qui solvit Christum, which does away with Christ that He came in the flesh, is not of God.”
A doing away in deeds is meant.
What has he shown you?
“That denies”: in that he says, “does away with” (or, “unmakes”).
He came to gather into one; you come to unmake.
You would pull Christ’s members apart.
How can it be said that you do not deny that Christ has come in the flesh, you who tear apart the Church of God which He has gathered together?
Therefore you go against Christ; you are an antichrist.
Whether you are inside or outside, you are an antichrist: only, when you are inside, you are hidden; when you are outside, you are made manifest.
You unmake Jesus and deny that He came in the flesh; you are not of God.
Therefore He says in the Gospel: “Whoever shall break one of these least commandments, and shall teach so, shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven.”
What is this breaking?
What is this teaching? A breaking in the deeds, and a teaching, as it were, in words.
“You who preach that men should not steal, do you steal?”
Therefore he who steals breaks or undoes the commandment in his deed, and as it were teaches so: “he shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven,” that is, in the Church of this present time.
Of him it is said, “What they say, do; but what they do, do not do.
But he who shall do and shall teach so shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven.”

From this, that He has said here fecerit, “shall do,” while in contrast to this He said there solverit, meaning non fecerit, “shall not do, and shall teach so”—to break, then, is not to do—what does He teach us, but that we should examine men’s deeds, and not take their words on trust?

The obscurity of the matters compels us to speak at great length, chiefly so that what the Lord deigns to reveal may be brought within reach even of the brethren of slower understanding, because all were bought by the blood of Christ.
And I am afraid the epistle itself will not be finished during these days, as I promised; but as the Lord wills, it is better to reserve the remainder than to overload your hearts with too much food.
“Now you are of God, little children, and have overcome him, because greater is He who is in you than he who is in this world.
They are of the world; therefore they speak of the world, and the world hears them.
We are of God; he who knows God hears us; he who is not of God does not hear us.
From this we know the spirit of truth, and [the spirit] of error.
Dearly beloved, let us love one another, for love is of God; and everyone who loves is born of God, and knows God.
He who does not love does not know God, for God is love.
In this the love of God was made manifest in us, that God sent His only-begotten Son into this world, that we may live through Him.
In this is love, not that we loved, but that He loved us, and sent His Son to be the Atoner for our sins.
Dearly beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.
No man has seen God at any time.”
1. This world is to all the faithful who are seeking their own country what the desert was to the people of Israel.
They were indeed still wandering, and were seeking their own country; but with God as their guide they could not wander astray.
Their way was God’s command.
For though they went about for forty years, the journey itself is made up of very few stages, and is known to all.
They were delayed because they were in training, not because they were forsaken.

That, therefore, which God promises us is an indescribable sweetness and a good, as the Scripture says, and as you have often heard us repeat, which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man.”
But we are exercised by temporal labors, and trained by the temptations of this present life.
However, if you would not die of thirst in this wilderness, drink charity.
It is the fountain which God has been pleased to place here, so that we do not faint on the way; and we shall drink of it more abundantly when we have come to our own land.
The Gospel has just been read; now, to speak of the very words with which the reading ended, what else did you hear but concerning charity?
For we have made an agreement with our God in prayer, that if we would have Him forgive us our sins, we also should forgive the sins which may have been committed against us.
Now that which forgives is none other than charity.
Take charity away from the heart; hatred possesses it; it does not know how to forgive.
Let charity be there, and she forgives fearlessly, not being cramped.
And this whole epistle which we have undertaken to explain to you—see whether it commends anything else than this one thing, charity.
Nor need we fear that by much speaking of it, it may come to be hateful.
For what is there to love, if charity comes to be hateful?
It is by charity that other things come to be rightly loved; then how must it itself be loved!
Therefore let not that which ought never to depart from the heart depart from the tongue.
2. “Now,” he says, “you are of God, little children, and have overcome him”: whom but Antichrist?
For above he had said, “Whoever unmakes Jesus Christ and denies that He has come in the flesh is not of God.”
Now we explained, if you remember, that all those who violate charity deny that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.

For Jesus had no need to come except because of charity; as indeed the charity we are commending is that which the Lord Himself commends in the Gospel: “Greater love than this no man can have, that a man lay down his life for his friends.”
How was it possible for the Son of God to lay down His life for us without putting on flesh in which He might die?

Whoever therefore violates charity, let him say what he will with his tongue, his life denies that Christ has come in the flesh; and this is an antichrist, wherever he may be, by whatever way he has come in.
But what does the apostle say to those who are citizens of that country for which we sigh?
“You have overcome him.”
And by what have they overcome?
“Because greater is He who is in you than he who is in this world.”

Lest they should attribute the victory to their own strength, and be overcome by the arrogance of pride (for whomever the devil makes proud, he overcomes), wishing them to keep humility, what does he say?
“You have overcome him.”
Every man now, on hearing this saying, “You have overcome,” lifts up his head, lifts up his neck, wishes himself to be praised.
Do not exalt yourself; see who it is that has overcome in you.
Why have you overcome?
“Because greater is He who is in you than he who is in the world.”
Be humble, carry your Lord; be the beast for Him to sit on.
It is good for you that He should rule, and He guide.
For if you do not have Him to sit on you, you may lift up your neck, you may kick out your heels; but woe to you without a ruler, for this liberty sends you among the wild beasts to be devoured!
3. “These are of the world.”
Who? The antichrists. You have already heard who they are.
And if you are not such, you know them; but whoever is such does not know.
“These are of the world; therefore they speak of the world, and the world hears them.”
Who are they who “speak of the world”?
Mark who are against charity.
Behold, you have heard the Lord saying, “If you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your trespasses.
But if you do not forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.”
It is the sentence of Truth; or if it is not Truth that speaks, contradict it.
If you are a Christian and believe Christ, He has said, “I am the truth.”
This sentence is true, is firm.
Now hear men who “speak of the world.”
“And will you not avenge yourself?
And will you let him say that he has done this to you?
No: let him feel that he has to deal with a man.”
Every day such things are said. Those who say such things, “of the world they speak, and the world hears them.”
None say such things but those who love the world, and such things are heard by none but those who love the world.
And you have heard that to love the world and neglect charity is to deny that Jesus came in the flesh.

Or say whether the Lord Himself in the flesh did that? Whether, when struck, He willed to be avenged? Whether, hanging on the cross, He did not say, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do”?
But if He did not threaten, who had the power, why do you threaten, why are you puffed up with anger, you who are under the power of another?
He died because it was His will to die, yet He did not threaten; you do not know when you will die, and do you threaten?
4. “We are of God.”
Let us see why; see whether it is for any other reason than charity.
“We are of God: he who knows God hears us; he who is not of God does not hear us.
By this we know the spirit of truth, and of error”: namely by this, that he who hears us has the spirit of truth; he who does not hear us has the spirit of error.
Let us see what he advises, and let us choose rather to hear him advising in the spirit of truth, and not antichrists, not lovers of the world, not the world.
If we are born of God, “beloved,” he goes on—see above from what point: “We are of God: he who knows God hears us; he who is not of God does not hear us.

By this we know the spirit of truth, and of error”: yes, now he makes us eagerly attentive: to be told that he who knows God hears, but he who does not know Him does not hear; and that this is the discerning between the spirit of truth and the spirit of error: well then, let us see what he is about to advise; in what we must hear him—“Beloved, let us love one another.”
Why? Because a man advises it?
“Because love is of God.”
He has greatly commended love, in that he has said, “Is of God”: but he is going to say more; let us hear eagerly.
So far he has said, “Love is of God; and everyone who loves is born of God, and knows God.
He who does not love does not know God.”
Why? “For God is love” [Love is God].
What more could be said, brethren?

If nothing were said in praise of love throughout the pages of this epistle, if nothing whatever throughout the other pages of the Scriptures, and this one thing only were all we were told by the voice of the Spirit of God, “For Love is God,” we ought to require nothing more.
5. Now see that to act against love is to act against God.
Let no one say, “I sin against man when I do not love my brother (mark it!), and sin against man is a thing to be taken lightly; only let me not sin against God.”
How do you not sin against God, when you sin against love?
“Love is God.” Do “we” say this?
If we said, “Love is God,” perhaps one of you might be offended and say, What has he said?
What did he mean by saying that “Love is God”?
God “gave” love; as a gift God bestowed love.
“Love is of God: Love IS God.”

Look, here you have, brethren, the Scriptures of God: this epistle is canonical; it is read aloud throughout all nations, it is held by the authority of the whole earth, it has built up the whole earth.
Here you are told by the Spirit of God, “Love is God.”
Now, if you dare, go against God, and refuse to love your brother!
6. In what sense, then, was it said a while ago, “Love is of God,” and now, “Love IS God”?
For God is Father and Son and Holy Spirit: the Son, God of God; the Holy Spirit, God of God; and these three are one God, not three Gods.
If the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, and that person loves in whom the Holy Spirit dwells: therefore “Love is God”; but “IS God,” because “Of God.”
For you have both in the epistle; both “Love is of God,” and “Love is God.”
Of the Father alone the Scripture does not say that He is “of God”; but when you hear that expression, “Of God,” either the Son is meant, or the Holy Spirit.
Because while the apostle says, “The love of God is poured out in our hearts by the Holy Spirit who is given to us,” let us understand that He who subsists in love is the Holy Spirit.
For it is this very Holy Spirit, whom the wicked cannot receive; He is that Fountain of which the Scripture says, “Let the fountain of your water be your own, and let no stranger share it with you.”
For all who do not love God are strangers, are antichrists.
And though they come to the churches, they cannot be numbered among the children of God; that Fountain of life does not belong to them.
To have baptism is possible even for a bad man; to have prophecy is possible even for a bad man.
We find that King Saul had prophecy: he was persecuting holy David, yet he was filled with the spirit of prophecy and began to prophesy.
To receive the sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord is possible even for a bad man: for of such it is said, “He who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself.”
To have the name of Christ is possible even for a bad man; that is, even a bad man can be called a Christian: like those of whom it is said, “They polluted the name of their God.”
I say, to have all these sacraments is possible even for a bad man; but to have charity and to be a bad man is not possible.
This, then, is the special gift; this is the “Fountain” that is uniquely one’s “own.”
The Spirit of God urges you to drink of this; the Spirit of God urges you to drink of Himself.
7. “In this the love of God was made manifest in us.”
See, in order that we may love God, we have exhortation.
Could we love Him, unless He first loved us?
If we were slow to love, let us not be slow to love in return.
He loved us first; not even so do we love.

He loved the unrighteous, but He did away with the unrighteousness: He loved the unrighteous, but He did not gather them together to unrighteousness: He loved the sick, but He visited them to make them well.
“Love,” then, “is God.”
“In this the love of God was made manifest in us, because God sent His only-begotten Son into the world, that we might live through Him.”

As the Lord Himself says: “Greater love than this no man can have, that a man lay down his life for his friends”: and there the love of Christ toward us was proved, in that He died for us: how is the love of the Father toward us proved?

In that He “sent His only Son” to die for us: so also the apostle Paul says: “He who did not spare His own Son, but delivered Him up for us all, how has He not with Him also freely given us all things?”
See, the Father delivered up Christ; Judas delivered Him up; does it not seem as if the thing done were of the same kind?
Judas is a “traditor,” one who delivered up [or, a traitor]: is God the Father that?
God forbid! you say.
I do not say it, but the apostle says, “He who did not spare His own Son, but ‘tradidit Eum,’ delivered Him up for us all.”
Both the Father delivered Him up, and He delivered up Himself.
The same apostle says: “Who loved me, and delivered Himself up for me.”
If the Father delivered up the Son, and the Son delivered up Himself, what has Judas done?

There was a “traditio” (delivering up) by the Father; there was a “traditio” by the Son; there was a “traditio” by Judas: the thing done is the same, but what is it that distinguishes the Father delivering up the Son, the Son delivering up Himself, and Judas the disciple delivering up his Master?
This: that the Father and the Son did it in love, but Judas did it in treacherous betrayal.
You see that what a man does is not the thing to be considered, but with what mind and will he does it.
We find God the Father in the same deed in which we find Judas; the Father we bless, Judas we detest.
Why do we bless the Father, and detest Judas?
We bless charity; we detest iniquity.
How great a good was conferred on mankind by the delivering up of Christ!
Did Judas have this in his thoughts, that he therefore delivered Him up?
God had in His thoughts our salvation, by which we were redeemed; Judas had in his thoughts the price for which he sold the Lord.
The Son Himself had in His thoughts the price He gave for us; Judas, in his, the price he received to sell Him.
The different intention, therefore, makes the things done different.

Though the thing is one, yet if we measure it by the different intentions, we find the one a thing to be loved, the other to be condemned; the one we find a thing to be glorified, the other to be detested.
Such is the power of charity.
See that it alone discriminates; it alone distinguishes the deeds of men.
8. This we have said in the case where the things done are similar.
In the case where they are different, we find a man made fierce by charity, and made winningly gentle by iniquity.
A father beats a boy, and a child-stealer caresses one.
If you name the two things, blows and caresses, who would not choose the caresses and decline the blows?
If you mark the persons, it is charity that beats, iniquity that caresses.
See what we are insisting upon: that the deeds of men are discerned only by the root of charity.
For many things may be done that have a good appearance, and yet do not proceed from the root of charity.
For thorns also have flowers: some actions truly seem rough, seem savage; yet they are done for discipline at the bidding of charity.

Once for all, then, a short precept is given you: Love, and do what you will: whether you hold your peace, hold your peace through love; whether you cry out, cry out through love; whether you correct, correct through love; whether you spare, spare through love: let the root of love be within; from this root nothing can spring but what is good.

9. “In this is love—in this the love of God toward us was made manifest, because God sent His only-begotten Son into this world, that we might live through Him.—In this is love, not that we loved God, but that He loved us”: we did not love Him first: for to this end He loved us, that we might love Him: “And sent His Son to be the Atoner for our sins”: “litatorem,” that is, one who sacrifices.
He sacrificed for our sins.
Where did He find the sacrifice?
Where did He find the victim which He would offer pure?
Other He found none; His own self He offered.
“Beloved, if God so loved us, we ought also to love one another.
Peter,” He says, “do you love me?”
And he said, “I love.”
“Feed my sheep.”
10. “No one has seen God at any time”: He is a thing invisible; not with the eye but with the heart must He be sought.
But just as, if we wished to see the sun, we would cleanse the eye of the body, so, wishing to see God, let us cleanse the eye by which God can be seen.
Where is this eye?
Hear the Gospel: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.”
But let no one imagine God for himself according to the lust of his eyes.

For so he makes for himself either a huge form, or a certain incalculable magnitude which, like the light he sees with his bodily eyes, he makes extend in all directions; field after field of space he gives it all the bigness he can; or he represents it to himself as if it were an old man of venerable form.
Do not imagine any of these things.
There is something you may imagine, if you would see God: “God is love.”
What sort of face has love? What form has it? What stature? What feet? What hands has it? No one can say.

And yet it has feet, for these carry men to church; it has hands, for these reach out to the poor; it has eyes, for by them we consider the needy: “Blessed is the man,” it is said, “who considers the needy and the poor.”
It has ears, of which the Lord says, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”
These are not members distinct in place; but he who has charity sees the whole at once with the understanding.
Inhabit, and you shall be inhabited; dwell, and you shall be dwelt in.
For what do you say, my brethren? Who loves what he does not see?
Now why, when charity is praised, do you lift up your hands, shout acclaim, praise?
What have I shown you?
What I brought forth, was it a gleam of colors?
What I set before you, was it gold and silver?
Have I dug out jewels from hidden treasures?
What of this sort have I shown to your eyes?
Is my face changed while I speak?
I am in the flesh; I am in the same form in which I came out to you; you are in the same form in which you came here: charity is praised, and you shout applause.
Certainly you see nothing.
But as it pleases you when you praise, so let it please you to keep it in your heart.
For mark well what I say, brethren; I urge you all, as God enables me, toward a great treasure.

If a beautiful little vase were shown you, embossed, inlaid with gold, finely wrought, and it charmed your eyes, and drew toward it the eager desire of your heart, and you were pleased with the hand of the craftsman, and the weight of the silver, and the splendor of the metal, would not each one of you say, “O, if only I had that vase!”
And you would say it to no purpose, for it would not be in your power to have it.
Or if one should wish to have it, he might think of stealing it from another’s house.
Charity is praised to you; if it pleases you, have it, possess it: there is no need for you to rob anyone, no need for you to think of buying it; it is to be had freely, without cost.
Take it, embrace it; there is nothing sweeter.
If it is such when it is only spoken of, what must it be when one has it?

11. If any of you perhaps wish to keep charity, brethren, above all things do not imagine it to be an abject and sluggish thing; nor that charity is to be preserved by a sort of gentleness—no, not gentleness, but tameness and listlessness.
It is not preserved in that way.

Do not imagine that you love your servant when you do not beat him, or that you love your son when you do not give him discipline, or that you love your neighbor when you do not rebuke him: this is not charity, but mere feebleness.
Let charity be fervent to correct, to amend: but if the conduct is good, let it delight you; if bad, let it be amended, let it be corrected.
Do not love the error in the man, but the man: for God made the man; the man himself made the error.
Love that which God made; do not love that which the man himself made.
When you love that, you take away this; when you value that, you amend this.
But even if you are severe at any time, let it be because of love, for correction.
For this reason charity was signified by the Dove which descended upon the Lord.
That likeness of a dove, the likeness in which the Holy Spirit came, by whom charity was to be poured into us: why was this?
The dove has no gall: yet with beak and wings she fights for her young; hers is a fierceness without bitterness.
And so also does a father; when he chastises his son, he chastises him for discipline.
As I said, the kidnapper, in order that he may sell, lures the child with bitter endearments; a father, in order that he may correct, chastises without gall.
Be such toward all men.

See here, brethren, a great lesson, a great rule: each one of you has children, or wishes to have them; or if he has altogether determined to have no children after the flesh, at least he desires to have children spiritually:—what father does not correct his son? What son does his father not discipline?
And yet he seems to be fierce with him.
It is the fierceness of love, the fierceness of charity: a sort of fierceness without gall, after the manner of the dove, not of the raven.
Hence it came into my mind, my brethren, to tell you that those violators of charity are the ones who have made the schism: as they hate charity itself, so they also hate the dove.
But the dove convicts them: it comes forth from heaven, the heavens open, and it remains on the head of the Lord.
Why this? That John may hear, “This is He who baptizes.”
Away, you robbers; away, you invaders of the possession of Christ!
On your own possessions, where you insist on being lords, you have dared to fix the titles of the great Owner.
He recognizes His own titles; He claims for Himself His own possession.
He does not cancel the titles, but enters in and takes possession.
So in one who comes to the Catholic Church, his baptism is not canceled, so that the title of the commander may not be canceled: but what is done in the Catholic Church?
The title is acknowledged; the Owner enters in under His own titles, where the robber was entering in under titles not his own.
“If we love one another, God abides in us, and His love will be perfected in us.
By this we know that we abide in Him, and He in us, because He has given us of His Spirit.
And we have seen and are witnesses that the Father sent the Son to be the Savior of the world.
Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God.
And we have known and believed the love that God has for us.
God is love; and he who abides in love abides in God, and God abides in him.”
1. Love is a sweet word, but sweeter the deed.

To be always speaking of it is not in our power: for we have many things to do, and various affairs draw us different ways, so that our tongue does not have leisure to be always speaking of love: though indeed our tongue could have nothing better to do.
But though we may not always be speaking of it, we may always keep it.
Just as it is with the Alleluia which we sing at this present time: are we always doing this?
Not for one hour—I do not say for the whole length of it—do we sing Alleluia, but barely for a few moments of one hour, and then we give ourselves to something else.
Now Alleluia, as you already know, means, Praise the Lord.
He who praises God with his tongue cannot be always doing this; he who praises God by his life and conduct can be doing it always.

Works of mercy, affections of charity, sanctity of piety, purity of chastity, modesty of sobriety—these things are always to be practiced: whether we are in public or at home; whether before men or in our room; whether speaking or keeping silent; whether occupied with something or free from occupation: these are always to be kept, because all these virtues which I have named are within.
But who is able to name them all?
There is, as it were, the army of an emperor stationed within, in your mind.
For as an emperor does what he will by his army, so the Lord Jesus Christ, once He begins to dwell in our inner man (that is, in the mind through faith), uses these virtues as His ministers.

And by these virtues, which cannot be seen with the eyes and yet are praised when they are named—and they would not be praised unless they were loved, nor loved unless they were seen; and if not loved unless seen, they are seen with another eye, that is, with the inward beholding of the heart—by these invisible virtues the members are visibly set in motion: the feet to walk, but where? Where they are moved by the good will which serves the good emperor like a soldier: the hands to work; but at what? At that which is commanded by charity, which is inspired within by the Holy Spirit.

The members, then, are seen when they are set in motion; He who orders them within is not seen: and who He is that orders them within is known almost only to Him who orders, and to him who is ordered within.
2. For, brethren, you heard just now when the Gospel was read, at least if you had for it the ear not only of the body but also of the heart.
What did it say? “Take heed that you do not do your righteousness before men, to be seen by them.”
Did He mean to say this, that whatever good things we do, we should hide them from the eyes of men, and be afraid to be seen?
If you fear spectators, you will not have imitators: you ought therefore to be seen.
But you must not do it for the purpose of being seen.
Not there should be the end of your joy, not there the goal of your rejoicing, that you should count yourself to have gained the whole fruit of your good work when you are seen and praised.
This is nothing. Despise yourself when you are praised; let Him be praised in you who works through you.
Therefore do not do the good you do for your own praise, but to the praise of Him from whom you have the power to do good.
From yourself you have the doing of ill; from God you have the doing of good.
On the other hand, look at perverse men, how backward they are.
What they do well, they insist on ascribing to themselves; if they do ill, they insist on accusing God.
Reverse this distorted and backward procedure, which puts the thing, as one might say, head downwards, which makes that lowermost which is uppermost, and that upward which is downward.
Do you want to make God lowermost and yourself uppermost?
You fall headlong; you do not elevate yourself; for He is always above.
What then? You well, and God ill? No, rather say this, if you would speak more truly: I ill, He well; and what I do well, the well-doing is from Him: for whatever I do from myself is ill.
This confession strengthens the heart and makes a firm foundation of love.
For if we ought to hide our good works lest they be seen by men, what becomes of that saying of the Lord in the sermon which He delivered on the mount?
Where He said this, there He also said a little before, “Let your good works shine before men.”
And He did not stop there, did not make an end there, but added, “And glorify your Father who is in heaven.”
And what does the apostle say?
“And I was unknown by face to the churches of Judea which were in Christ: but they only heard, He who persecuted us in times past now preaches the faith which he once destroyed.
And they glorified God in me.”
See how he also, since he had become so widely known, did not place the good in his own praise, but in the praise of God.
And as for himself, in his own person, that he was one who laid waste the Church, a persecutor, envious, malicious—it is he himself who confesses this, not we who reproach him with it.
Paul loves to have his sins spoken of by us, that He may be glorified who healed such a disease.
For it was the hand of the Physician that cut and healed the greatness of the sore.
That voice from heaven laid low the persecutor and raised up the preacher; killed Saul and brought Paul to life.
For Saul was the persecutor of a holy man; from him this man had his name when he persecuted the Christians: afterward, from Saul he became Paul.
What does the name Paulus mean?
Little. Therefore when he was Saul, he was proud, lifted up; when he was Paul, he was lowly, little.
So we say, I will see you “paulo post,” that is, after a little while.
Hear that he was made little: “For I am the least of the apostles”; and, “To me, the least of all saints,” he says in another place.
So he was among the apostles as the hem of the garment: but the Church of the Gentiles touched it, as did the woman who had the flow of blood, and was made whole.

3. So then, brethren, this I would say, this I do say, this, if I could, I would not leave unsaid: Let there be in you now these works, now those, according to the time, according to the hours, according to the days.

Are you always to be speaking? Always to keep silence? Always to be refreshing the body? Always to be fasting? Always to be giving bread to the needy? Always to be clothing the naked? Always to be visiting the sick? Always to be bringing into agreement those who disagree? Always to be burying the dead?
No: but now this, now that.
These things are taken in hand, and they stop: but that which, as emperor, commands all the forces within neither has a beginning nor ought to stop.
Let charity within have no intermission: let the duties of charity be carried out according to the time.
Let “brotherly love,” then, as it is written, let “brotherly love continue.”
4. But perhaps it will have struck some of you all along, while we have been expounding this epistle of blessed John to you, why it is only “brotherly” love that he so emphatically commends.
“He who loves his brother,” he says; and, “a commandment is given us that we love one another.”

Again and again it is brotherly love that he speaks of: but the love of God, that is, the love with which we ought to love God, he has not so constantly named; yet he has not altogether left it unspoken.
But concerning love of an enemy, almost throughout the epistle, he has said nothing.
Although he vehemently preaches and commends charity to us, he does not tell us to love our enemies, but tells us to love our brethren.
But just now, when the Gospel was read, we heard, “For if you love those who love you, what reward shall you have?
Do not even the tax collectors do this?”

How is it then that John the apostle commends brotherly love as the thing of great concern to us for a certain perfection; whereas the Lord says it is not enough that we love our brethren, but that we ought to extend that love so that we may reach even to enemies?
He who reaches even to enemies does not pass over the brethren.
It must, like fire, first seize upon what is nearest, and so extend to what is further off.
A brother is nearer to you than any chance person.
Again, that person whom you do not know, who yet is not against you, has more hold upon you than an enemy who is also against you.
Extend your love to those who are nearest, yet do not call this extending: for it is almost loving yourself, to love those who are close to you.
Extend it to the unknown, who have done you no harm.
Pass even them: reach on to love your enemies.
This at least the Lord commands.
Why has the apostle here said nothing about loving an enemy?

5. All love—whether that which is called carnal, which is usually called not “dilectio” but “amor” (for the word “dilectio” is usually used of better objects, and understood of better objects)—yet all love, dear brethren, has in it a wishing well to those who are loved.
For we ought not so to love, nor are we able so to love (whether “diligere” or “amare”: for this latter word the Lord used when He said, “Petra, amas me?”
“Peter, do you love me?”)—we ought not so to love men as we hear gluttons say, I love thrushes.
You ask why he loves them?
That he may kill them, that he may consume them.
He says he loves them, and to this end he loves them, that they may cease to be; to this end he loves them, that he may do away with them.
And whatever we love by way of food, we love it to this end, that it may be consumed and we restored.
Are men to be loved in such a way as to be consumed?
But there is a certain friendliness of well-wishing, by which we desire at some time or other to do good to those whom we love.
What if there is no good that we can do?
The benevolence, the wishing well, of itself suffices for him who loves.
For we ought not to wish men to be wretched, that we may be able to practice works of mercy.
You give bread to the hungry: but it would be better that none hungered, and you had no one to give to.
You clothe the naked: oh, that all were clothed, and this need did not exist!
You bury the dead: oh, that it had come at last, that life where none shall die!
You reconcile those who quarrel: oh, that it were here at last, that eternal peace of Jerusalem, where none shall disagree!
For all these are services rendered to necessities.
Take away the wretched; there will be an end to works of mercy.
The works of mercy will be at an end: shall the ardor of charity be quenched?
With a truer touch of love you love the happy man, for whom there is no good service you can do; purer will that love be, and far more unalloyed.
For if you have done a kindness to the wretched, perhaps you desire to lift yourself up over against him, and wish him to be subject to you, who have done the kindness to him.
He was in need, you bestowed; you seem to yourself greater, because you bestowed, than he on whom it was bestowed.
Wish him your equal, that you both may be under the One Lord, on whom nothing can be bestowed.
6. For in this the proud soul has passed its bounds and, in a manner, become avaricious.
For, “The root of all evils is avarice”; and again it is said, “The beginning of all sin is pride.”
And we ask, it may be, how these two sayings agree: “The root of all evils is avarice,” and, “The beginning of all sin is pride.”
If pride is the beginning of all sin, then pride is the root of all evils.
Now certainly, “the root of all evils is avarice.”
We find that in pride there is also avarice (or grasping); for man has passed his bounds: and what is it to be avaricious? To go beyond that which suffices.
Adam fell by pride: “the beginning of all sin is pride,” it says: did he fall by grasping?
What more grasping than he for whom God could not suffice?
In fact, my brethren, we read how man was made after the image and likeness of God: and what did God say of him?
“And let him have power over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the heaven, and over all cattle that move upon the earth.”
Did He say, Have power over men?
“Have power,” He says: He has given him natural power: “have power” over what? “Over the fish of the sea, the birds of the heaven, and all moving things that move upon the earth.”
Why is this power over these things a natural power?
Because man has the power from this: that he was made after the image of God.
And in what was he made after God’s image?

In the intellect, in the mind, in the inner man; in that he understands truth, distinguishes between right and wrong, knows by whom he was made, is able to understand his Creator, to praise his Creator: he has this intelligence who has prudence.

Therefore, when many by evil lusts wore out the image of God in themselves, and by the perversity of their conduct extinguished the very flame, so to speak, of intelligence, the Scripture cried aloud to them, “Do not become like the horse and mule, which have no understanding.”
That is to say, I have set you above the horse and mule; you I made after my image; I have given you power over these.

Why? Because they do not have the rational mind: but you, by the rational mind, are capable of truth, and understand what is above you: be subject to Him who is above you, and beneath you shall be those things over which you were set.
But because by sin man deserted Him whom he ought to be under, he is made subject to the things which he ought to be above.
7. Mark what I say: God, man, beasts: that is, above you, God; beneath you, the beasts.
Acknowledge Him who is above you, that those who are beneath you may acknowledge you.
Thus, because Daniel acknowledged God above him, the lions acknowledged him above them.
But if you do not acknowledge Him who is above you, you despise your superior, you become subject to your inferior.
Accordingly, how was the pride of the Egyptians subdued?
By means of frogs and flies.
God might have sent lions: but a great man may be scared by a lion.
The prouder they were, the more by means of things contemptible and feeble was their wicked neck broken.
But Daniel the lions acknowledge, because he was subject to God.

What then of the martyrs who were cast to the wild beasts to fight with them, and were torn by the teeth of savage creatures—were they not under God? Or were those three men servants of God, and the Maccabees not servants of God?
The fire acknowledged as God’s servants the three men, whom it did not burn, nor did it hurt their garments; and did it not acknowledge the Maccabees?
It acknowledged the Maccabees; it did, my brethren, acknowledge them also.
But there was need of a scourge, by the Lord’s permission: He has said in Scripture, “He scourges every son whom He receives.”
For do you think, my brethren, that the iron would have pierced into the vitals of the Lord unless He had permitted it, or that He would have hung fastened to the tree unless it had been His will?
Did not His own creature acknowledge Him?
Or did He set an example of patience for His faithful ones?
You see, then, God delivered some visibly, some He did not deliver visibly: yet all He delivered spiritually; spiritually He deserted none.
Visibly He seemed to have deserted some; some He seemed to have rescued.
He rescued some for this reason, that you may not think He did not have the power to rescue.
He has given proof that He has the power, so that where He does not do it, you may understand a more hidden will, not surmise a difficulty in doing it.

But what, brethren? When we shall have come out of all these snares of mortality, when the times of temptation shall have passed away, when the river of this world shall have flowed by, and we shall have received again that “first robe,” that immortality which we lost by sinning—“when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption,” that is, this flesh shall have put on incorruption, “and this mortal shall have put on immortality”—all creatures shall acknowledge the now perfected sons of God, in whom there is no more need to be tempted or to be scourged: all things shall be subjected to us, if here we are subjected to God.
8. So then the Christian ought to be such that he does not glory over other “men.”
For God has given it to you to be over the beasts, that is, to be better than the beasts.
This you have by nature; you will always be better than a beast.
If you wish to be better than another man, you will begrudge him when you see him to be your equal.
You ought to wish all men to be your equals; and if by wisdom you surpass anyone, you ought to wish that he also may be wise.

As long as he is slow, he learns from you; as long as he is untaught, he has need of you; and you are seen to be the teacher, he the learner; therefore you seem to be the superior, because you are the teacher; he the inferior, because he is the learner.
Unless you wish him to be your equal, you wish to have him always a learner.
But if you wish to have him always a learner, you will be an envious teacher.
If an envious teacher, how will you be a teacher?
I beg you, do not teach him your envy.
Hear the apostle speaking from the deep affections of charity: “I would that all were even as I.” In what sense did he wish all to be his equals?
In this he was superior to all, that by charity he wished all to be his equals.
I say, then, man has passed his bounds; he would insist on being greedy for more than his due, on being above men, he who was made above the beasts: and this is pride.
9. And see what great works pride does.
Lay it up in your hearts how alike, how nearly on a par, as it were, are the works it does and the works of charity.
Charity feeds the hungry, and so does pride: charity, that God may be praised; pride, that itself may be praised.
Charity clothes the naked, so does pride; charity fasts, so does pride; charity buries the dead, so does pride.
All the good works which charity wishes to do, and does, pride on the other hand drives at the same, and, so to speak, keeps her horses up to the mark.
But charity stands between her and it, and leaves no room for ill-driven pride; not ill-driving, but ill-driven.
Woe to the man whose charioteer is pride, for he must go headlong!

But in the good that is done, that it may not be pride that sets us on, who knows? Who sees it? Where is it? The works we see: mercy feeds, pride also feeds; mercy takes in the stranger, pride also takes in the stranger; mercy intercedes for the poor, pride also intercedes.
How is this? In the works we see no difference.
I dare to say something, but not I; Paul has said it: charity dies, that is, a man having charity confesses the name of Christ and suffers martyrdom; pride also confesses, and also suffers martyrdom.
The one has charity, the other does not have charity.
But let him who does not have charity hear from the apostle: “If I distribute all my goods to the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, and do not have charity, it profits me nothing.”
So then the divine Scripture calls us away from the outward display of the face to that which is within; from this surface which is paraded before men, it calls us away to that which is within.
Return to your own conscience; question it.
Do not consider what blossoms outwardly, but what root there is in the ground.
Is lust rooted there?
There may be a show of good deeds; truly good works there cannot be.
Is charity rooted there?
Have no fear: nothing evil can come of that.
The proud man caresses; love is severe.
The one clothes, the other strikes.
For the one clothes in order to please men, the other strikes in order to correct by discipline.
More acceptable is the blow of charity than the alms of pride.
Come within, then, brethren; and in all things, whatever you do, look to God your witness.
See whether He sees with what mind you do it.
If your heart does not accuse you of doing it for the sake of display, it is well: do not fear.
But when you do good, do not fear that another may see you.
Fear lest you do it to the end that you may be praised; let the other see it, that God may be praised.
For if you hide it from the eyes of man, you hide it from the imitation of man; you withdraw from God His praise.
There are two to whom you give the alms; two hunger, one for bread, the other for righteousness.

Between these two famishing souls (as it is written, “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled”), between these two famishing persons you, the doer of the good work, are set; if charity does the work on occasion of the one, in it she has pity on both; she would help both.
For the one craves what he may eat, the other craves what he may imitate.

You feed the one; give yourself as a pattern to the other; so you have given alms to both: the one you have caused to thank you for killing his hunger, the other you have made to imitate you by setting him an example.
10. Show mercy, then, as men of merciful hearts; because in loving enemies also, you love brethren.
Do not think that John has given no precept concerning love of our enemy because he has not ceased to speak of brotherly love.
You love brethren. “How,” you say, “do we love brethren?”
I ask why you love an enemy.
Why do you love him?
That he may be healthy in this life? What if it is not expedient for him?
That he may be rich? What if he is blinded by his very riches?
That he may marry a wife? What if he has a bitter life of it?
That he may have children? What if they turn out bad?
Uncertain, therefore, are these things which you seem to wish for your enemy in loving him; they are uncertain.
Wish for him that he may have eternal life with you; wish for him that he may be your brother: then, when you love him, you love a brother.
For you love in him not what he is, but what you wish him to be.

I once said to you, my beloved, if I am not mistaken: There is a log of timber lying in sight; a good workman has seen the log, not yet planed, just as it was hewn from the forest; he has taken a liking to it; he would make something out of it.
For indeed he did not love it so that it should always remain as it is.
In his art he has seen what it shall be, not in his liking what it is; and his liking is for the thing he will make of it, not for the thing it is.
So God loved us sinners.
We say that God loved sinners, for He says, “Those who are well have no need of the Physician, but those who are sick.”
Did He love us sinners so that we should still remain sinners?
Our Carpenter saw us as timber from the wood, and had in His thoughts the building He would make of it, not the unwrought timber that it was.
So too you see your enemy striving against you, raging, biting with words, provoking with insults, harassing with hatred: you have regard to this in him, that he is a man.
You see all these things that are against you, that they were done by man; and you see in him that he was made by God.
Now, that he was made a man was God’s doing; but that he hates you is his own doing; that he bears you ill will is his own doing.
And what do you say in your mind?
“Lord, be merciful to him, forgive him his sins, strike terror into him, change him.”
You do not love in him what he is, but what you wish him to be.
Consequently, when you love an enemy, you love a brother.
Therefore, perfect love is the loving of an enemy; and this perfect love is in brotherly love.
And let no one say that John the apostle has admonished us somewhat less, and the Lord Christ somewhat more.
John has admonished us to love the brethren; Christ has admonished us to love even enemies.
Mark to what end Christ has bidden you to love your enemies.
That they may remain enemies always?
If He bade it to this end, that they should remain enemies, you hate, you do not love.
Mark how He Himself loved: because He would not have them remain the persecutors they were, He said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do.”
Those whom He willed to be forgiven, He willed to be changed; those whom He willed to be changed, He deigned to make brethren out of enemies, and did in truth make them so.

He was killed, was buried, rose again, ascended into heaven; He sent the Holy Spirit to His disciples; they began to preach His name with boldness; they did miracles in the name of Him who was crucified and slain; those slayers of the Lord saw them; and those who in rage had shed His blood drank it by believing.
11. These things I have said, brethren, and at some length; yet because charity was to be commended to you more earnestly, beloved, in this way it had to be commended.
For if there is no charity in you, we have said nothing.
But if it is in you, we have, as it were, poured oil on the flames.
And in whom it was not, perhaps it has been kindled by words.
In one, what was there has grown; in another, what was not has begun to be.
To this end, therefore, we have said these things, that you may not be slow to love your enemies.
Does anyone rage against you? He rages, you pray; he hates, you pity.
It is the fever of his soul that hates you: he will be well, and will thank you.
How do physicians love those who are sick?
Is it the sick that they love?
If they love them as sick, they wish them to be always sick.
To this end they love the sick: not that they should remain sick, but that from being sick they should be made well.
And how much they very often have to suffer from the frenzied!
What insulting language! Very often they are even struck by them.
He attacks the fever, forgives the man.
And what shall I say, brethren? Does he love his enemy?
No, he hates his enemy, the disease; for it is this that he hates, and he loves the man by whom he is struck: he hates the fever.
For by whom or by what is he struck? By the disease, by the sickness, by the fever.
He takes away that which strives against him, that there may remain that from which he will have thanks.
So you do likewise. If your enemy hates you, and hates you unjustly, know that the lust of the world reigns in him; therefore he hates you.
If you also hate him, you in turn render evil for evil.
What does it achieve, to render evil for evil?
I wept for one sick man who hated you; now I mourn for you, if you also hate.
But he attacks your property; he takes from you I know not what things that you have on earth; therefore you hate him, because he puts you in straits on earth.
Do not be straitened; move yourself to heaven above; there you will have your heart where there is wide room, so that you may not be straitened in the hope of eternal life.
Consider what the things are that he takes from you: he would not take even these from you except by permission of Him who “scourges every son whom He receives.”
He, this same enemy of yours, is in a manner the instrument in the hands of God by which you may be healed.

If God knows it to be good for you that he should despoil you, He permits him; if He knows it to be good for you that you should receive blows, He permits him to strike you: by means of him He cares for you. Wish that he may be made well.
12. “No one has seen God at any time.”
See, beloved: “If we love one another, God will dwell in us, and His love will be perfected in us.”
Begin to love; you will be perfected.
Have you begun to love?
God has begun to dwell in you: love Him who has begun to dwell in you, that by dwelling in you more perfectly He may make you perfect.
“By this we know that we dwell in Him and He in us, because He has given us of His Spirit.”
It is well: thanks be to God!
We come to know that He dwells in us.
And how do we come to know this very thing, namely, that we do know that He dwells in us?
Because John himself has said this: “Because He has given us of His Spirit.”
How do we know that He has given us of His Spirit?
This very thing, that He has given you of His Spirit, how do you come to know it?
Ask your own inmost heart: if it is full of charity, you have the Spirit of God.
How do we know that by this you know that the Spirit of God dwells in you?
“Because the love of God is poured out in our hearts by the Holy Spirit who is given to us.”
13. “And we have seen and are witnesses that God has sent His Son to be the Savior of the world.”
Set your minds at rest, you who are sick: such a Physician has come, and do you despair?
Great were the diseases, incurable were the wounds, desperate was the sickness.
Do you note the greatness of your ill, and not note the omnipotence of the Physician?
You are desperate, but He is omnipotent; His witnesses are these who were first healed and who announce the Physician; yet even they are made well in hope rather than in reality.
For so says the apostle: “For we are saved by hope.”
We have begun, therefore, to be made well in faith; but our wholeness will be perfected “when this corruptible has put on incorruption, and this mortal has put on immortality.”
This is hope, not the reality.
But he who rejoices in hope will hold the reality also; whereas he who does not have the hope will not be able to attain to the reality.
14. “Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God dwells in him, and he in God.”
Now we may say it in few words: “Whoever confesses”; not in word but in deed, not with the tongue but with the life.
For many confess in words but deny in deeds: “And we have known and believed the love that God has in us.”
And again, by what have you come to know this?
“Love is God.” He has already said it above; behold, he says it again.
Love could not be more highly commended to you than by being called God.
Perhaps you were ready to despise a gift of God.
And do you despise God?
“Love is God, and he who dwells in love dwells in God, and God dwells in him.”
Each mutually inhabits the other: He who holds, and he who is held.
You dwell in God, but in order that you may be held; God dwells in you, but in order that He may hold you, lest you fall.

Lest perhaps you imagine that you become a house of God in the same way that your house supports your flesh: if the house in which you are withdraws itself from under you, you fall; but if you withdraw yourself, God does not fall.
When you forsake Him, He is none the less; when you have returned to Him, He is none the greater.

You are healed, yet on Him you will bestow nothing; you are made clean, you are made new, you are set right: He is a medicine for the unhealthy, a rule for the crooked, light for the darkened, a dwelling for the forsaken.
All, therefore, is conferred on you: see that you do not imagine that anything is conferred on God by your coming to Him; no, not so much as a slave.
Shall God, indeed, not have servants if you are unwilling, if all are unwilling?
God does not need the servants, but the servants need God; therefore the Psalm says, “I have said to the Lord, You are my God.”
He is the true Lord.
And what does it say?
“For You have no need of my goods.”
You need the good you have from your servant.
Your servant needs the good he has from you, that you may feed him; you also need the good you have from your servant, that he may help you.
You cannot draw water for yourself, cannot cook for yourself, cannot run before your horse, cannot tend your beast.
You see that you need the good you have from your servant; you need his service.
Therefore you are not a true lord, while you have need of an inferior.
He is the true Lord, who seeks nothing from us; and woe to us if we do not seek Him!
