He seeks nothing from us; yet He sought us when we did not seek Him.
One sheep had strayed; He found it, He brought it back on His shoulders rejoicing.
And was the sheep necessary for the Shepherd, and not rather the Shepherd necessary for the sheep? The more I love to speak of charity, the less willing I am that this epistle should be finished.
No one is more ardent in commending charity.
Nothing sweeter is preached to you, nothing more wholesome is drunk by you; but only if by godly living you confirm in yourselves the gift of God.

Do not be ungrateful for His so great grace, who, though He had one Only Son, would not have Him be a Son alone; but, that He might have brethren, adopted to Himself those who should possess eternal life with Him.
“In this love is made perfect in us, that we may have boldness in the day of judgment; because as He is, so are we in this world.
There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has torment.
He who fears is not made perfect in love.
Let us love Him, because He first loved us.
If someone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?
And this commandment we have from Him: that he who loves God should love his brother also.”
1. You remember, beloved, that of the epistles of John the apostle the last part remains to be handled by us and expounded to you, as the Lord grants.
Of this debt, then, we are mindful; and you ought to be mindful of your claim.
For indeed this same charity, which in this epistle is chiefly and almost alone commended, at once makes us most faithful in paying our debts, and you most sweet in exacting your rights.

I have said “most sweet in exacting,” because where charity is not, he who exacts is bitter; but where charity is, both he who exacts is sweet, and he from whom it is exacted, although he undertakes some labor, yet charity makes the very labor almost no labor, and light.

Do we not see how, even in dumb and irrational animals, where the love is not spiritual but carnal and natural, the mother yields herself with great affection to her young ones when they would have the milk which is their right; and however impetuously the suckling rushes at the teats, yet that is better for the mother than that it should not suck nor exact what is due from love?

Often we see great calves driving their heads at the cow’s udders with a force that almost lifts up the mother’s body, yet she does not kick them off; indeed, if the young one is not there to suck, the lowing of the mother calls for it to come to the teats.
If, then, there is in us that spiritual charity of which the apostle says, “I became small in your midst, even as a nurse cherishing her young ones,” we love you the more when you are exacting.
We do not like the sluggish, because for the languid ones we are afraid.

We have been obliged, however, to interrupt the continuous reading of this epistle, because of certain appointed lessons coming in between, which had to be read on their holy days, and preached upon as well.
Let us now come back to the order which was interrupted; and what remains, holy brethren, receive with all attention.
I do not know whether charity could be more magnificently commended to us than by its being said, “Charity is God.”
Brief praise, yet mighty praise: brief in utterance, mighty in meaning!
How quickly it is said, “Love is God!”
This also is short: if you count it, it is one; if you weigh it, how great it is!
“Love is God, and he who dwells,” he says, “in love dwells in God, and God dwells in him.”
Let God be your house, and be yourself a house of God; dwell in God, and let God dwell in you.
God dwells in you that He may hold you; you dwell in God that you may not fall; for thus the apostle says of this same charity, “Charity never falls.”
How should he fall whom God holds?
2. “In this our love is made perfect in us, that we may have boldness in the day of judgment; because as He is, so are we in this world.”
He tells how each may test himself, what progress charity has made in him, or rather what progress he has made in charity.
For if charity is God, God is capable neither of progress nor of decline: that charity is said to be making progress in you means only that you are making progress in it.
Ask, therefore, what progress you have made in charity, and what your heart will answer you, that you may know the measure of your progress.
For he has promised to show us by what we may know Him, and has said, “In this love is made perfect in us.”
Ask: in what? “That we may have boldness in the day of judgment.”
Whoever has boldness in the day of judgment, in that man charity is made perfect.
What is it to have boldness in the day of judgment?
Not to fear that the day of judgment should come.
There are men who do not believe in a day of judgment; these cannot have boldness in a day which they do not believe will come.
Let us pass these by: may God awaken them, that they may live; why do we speak of the dead?
They do not believe that there will be a day of judgment; they neither fear nor desire what they do not believe.
A man has begun to believe in a day of judgment: if he has begun to believe, he has also begun to fear.
But because he still fears, because he does not yet have boldness in the day of judgment, charity is not yet made perfect in that man.
But for all that, should one despair?
In one in whom you see the beginning, why do you despair of the end?
“What beginning do I see?” you say.
That very fear. Hear the Scripture: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.”

Well then, he has begun to fear the day of judgment: by fearing let him correct himself, let him watch against his enemies, that is, his sins; let him begin to come to life again inwardly, and to put to death his members which are on the earth, as the apostle says, “Put to death your members which are on the earth.”
By the members on earth he means spiritual wickedness; for he goes on to explain it: “Covetousness, uncleanness,” and the rest which he lists there.
Now in proportion as this man who has begun to fear the day of judgment puts to death his members which are on the earth, in that proportion the heavenly members rise up and are strengthened.
But the heavenly members are all good works.
As the heavenly members rise up, he begins to desire what he once feared.
Once he feared lest Christ should come and find in him the ungodly man whom He must condemn; now he longs for Him to come, because He will find the godly man whom He may crown.
Having now begun to desire Christ’s coming, the chaste soul which desires the embrace of the Bridegroom renounces the adulterer and becomes a virgin within by faith, hope, and charity.
Now the man has boldness in the day of judgment: he does not fight against himself when he prays, “Your kingdom come.”
For he who fears lest the kingdom of God should come fears lest his prayer be heard.
How can he be said to pray who fears lest his prayer be heard?
But he who prays with the boldness of charity wishes now that He may come.
Of this same desire one said in the Psalm, “And You, O Lord, how long?
Turn, O Lord, and deliver my soul.”
He groaned at being so put off.
For there are men who with patience submit to die; but there are some perfect ones who with patience endure to live.
What do I mean?

When a person still desires this life, that person, when the day of death comes, patiently endures death: he struggles against himself that he may follow the will of God, and in his mind desires what God chooses, not what man’s will chooses; from desire of the present life there comes a reluctance toward death, but yet he takes to himself patience and fortitude, that he may meet death with an even mind; he dies patiently.
But when a man desires, as the apostle says, “to be dissolved and to be with Christ,” that person does not die patiently, but lives patiently and dies with delight.
See the apostle living patiently, that is, how with patience he here does not love life but endures it.
“To be dissolved,” he says, “and to be with Christ is far better; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sakes.”
Therefore, brethren, make every effort; settle it inwardly within yourselves to make this your concern, that you may desire the day of judgment.
In no other way is charity proved to be perfect than when one has begun to desire that day.
But that man desires it who has boldness in it, whose conscience feels no alarm, in perfect and sincere charity.
3. “In this His love is perfected in us, that we may have boldness in the day of judgment.”
Why shall we have boldness?
“Because as He is, so are we also in this world.”
You have heard the ground of your boldness: “Because as He is,” says the apostle, “so are we also in this world.”
Does he not seem to have said something impossible?
For is it possible for man to be as God?
I have already explained to you that “as” is not always said of equality, but is said of a certain resemblance.
For how do you say, “As I have ears, so has my image”?
Is it quite so? And yet you say “so, as.”
If, then, we were made after God’s image, why are we not as God?
Not to the point of equality, but in proportion to our measure.
From where, then, are we given boldness in the day of judgment?
“Because as He is, so are we also in this world.”
We must refer this to the same charity, and understand what is meant.
The Lord says in the Gospel, “If you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not the tax collectors do this?”
Then what would He have us do?
“But I say to you, Love your enemies, and pray for those who persecute you.”
If, then, He bids us love our enemies, from where does He bring an example to set before us?
From God Himself; for He says, “That you may be the children of your Father who is in heaven.”
How does God do this?
He loves His enemies, He “who makes His sun rise on the good and the bad, and sends rain on the just and the unjust.”

If, then, this is the perfection to which God invites us, that we love our enemies as He loved His, this is our boldness in the day of judgment, that “as He is, so are we also in this world”; because, as He loves His enemies in making His sun rise on good and bad, and in sending rain on the just and unjust, so we, since we cannot bestow sun and rain on them, bestow on them our tears when we pray for them.
4. Now, therefore, concerning this same boldness, let us see what he says.
How do we understand that charity is perfect?
“There is no fear in charity.”
Then what do we say of him who has begun to fear the day of judgment?
If charity in him were perfect, he would not fear.
For perfect charity would make perfect righteousness, and he would have nothing to fear; rather, he would have something to desire: that iniquity may pass away, and God’s kingdom come.
So then, “there is no fear in charity.”
But in what charity?
Not in charity begun. In what, then?
“But perfect charity,” he says, “casts out fear.”
Then let fear make the beginning, because “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.”
Fear, so to speak, prepares a place for charity.
But once charity has begun to dwell there, the fear which prepared the place for it is cast out.
For in proportion as this increases, that decreases; and the more this comes to be within, the more fear is cast out.
Greater charity, less fear; less charity, greater fear.
But if there is no fear, there is no way for charity to come in.

As we see in sewing, the thread is brought in by means of the bristle: the bristle enters first, but unless it comes out, the thread does not come into its place; so fear first occupies the mind, but the fear does not remain there, because it enters only in order to bring in charity.
Once there is a sense of security in the mind, what joy we have, both in this world and in the world to come!
Even in this world, who shall hurt us, being full of charity?

See how the apostle exults concerning this very charity: “Who shall separate us from the charity of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?”
And Peter says: “And who is he who will harm you, if you are followers of what is good?—There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has torment.”
The consciousness of sins torments the heart: justification has not yet taken place.
There is something in it that itches, that pricks.
Accordingly, in the Psalm, what does he say concerning this same perfection of righteousness?
“You have turned my mourning into joy for me; You have put off my sackcloth and girded me with gladness, to the end that my glory may sing to You, and that I may not be pricked.”
What is this, “That I may not be pricked”?
That there may not be anything that will goad my conscience.
Fear goads; but do not fear: charity enters in, and she heals the wound that fear inflicts.
The fear of God wounds as the physician’s knife does; it takes away the rottenness, and seems to make the wound greater.
Behold, when the rottenness was in the body, the wound was smaller, but dangerous; then comes the knife; the wound hurt less then than it hurts now while the physician is cutting it.
It hurts more while he is operating on it than it would if it were not operated on; it hurts more under the healing operation, but only so that it may never hurt once the healing is accomplished.
Then let fear occupy your heart, that it may bring in charity; let the scar follow the physician’s knife.
He is such a Healer that the scars do not even appear; only put yourself under His hand.
For if you are without fear, you cannot be justified.
It is a sentence pronounced by the Scriptures: “For he who is without fear cannot be justified.”
Fear, then, must enter first, that by it charity may come.
Fear is the healing operation; charity, the sound condition.
“But he who fears is not made perfect in love.”
Why? “Because fear has torment,” just as the cutting of the surgeon’s knife has torment.
5. But there is another saying which seems contrary to this, if it does not have someone who understands it.
Namely, it is said in a certain place in the Psalms, “The fear of the Lord is chaste, enduring forever.”
He shows us an eternal fear, but a chaste one.
But if he there shows us an eternal fear, does this epistle perhaps contradict him when it says, “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear”?
Let us question both utterances of God.
The Spirit is one, though the books are two, though the mouths are two, though the tongues are two.
For this is said by the mouth of John, that by the mouth of David; but do not think that the Spirit is more than one.
If one breath fills two pipes [of the double flute], cannot one Spirit fill two hearts and move two tongues?
But if two pipes filled by one breathing sound in unison, can two tongues filled with the Spirit or Breath of God make a discord?
There is, then, a unison there, there is a harmony; only it requires someone who can hear.

Behold, this Spirit of God has breathed into and filled two hearts, has moved two tongues; and we have heard from the one tongue, “There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear”; we have heard from the other, “The fear of the Lord is chaste, enduring forever.”
How is this? The notes seem to jar.
Not so: rouse your ears; mark the melody.

It is not without cause that in the one place the word “chaste” is added, and in the other it is not added; but it is because there is one fear which is called chaste, and there is another fear which is not called chaste.
Let us mark the difference between these two fears, and so understand the harmony of the flutes.
How are we to understand, or how to distinguish?
Mark, my beloved. There are men who fear God lest they be cast into hell, lest perhaps they burn with the devil in everlasting fire.
This is the fear which brings in charity; but it comes in order to depart.
For if you still fear God because of punishments, you do not yet love Him whom you fear in this way.
You do not desire the good things, but are afraid of the evil things.
Yet because you are afraid of the evil things, you correct yourself and begin to desire the good things.
Once you have begun to desire the good, there will be in you the chaste fear.
What is the chaste fear?
The fear lest you lose the good things themselves.
Mark! It is one thing to fear God lest He cast you into hell with the devil, and another thing to fear God lest He forsake you.

The fear by which you fear lest you be cast into hell with the devil is not yet chaste, for it does not come from the love of God but from the fear of punishment; but when you fear God lest His presence forsake you, you embrace Him, you long to enjoy God Himself.

6. One cannot better explain the difference between these two fears, the one which charity casts out, the other chaste, which endures forever, than by putting the case of two married women, one of whom, you may suppose, is willing to commit adultery, delights in wickedness, and only fears lest she be condemned by her husband.
She fears her husband; but because she still loves wickedness, that is the reason why she fears her husband.
To this woman the presence of her husband is not welcome but burdensome; and if she happens to live wickedly, she fears her husband, lest he should come.
Such are those who fear the coming of the day of judgment.
Put the case that the other loves her husband, that she feels she owes him chaste embraces, that she stains herself with no uncleanness of adultery: she wishes for the presence of her husband.
And how are these two fears distinguished?
The one woman fears, the other also fears.
Question them: they seem to give one answer. Question the one: “Do you fear your husband?” She answers, “I do.”
Question the other, whether she fears her husband; she answers, “I do fear him.”
The voice is one, the mind different.
Now then let them be questioned: “Why?”
The one says, “I fear my husband, lest he should come”; the other says, “I fear my husband, lest he depart from me.”
The one says, “I fear to be condemned”; the other, “I fear to be forsaken.”
Let the same take place in the mind of Christians, and you find a fear which love casts out, and another fear, chaste, enduring forever.
7. Let us speak first, then, to those who fear God just in the manner of that woman who delights in wickedness; that is, she fears her husband lest he condemn her. To such let us speak first.

O soul, you who fear God lest He condemn you, just as the woman fears who delights in wickedness—she fears her husband, lest she be condemned by her husband—as you are displeased with this woman, so be displeased with yourself.

If perhaps you have a wife, would you want your wife to fear you in this way, so that she may not be condemned by you? That, delighting in wickedness, she should be restrained only by the weight of her fear of you, not by condemning her own iniquity?
You would want her to be chaste so that she may love you, not so that she may fear you.
Show yourself to God such as you would want your wife to be to you.
And if you do not yet have a wife, and wish to have one, you would want her to be such.
And yet what are we saying, brethren?

That woman whose fear of her husband is the fear of being condemned by her husband perhaps does not commit adultery lest by some means or other it come to her husband’s knowledge, and he deprive her of this temporal light of life; yet the husband can be deceived and kept in ignorance, for he is only human, as she is who can deceive him.
She fears him from whose eyes she can be hidden: and do you not fear the face of your Husband, which is always upon you?
“The countenance of the Lord is against those who do evil.”

She seizes on her husband’s absence, and perhaps is stirred by the delight of adultery; and yet she says to herself, I will not do it: he is indeed absent, but it is hard to keep it from somehow coming to his knowledge.

She restrains herself lest it come to the knowledge of a mortal man—one who, it is also possible, may never know it; who, it is also possible, may be deceived, so that he will consider a bad woman good, and consider her chaste who is an adulteress: and do you not fear the eyes of Him whom no one can deceive? Do you not fear the presence of Him who cannot be turned away from you?
Pray God to look upon you, and to turn His face away from your sins: “Turn away Your face from my sins.”
But how do you deserve that He should turn His face away from your sins, if you do not turn your own face away from your sins?
For the same voice says in the Psalm: “For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me.”
Acknowledge it, and He forgives.

8. We have addressed that soul which still has the fear that does not endure forever, but which love shuts out and casts out: let us also address the soul which now has the fear that is chaste, enduring forever.
Shall we find that soul, do you think, so that we may address it? Is it here, do you think, in this congregation? Is it, do you think, here in this chancel? Is it here on earth, do you think?
It cannot but be here; only it is hidden.
Now it is winter: within, the greenness is in the root.
Perhaps we may reach the ears of that soul.
But wherever that soul is, oh, that I could find it, and instead of its listening to me, might myself listen to it!
It should teach me something, rather than learn from me!

A holy soul, a soul on fire, and longing for the kingdom of God: that soul it is not I who address, but God Himself addresses it, and thus consoles it while it patiently endures to live here on earth: “You would like Me to come even now, and I know that you wish I would come even now; I know what you are, such that you may wait for My coming without fear; I know that this is a trouble to you: but wait still longer, endure; I am coming, and coming quickly.”
But to the loving soul time moves slowly.
Hear her singing, like the lily she is, from among the thorns; hear her sighing and saying, “I will sing, and will understand in a blameless way: when will You come to me?”
But in a blameless way she may well not fear, because “perfect love casts out fear.”
And when He has come to her embrace, she still fears, but in the manner of one who feels secure.
What does she fear?
She will beware and guard herself against her own iniquity, so that she does not sin again: not lest she be cast into the fire, but lest she be forsaken by Him.
And there shall be in her—what? The “chaste fear, enduring forever.”
We have heard the two flutes sounding in unison.
That one speaks of fear, and this one speaks of fear: but that one, of the fear with which the soul fears lest she be condemned; this one, of the fear with which the soul fears lest she be forsaken.
That is the fear which charity casts out; this, the fear that endures forever.
9. “Let us love, because He first loved us.”
For how could we love, unless He had first loved us?
By loving we became friends: but He loved us as enemies, so that we might be made friends.
He first loved us, and gave us the gift of loving Him.
We did not yet love Him: by loving we are made beautiful.
If a deformed and ill-featured man loves a beautiful woman, what shall he do?
Or what shall a woman do if, being deformed and ill-featured and dark-complexioned, she loves a beautiful man?
Can she become beautiful by loving?
Can he become handsome by loving?
He loves a beautiful woman, and when he sees himself in a mirror, he is ashamed to lift his face to her, his lovely one, with whom he is in love.
What shall he do to become beautiful?
Does he wait for good looks to come?
No, rather, by waiting, old age is added to him and makes him uglier.

There is nothing, then, to be done, no way to advise him, except that he should restrain himself and not presume to love unequally; or if perhaps he does love her and wishes to take her as his wife, let him love chastity in her, not the face of the flesh.
But our soul, my brethren, is unlovely because of iniquity: by loving God it becomes lovely.
What a love that must be, which makes the lover beautiful!
But God is always lovely, never unlovely, never changeable.
He who is always lovely first loved us; and what were we when He loved us but foul and unlovely?
But not to leave us foul; no, but to change us, and to make us lovely instead of unlovely.
How shall we become lovely?
By loving Him who is always lovely.
As love increases in you, so loveliness increases: for love itself is the beauty of the soul.
“Let us love, because He first loved us.”
Hear the apostle Paul: “But God showed His love in us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us”: the just for the unjust, the beautiful for the foul.
How do we find Jesus beautiful?
“You are beautiful in loveliness beyond the sons of men; grace is poured upon Your lips.”
Why so? See again why it is that He is fair: “Beautiful in loveliness beyond the sons of men”: because “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

But in taking flesh, He took upon Himself, as it were, your foulness, that is, your mortality, so that He might adapt Himself to you and become suited to you, and stir you up to love the beauty within.
Where then in Scripture do we find Jesus uncomely and deformed, as we have found Him comely and “beautiful in loveliness beyond the sons of men”? Where do we also find Him deformed?
Ask Isaiah: “And we saw Him, and He had no form nor comeliness.”
Here now are two flutes which seem to make discordant sounds: yet one Spirit breathes into both.
By this one it is said, “Beautiful in loveliness beyond the sons of men”; by that one it is said in Isaiah, “We saw Him, and He had no form nor comeliness.”
Both flutes are filled by one Spirit; they make no dissonance.
Do not turn away your ears; apply your understanding.
Let us ask the apostle Paul, and let him explain to us the harmony of the two flutes.
Let him sound for us the note, “Beautiful in loveliness beyond the sons of men.—Who, being in the form of God, did not think it robbery to be equal with God.”

Let him sound for us also the note, “We saw Him, and He had no form nor comeliness.—He made Himself of no reputation, taking upon Himself the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and found in fashion as a man.
He had no form nor comeliness,” so that He might give you form and comeliness.
What form? What comeliness?
The love which is in charity: so that, loving, you may run; running, you may love.
You are fair now: but do not rest your gaze upon yourself, lest you lose what you have received; let your gaze end in Him by whom you were made fair.
Be fair only to the end that He may love you.
But direct your whole aim to Him, run to Him, seek His embraces, fear to depart from Him, so that there may be in you the chaste fear which endures forever.
“Let us love, because He first loved us.”
10. “If anyone says, I love God.”
What God? Why do we love?
“Because He first loved us,” and gave us the power to love.
He loved us ungodly, to make us godly; loved us unrighteous, to make us righteous; loved us sick, to make us whole.
Ask each individual; let him tell you whether he loves God.
He cries out, he confesses: I love; God knows.
There is another question to be asked.
“If anyone says, I love God, and hates his brother, he is a liar.”
How do you prove that he is a liar?
Listen. “For he who does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?”
What then? Does he who loves a brother love God also?
He must of necessity love God; he must of necessity love Him who is Love itself.
Can anyone love his brother and not love Love?
Of necessity he must love Love.
What then? Because he loves Love, does it follow that he loves God?
Certainly it follows.
In loving Love, he loves God.
Or have you forgotten what you said a little while ago, “Love is God”?
If “Love is God,” whoever loves Love loves God.
Love your brother, then, and feel assured.
You cannot say, “I love my brother, but I do not love God.”
Just as you lie if you say “I love God” when you do not love your brother, so you are deceived when you say, I love my brother, if you think that you do not love God.
You who love your brother must of necessity love Love itself: but “Love is God”; therefore whoever loves his brother must of necessity love God.
But if you do not love the brother whom you see, how can you love God whom you do not see?
Why does he not see God?
Because he does not have Love itself.
That he does not see God is because he does not have love; that he does not have love is because he does not love his brother.
The reason, then, why he does not see God is that he does not have Love.

For if he has Love, he sees God, for “Love is God”: and that eye is being more and more purified by love, to see that Unchangeable Substance in whose presence he shall always rejoice, which he shall enjoy forever, when he is joined with the angels.
Only let him run now, so that he may at last have gladness in his own country.

Let him not love his pilgrimage, not love the road: let everything be bitter except Him who calls us, until we hold Him fast and say what is said in the Psalm: “You have destroyed all who go whoring away from You”—and who are they that go whoring? Those who go away and love the world. But what will you do? He goes on and says: “But for me it is good to cling to God.”
All my good is to cling to God, freely.
For if you question him and say, For what do you cling to Him? and he should say, That He may give me—Give you what?
It is He who made the heaven, He who made the earth: what shall He give you?
You are already clinging to Him: find something better, and He will give it to you.
11. “For he who does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?
And this commandment we have from Him, that he who loves God should love his brother also.”
Marvelously fine talk it was, that you said, “I love God,” and you hate your brother!
O murderer, how do you love God?
Have you not heard above in this very epistle, “He who hates his brother is a murderer”?
Yes, but I truly do love God, however much I hate my brother.
You truly do not love God, if you hate your brother.
And now I will make it good by another proof.
This same apostle has said, “He gave us a commandment that we should love one another.”
How can you be said to love Him whose commandment you hate?
Who will say, I love the emperor, but I hate his laws?
The emperor recognizes whether you love him by this: that his laws are observed throughout the provinces.
Our Emperor’s law—what is it?
“A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another.”
You say, then, that you love Christ: keep His commandment, and love your brother.
But if you do not love your brother, how can you be said to love Him whose commandment you despise?
Brethren, I am never satisfied with speaking of charity in the name of the Lord.

In the measure that you have an insatiable desire for this thing, in that measure we hope the thing itself is growing in you and casting out fear, so that there may remain that chaste fear which is permanent forever.
Let us endure the world, endure tribulations, endure the stumbling blocks of temptations.
Let us not depart from the way; let us hold to the unity of the Church, hold to Christ, hold to charity.

Let us not be torn away from the members of His Bride, not be torn away from faith, so that we may glory in His coming; and we shall securely abide in Him, now by faith, then by sight, of whom we have so great a pledge, even the gift of the Holy Spirit.
“Whoever believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God; and everyone that loves Him that begot Him loves Him also that is begotten of Him.
By this we know that we love the children of God, because we love God and do His commandments.
For this is the love of God: that we keep His commandments.”

1. I suppose you remember, those of you who were present yesterday, what point in the course of this epistle our exposition has reached: namely, “He who does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?
And this commandment we have from Him, that he who loves God should love his brother also.”
Thus far we have discoursed.
Let us see, then, what comes next in order.
“Whoever believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God.”
Who is he that does not believe that Jesus is the Christ?
He who does not live as Christ commanded.
For many say, “I believe”: but faith without works does not save.
Now the work of faith is love, as Paul the apostle says, “And faith which works by love.”
Your past works, indeed, before you believed, were either none, or if they seemed good, were worth nothing.

For if they were none, you were like a man without feet, or with sore feet, unable to walk; but if they seemed good, before you believed, you did indeed run, but by running aside from the way you went astray instead of coming to the goal.
It is for us, then, both to run, and to run in the way.
He who runs aside from the way runs to no purpose, or rather runs only to toil.
He goes the more astray, the more he runs aside from the way.
What is the way by which we run?
Christ has told us, “I am the Way.”
What is the home to which we run?
“I am the Truth.”
By Him you run, to Him you run, in Him you rest.
But so that we might run by Him, He reached even to us: for we were far off, foreigners in a far country.
It was not enough that we were in a far country; we were also so feeble that we could not stir.
As a Physician, He came to the sick; as a Way, He extended Himself to those who were in a far country.
Let us be saved by Him; let us walk in Him.
This is what it is to “believe that Jesus is the Christ,” as Christians believe, who are Christians not in name only, but in deeds and in life—not as the devils believe.
For “the devils also believe and tremble,” as the Scripture tells us.
What more could the devils believe than to say, “We know who You are, the Son of God”?
What the devils said, Peter also said.
When the Lord asked them who He was, and whom men said that He was, the disciples answered Him, “Some say that You are John the Baptist; some, Elijah; and others, Jeremiah, or one of the prophets.
He says to them, But whom do you say that I am?
And Peter answered and said, You are the Christ, the Son of the Living God.”
And this he heard from the Lord: “Blessed are you, Simon Barjona; for flesh and blood did not reveal it to you, but My Father in heaven.”
See what praises follow this faith.
“You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build My Church.”
What does “Upon this rock I will build My Church” mean?
Upon this faith; upon what has been said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the Living God.
Upon this rock,” He says, “I will build My Church.”
Mighty praise! So then, Peter says, “You are the Christ, the Son of the Living God”; the devils also say, “We know who You are, the Son of God, the Holy One of God.”
Peter said this, and the devils said this too: the words the same, the mind not the same.
And how is it clear that Peter said this with love?
Because a Christian’s faith is with love, but a devil’s is without love.
How without love? Peter said this so that he might embrace Christ; the devils said it so that Christ might depart from them.
For before they said, “We know who You are, the Son of God,” they said, “What have we to do with You?
Why have You come to destroy us before the time?”
It is one thing, then, to confess Christ so that you may hold Christ, another thing to confess Christ so that you may drive Christ away from you.
So then you see that in the sense in which he says here, “Whoever believes,” it is a faith of one’s own, not a faith such as one has in common with many.
Therefore, brethren, let none of the heretics say to you, “We also believe.”
For this is why I have given you an example from the case of the devils: so that you may not rejoice in the words of believing, but examine well the deeds of the life.
2. Let us see, then, what it is to believe in Christ; what it is to believe that Jesus is the Christ.
He proceeds: “Whoever believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God.”
But what is it to believe that?
“And everyone that loves Him that begot Him loves Him also that is begotten of Him.”
To faith he has immediately joined love, because faith without love is worth nothing.
With love, it is the faith of a Christian; without love, the faith of a devil: but those who do not believe are worse than devils, more stupid than devils.
Some man will not believe in Christ: so far, he is not even on a par with the devils.
A person does now believe in Christ, but hates Christ: he has the confession of faith in fear of punishment, not in love of the crown; so the devils also feared to be punished.

Add love to this faith, so that it may become a faith such as the apostle Paul speaks of, a “faith which works by love”: you have found a Christian, found a citizen of Jerusalem, found a fellow citizen of the angels, found a pilgrim sighing on the way: join yourself to him, he is your fellow traveler; run with him, if indeed you also are this.
“Everyone that loves Him that begot Him loves Him also that is begotten of Him.”
Who “begot”? The Father.
Who “is begotten”? The Son.
What then does he say?
“Everyone that loves the Father loves the Son.”
3. “In this we know that we love the sons of God.”
What is this, brethren?

Just now he was speaking of the Son of God, not of sons of God: see, here one Christ was set before us to contemplate, and we were told, “Whoever believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God: and everyone that loves Him that begot,” that is, the Father, “loves Him also that is begotten of Him,” that is, the Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.
And he goes on: “In this we know that we love the sons of God,” as if he had been about to say, “In this we know that we love the Son of God.”

He has said “the sons of God,” whereas just before he was speaking of the Son of God—because the sons of God are the Body of the only Son of God, and since He is the Head and we the members, it is one Son of God.

Therefore he who loves the sons of God loves the Son of God, and he who loves the Son of God loves the Father; nor can anyone love the Father unless he loves the Son, and he who loves the sons also loves the Son of God.
What sons of God?
The members of the Son of God.
And by loving he himself becomes a member, and through love comes to be in the frame of the body of Christ, so that there shall be one Christ, loving Himself.
For when the members love one another, the body loves itself.
“And whether one member suffers, all the members suffer along with it; or one member is honored, all the members rejoice along with it.”
And then he goes on to say, “Now you are the body of Christ, and members.”
John was speaking just before of brotherly love, and said, “He who does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?”
But if you love your brother, perhaps you love your brother and do not love Christ?
How could that be, when you love members of Christ?
When therefore you love members of Christ, you love Christ; when you love Christ, you love the Son of God; when you love the Son of God, you love the Father also.
Love, therefore, cannot be separated into parts.
Choose what you will love; the rest follow you.
Suppose you say, I love God alone, God the Father.
You lie: if you love, you do not love Him alone; but if you love the Father, you love the Son also.

Look, you say, I love the Father, and I love the Son: but only this—God the Father and God the Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, who ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father, that Word by whom all things were made, and “the Word was made flesh, and dwelt in us”: this alone I love.
You lie; for if you love the Head, you love the members also; but if you do not love the members, neither do you love the Head.
Do you not tremble at the voice uttered by the Head from heaven on behalf of His members, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting ME?”
The persecutor of His members He called His persecutor; His lover, the lover of His members.
Now what His members are, you know, brethren: none other than the Church of God.
“In this we know that we love the sons of God, in that we love God.”
And how? Are not the sons of God one thing, and God Himself another?
But he who loves God loves His precepts.
And what are the precepts of God?
“A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another.”

Let no one excuse himself by another love, for another love; so, and only so, is it with this love: as the love itself is bound together in one, so it makes one all that hang upon it, and like fire it melts them down into one.
It is gold: the lump is melted and becomes some one thing.
But unless the heat of charity is applied, there can be no melting down of many into one.
“That we love God”—by this “we know that we love the sons of God.”
4. And by what do we know that we love the sons of God?
By this: “that we love God, and do His commandments.”
We sigh here, because of the hardness of doing the commandments of God.
Hear what follows. O man, at what do you toil in loving?
In loving avarice. What you love is loved with toil: there is no toil in loving God.
Avarice will command you to labors, perils, severe hardships and tribulations; and you will do its bidding.
To what end? So that you may have that with which you will fill your chest, and lose your peace of mind.
Perhaps you felt more secure before you had it than since you began to have it.
See what avarice has commanded you.
You have filled your house, and are in dread of robbers; you have gotten gold, and lost your sleep.
See what avarice has commanded you.
Do it—and you did.
What does God command you?
Love Me. You love gold; you will seek gold, and perhaps not find it: whoever seeks Me, I am with him.
You will love honor, and perhaps not attain it: who ever loved Me and did not attain?
God says to you: You would make yourself a patron, or a powerful friend; you seek a way to his favor by means of some other person of lower rank.
Love Me, God says to you: favor with Me is not had by working through someone else; your love itself makes Me present to you.
What is sweeter than this love, brethren?
It is not without reason that you heard just now in the Psalm, “The unrighteous told me of delights, but not as Your law is, O Lord.”
What is the Law of God?
The commandment of God.
What is the commandment of God?
That “new commandment,” which is called new because it makes new: “A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another.”
Hear that this is the law of God.
The apostle says, “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ.”
This, even this, is the consummation of all our works: love.
In it is the end: for this we run; to it we run; when we have come to it, we shall rest.
5. You have heard in the Psalm, “I have seen the end of all perfection.”
He has said, I have seen the end of all perfection: what had he seen?

Do we think that he had climbed to the peak of some very high and pointed mountain, and looked out from there and seen the compass of the earth and the circles of the round world, and therefore said, “I have seen the end of all perfection”?

If this is a thing to be praised, let us ask the Lord for eyes of flesh so sharp-sighted that we shall need only some exceedingly high mountain on earth, so that from its summit we may see the end of all perfection.
Do not go far: look, I tell you, it is here; climb the mountain, and see the end.
Christ is the Mountain; come to Christ: from there you see the end of all perfection.
What is this end?

Ask Paul: “But the end of the commandment is charity, from a pure heart, and a good conscience, and faith without pretense”; and in another place, “Charity is the fullness,” or fulfillment, “of the law.”
What is so finished and complete as “fullness”?
For, brethren, the apostle here uses “end” in a way of praise.
Think not of consumption, but of consummation.
For it is in one sense that one says, I have finished my bread, and in another, I have finished my coat.
I have finished the bread by eating it; the coat, by making it.
In both cases the word is “end,” “finish”: but the bread is finished by being consumed, the coat is finished by being made; the bread, so as to be no more; the coat, so as to be complete.
In this sense, therefore, take this word “end” also, when the Psalm is read and you hear it said, “On the end, a Psalm of David.”
You are forever hearing this in the Psalms, and you should know what you hear.
What does “On the end” mean?—“For Christ is the end of the law to everyone who believes.”
And what does “Christ is the end” mean?
Because Christ is God, and “the end of the commandment is charity,” and “Charity is God”: because Father and Son and Holy Spirit are One.
There He is the End for you; elsewhere He is the Way.
Do not get stuck in the way, and so never come to the end.
Whatever else you come to, pass beyond it, until you come to the end.
What is the end?
It is good for me to “hold fast to God.”
Have you laid fast hold on God? You have finished the way: you shall abide in your own country.
Mark well! Someone seeks money: let it not be the end for you; pass on, as a traveler in a strange land.
But if you love it, you are entangled by avarice; avarice will be shackles on your feet: you can make no more progress.
Pass this also, therefore: seek the end.
You seek health of body: still, do not stop there.
For what is it, this health of the body, which death brings to an end, which sickness weakens—a feeble, mortal, fleeting thing?
Seek it, indeed, lest perhaps ill health hinder your good works: but for that very reason the end is not there, for it is sought for the sake of something else.
Whatever is sought for the sake of something else, the end is not there: whatever is loved for its own sake, and freely, the end is there.
You seek honors; perhaps you seek them in order to do something, so that you may accomplish something and so please God: do not love the honor itself, lest you stop there.
Do you seek praise? If you seek God’s, you do well; if you seek your own, you do ill; you stop short on the way.
But look, you are loved, you are praised: do not count it joy when you are praised in yourself; be praised in the Lord, so that you may sing, “In the Lord shall my soul be praised.”
You deliver some good discourse, and your discourse is praised.
Let it not be praised as yours; the end is not there.
If you set the end there, there is an end of you: but an end, not so that you are perfected, but so that you are consumed.
Then let your discourse not be praised as coming from you, as being yours.
But how should it be praised? As the Psalm says, “In God will I praise the discourse, in God will I praise the word.”
By this, what follows there will come to pass in you: “In God have I hoped; I will not fear what man can do to me.”
For when all that is yours is praised in God, there is no fear that your praise will be lost, since God does not fail.
Pass this also, therefore.
6. See, brethren, how many things we pass in which the end is not.
These we use as by the way; we take, as it were, our refreshment at the resting places on our journey, and pass on.
Where, then, is the end?
“Beloved, we are sons of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be”; this is said here, in this epistle.
As yet, then, we are on the way; as yet, wherever we come, we must pass on, until we attain to some end.
“We know that when He shall appear, we shall be like Him, for we shall see Him as He is.
That is the end; there, perpetual praising; there, Alleluia always without fail.
This, then, is the end he has spoken of in the Psalm: “I have seen the end of all perfection”; and as though it were said to him, What is the end you have seen?
“Your commandment, exceedingly broad.”
This is the end: the breadth of the commandment.
The breadth of the commandment is charity, because where charity is, there is no confinement.
In this breadth, this wide room, was the apostle when he said, “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians, our heart is enlarged: you are not confined in us.”
In this, then, is “Your commandment exceedingly broad.”
What is the broad commandment?
“A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another.”
Charity, then, is not confined.
Would you rather not be confined here on earth?
Dwell in the broad room.
For whatever man may do to you, he shall not confine you, because you love what man cannot harm: you love God, love the brotherhood, love the law of God, love the Church of God: it shall be forever.
You labor here on earth, but you shall come to the promised enjoyment.
Who can take from you what you love?
If no one can take from you what you love, you sleep secure: or rather, you keep watch secure, lest by sleeping you lose what you love.
For not without reason is it said, “Enlighten my eyes, lest at any time I sleep in death.”
Those who shut their eyes against charity fall asleep in the lusts of carnal delights.
Be wakeful, therefore. For these are the delights: to eat, to drink, to revel in luxury, to play, to hunt; all evils follow these vain pomps.
Are we ignorant that they are delights? Who can deny that they delight?
But the law of God is more beloved.
Cry out against such persuaders: “The unrighteous have told me of delights: but not such as Your law, O Lord.”
This delight remains. It not only remains as the goal to which you may come, but also calls you back when you flee.
7. “For this is the love of God, that we keep His commandments.”
You have already heard, “On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.”
See how He would not have you divide yourself over a multitude of pages: “On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.”
On what two commandments?
“You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind.
And, you shall love your neighbor as yourself.
On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.”
See here what commandments this whole epistle speaks of.
Therefore hold fast to love, and set your minds at rest.
Why are you afraid that you may do evil to someone?
Who does evil to the man he loves?
Love: it is impossible to do this without doing good.
But perhaps you rebuke him?
It is kindness that does it, not fierceness.
But perhaps you beat him?
You do this for discipline’s sake, because the kindness of your love will not let you leave him undisciplined.
And indeed these different and contrary results somehow come about: sometimes hatred uses winning ways, and charity shows itself fierce.

A person hates his enemy and feigns friendship for him: he sees him doing some evil, and he praises him; he wants him to go headlong, wants him to go blindly over the precipice of his lusts, perhaps never to return; he praises him, “For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul”; he applies to him the ointment of flattery; see, he hates, and he praises.

Another sees his friend doing something of the same sort; he calls him back; if he will not listen, he uses even words of reproof, he scolds, he quarrels: there are times when it comes to this, that one must even quarrel!
See, hatred shows itself winningly gentle, and charity quarrels!
Do not fix your attention on the words of seeming kindness, or on the seeming cruelty of the rebuke; look into the vein they come from; seek the root from which they proceed.
The one is gentle and smooth in order to deceive; the other quarrels in order to correct.
Well then, brethren, it is not for us to enlarge your heart: obtain from God the gift of loving one another.

Love all men, even your enemies, not because they are your brethren, but so that they may be your brethren; so that you may at all times be on fire with brotherly love, whether toward him who has become your brother, or toward your enemy, so that by being loved he may become your brother.
Wherever you love a brother, you love a friend.
Now he is with you, now he is bound to you in unity, yes, catholic unity.
If you are living rightly, you love a brother made out of an enemy.
But you love some man who has not yet believed in Christ, or, if he has believed, believes as the devils do: you rebuke his vanity.
Love him, and that with a brotherly love: he is not yet a brother, but you love him so that he may be a brother.
Well then, all our love is a brotherly love, toward Christians, toward all His members.
The discipline of charity, my brethren—its strength, flowers, fruit, beauty, pleasantness, food, drink, nourishment, embracing—has no satiety in it.
If it delights us so while we are in a foreign land, how we shall rejoice in our own country!
8. Let us run then, my brethren, let us run, and love Christ.
What Christ? Jesus Christ.
Who is He? The Word of God.
And how did He come to the sick?
“The Word was made flesh, and dwelt in us.”
What the Scripture foretold is fulfilled, then: “Christ must suffer, and rise again from the dead on the third day.”
His body, where is it?
His members, where do they toil?
Where must you be, so that you may be under your Head?
“And that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in His name through all nations, beginning at Jerusalem.”
There let your charity be spread abroad.
Christ says, and the Psalm—that is, the Spirit of God—says, “Your commandment is exceedingly broad”; and yet, if you please, some man would have charity confined to Africa!
Extend your charity over the whole earth if you would love Christ, for Christ’s members are throughout all the earth.
If you love only a part, you are divided; if you are divided, you are not in the body; if you are not in the body, you are not under the Head.
What does it profit you that you believe and blaspheme?
You adore Him in the Head, and blaspheme Him in the Body.
He loves His Body.
If you have cut yourself off from His Body, the Head has not cut itself off from its Body.
To no purpose do you honor Me, your Head cries to you from on high, to no purpose do you honor Me.

It is just as if a man wanted to kiss your head and tread on your feet: perhaps with hobnailed boots he would crush your feet while he clasps your head and kisses it: would you not cry out in the middle of the words with which he honors you, and say, What are you doing, man? You are treading on me.
You would not say, You are treading on my head; for the head he honored; but the head would cry out more for the members trodden on than for itself because it was honored.
Does not the head itself cry out, I want none of your honor; do not tread on me?
Now say, if you can, How have I trodden on you? Say that to the head: I wanted to kiss you, I wanted to embrace you.
But do you not see, you fool, that what you would embrace reaches, by virtue of a certain unity which binds the whole frame together, to that which you tread on?
Above you honor me, below you tread on me.
What you tread on feels more pain than what you honor feels joy.
In what way does the tongue cry out?
“It hurts me.” It does not say, “It hurts my foot,” but, “It hurts me,” it says.
O tongue, who has touched you? Who has struck? Who has goaded? Who has pricked?
No one; but I am bound together with the parts that are trodden on.
How would you have me not be pained, when I am not separate?

9. Our Lord Jesus Christ, then, ascending into heaven on the fortieth day, commended to us His Body, where it would continue to lie, for this reason: because He saw that many would honor Him because He has ascended into heaven, and He saw that their honoring Him is useless if they trample on His members here on earth.
And so that no one would err and, while adoring the Head in heaven, trample on the feet on earth, He told us where His members would be.
For when He was about to ascend, He spoke His last words on earth: after those same words He spoke no more on earth.
The Head, about to ascend into heaven, commended His members on earth to us and departed.
From then on you do not find Christ speaking on earth; you find Him speaking, but from heaven.
And even from heaven, why?
Because His members on earth were being trodden on.
For to Saul the persecutor He said from on high, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?”
I have ascended into heaven, but I still lie on earth: here I sit at the right hand of the Father, but there I still hunger, thirst, and am a stranger.
In what way, then, did He commend His Body to us when He was about to ascend into heaven?
When the disciples asked Him, saying, “Lord, will You at this time present Yourself, and when will the kingdom of Israel be?”

He answered, now at the point of departing, “It is not for you to know the time which the Father has put in His own power; but you shall receive strength from the Holy Spirit coming upon you, and you shall be witnesses to Me.”
See where His Body is spread abroad; see where He will not be trodden on: “You shall be witnesses to Me, to Jerusalem, and to Judea, and even to all the earth.”
See where I lie, I who am ascending!
For I ascend, because I am the Head: My Body still lies below.
Where does it lie? Throughout the whole earth.
Beware that you do not strike, beware that you do not hurt, beware that you do not trample: these are the last words of Christ as He was about to go into heaven.

Look at a sick man languishing on his bed, lying in his house, worn out with sickness, at death’s door, his soul as it were already between his teeth: anxious, it may be, about something dear to him, which he greatly loves, when it comes into his mind he calls his heirs and says to them, I beg you, do this.
He, as it were, holds back his soul by a violent effort, so that it may not depart before those words are made sure.
When he has dictated those last words, he breathes out his soul, and he is carried as a corpse to the tomb.
His heirs—how do they remember the last words of the dying man?
What if someone should stand up and say to them, Do not do it: what would they say?
“What? Shall I not do what my father, in the act of breathing out his soul, commanded me with his last breath, the last word of his that sounded in my ears as my father was departing this life?
Whatever other words of his I may disregard, his last ones have a stronger hold on me: since then I never saw him again, never again heard him speak.”

Brethren, think with Christian hearts: if to a man’s heirs his words, spoken when he was about to go to the tomb, are so sweet, so welcome, so weighty, what must we think of the last words of Christ, spoken not when He was about to go back to the tomb, but to ascend into heaven!

As for the man who lived and is dead, his soul is hurried off to other places, his body is laid in the earth, and whether these words of his are carried out or not makes no difference to him: he now has something else to do, or something else to suffer: either he rejoices in Abraham’s bosom, or in eternal fire he longs for a drop of water, while his corpse lies there without feeling in the tomb; and yet the last words of the dying man are kept.
What can those expect who do not keep the last words of Him who sits in heaven, who sees from on high whether they are despised or not despised?
The words of Him who said, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?”—who keeps account, until the judgment, of all that He sees His members suffer?
10. And what have we done? they say.
We are the persecuted, not the persecutors.
You are the persecutors, you wretched men.
In the first place, in that you have divided the Church.
The sword of the tongue is mightier than the sword of steel.
Hagar, Sarah’s maid, was proud, and she was afflicted by her mistress for her pride.
That was discipline, not punishment.
Accordingly, when she had gone away from her mistress, what did the angel say to her?
“Return to your mistress.”
Then, O carnal soul, like a proud bondwoman, suppose you have suffered some trouble for discipline’s sake, why do you rage?
“Return to your mistress”: hold fast the peace of the Church.
See, the Gospels are brought out, we read where the Church is spread abroad: men argue against us and say to us, “Betrayers!”
Betrayers of what? Christ commends His Church to us, and you do not believe: shall I believe you when you revile my parents?
Would you have me believe you about the “betrayers”?
First believe Christ yourself.
What is worth believing?
Christ is God, you are man: which ought to be believed first?
Christ has spread His Church abroad over all the earth: I say it—despise me; the gospel speaks—beware.
What does the gospel say?
“It was necessary for Christ to suffer, and to rise again from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in His name.”
Where there is remission of sins, there the Church is.

How the Church? Why, to her it was said, “To you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven.”
Where is this remission of sins spread abroad?
“Through all nations, beginning at Jerusalem.”

See, believe Christ! But because you are well aware that if you believe Christ you will have nothing to say about “betrayers,” you insist on having me believe you when you speak evil against my parents, rather than believing for yourself what Christ foretold!
1. All the faithful know the marriage of the king’s son and his feast, and the Lord’s Table is spread and open to all of them who are willing.
But it matters for each one to see how he approaches, even when he is not forbidden to approach It.
For the Holy Scriptures teach us that there are two feasts of the Lord: one to which the good and the evil come, the other to which the evil do not come.
So then the feast of which we have just now heard when the Gospel was being read has both good and evil guests.
All who excused themselves from this feast are evil; but not all those who entered in are good.
You therefore who are the good guests at this feast I address, you who have in your minds the words, “He who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself.”
All of you who are such I address, that you do not look for the good outside, and that you bear with the evil within.
2. I do not doubt that you wish to hear, beloved, who they are of whom I have spoken in my address, saying that they should not look for the good outside and should bear with the evil within.
If all within are evil, whom do I address?
If all within are good, whom did I advise them to bear with as evil?
Let me first, then, with the Lord’s help, get out of this difficulty as best I can.
If you consider “good” perfectly and strictly speaking, no one is good but God alone.
You have the Lord saying most plainly, “Why do you call Me good? No one is good but One, that is, God.”
How then can that marriage feast have good and bad guests, if “no one is good but God alone”?
In the first place you ought to know that in a certain sense we are all evil.
Yes, doubtless in a certain sense we are all evil; but in no sense are we all good.
For can we compare ourselves with the Apostles, to whom the Lord Himself said, “If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children”?
If we consider the Scriptures, there was only one evil man among the twelve Apostles, with reference to whom the Lord said in a certain place, “And you are clean, but not all.”
But yet in addressing them all together, He said, “If you, being evil.”
Peter heard this, John heard this, Andrew heard this, all the rest of the eleven Apostles heard it.
What did they hear?
“If you, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask Him?”
When they heard that they were evil, they were in despair; but when they heard that God in heaven was their Father, they revived.
“You, being evil”—what then is due to the evil but punishment?
“How much more will your Father who is in heaven?”
What is due to children but reward?
In the name “evil” is the dread of punishment; in the name “children” is the hope of heirs.
3. In a certain respect, then, they were evil who in another respect were good.
For to those to whom it is said, “You, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children,” is added immediately, “How much more will your Father who is in heaven?”
He is then the Father of the evil, but not of those who are to be left so; because He is the Physician of those who are to be cured.
In a certain sense, then, they were evil.

And yet those guests of the Householder at the King’s marriage were not, I suppose, of that number of whom it was said, “they invited good and bad,” so as to be reckoned among the number of the bad, who, as we have heard, were shut out in the person of the one who was found not to have a wedding garment.
In a certain respect, I repeat, they were bad who yet were good; and in a certain respect they were good who yet were bad.
Hear John on the respect in which they were bad: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”
See in what respect they were bad: because they had sin.
In what respect were they good?
“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”

If then we should say, on the principle of this interpretation which you have now heard me bring, as I think, out of the sacred Scriptures—namely, that the same men are in a certain way good and in a certain way bad—if we should wish to take in this sense the words, “they invited good and bad,” meaning the same persons as at once good and bad; if we should wish to take them so, we are not permitted to do so, because of that one who was found “not having a wedding garment,” and who was not merely “cast out” so as to be deprived of that feast, but so as to be condemned to the punishment of everlasting darkness.
4. But someone will say, What of one man? What strange, what great matter is it, if one among the crowd “not having a wedding garment” crept in unnoticed by the servants of the Householder?
Could it be said because of that one, “they invited good and bad”?
Pay attention, therefore, my brethren, and understand.
That one man represented one class; for they were many.
Here some attentive hearer may answer me and say, “I have no wish for you to tell me your guesses; I want to have it proved to me that that one represented many.”
With the Lord’s present help, I will prove it clearly; nor will I search far in order to be able to prove it.
God will help me with His own words in this place, and through my ministry He will furnish you with a plain proof of it.
“The Master of the house came in to see the guests.”

See, my brethren, the servants’ business was only to invite and bring in the good and bad; see that it is not said that the servants took notice of the guests, found among them a man who did not have on a wedding garment, and spoke to him.
This is not written.
The Master of the house saw him, the Master of the house discovered him, the Master of the house inspected him, the Master of the house separated him out.
It was not right to pass over this.
But I have undertaken to establish another point: how that one signifies many.
“The Master of the house” then “came in to see the guests, and He found there a man who did not have on a wedding garment.
And He said to him, Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?
And he was speechless.”
For He who questioned him was One to whom he could give no false reply.
The garment that was looked for is in the heart, not on the body; for had it been put on outwardly, it could not have been hidden even from the servants.
Where that wedding garment must be put on, hear in the words, “Let Your priests be clothed with righteousness.”
Of that garment the Apostle speaks: “If indeed we shall be found clothed, and not naked.”
Therefore he who escaped the notice of the servants was discovered by the Lord.
Being questioned, he is speechless: he is bound, cast out, and condemned, one for many.
I have said, Lord, that You teach us that in this You give warning to all.
Recall with me, then, my brethren, the words which you have heard, and you will at once discover, at once determine, that that one was many.
True, it was one man whom the Lord questioned; to one He said, “Friend, how did you come in here?”
It was one who was speechless, and of that same one it was said, “Bind him hand and foot, and cast him into outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”
Why? “For many are called, but few chosen.”
How can anyone contradict this plain showing of the truth?
“Cast him,” He says, “into outer darkness.”
“Him”—that one man, assuredly—of whom the Lord says, “for many are called, but few chosen.”
So then it is the few who are not cast out.
It is true he was only one man “who did not have the wedding garment.
Cast him out.” But why is he cast out?
“For many are called, but few chosen.”
Leave the few alone; cast out the many.
It is true that man was only one.
Yet undoubtedly that one not only was many, but those many far surpassed in number the number of the good.
For the good are also many; but in comparison with the bad, they are few.
In the crop there is much wheat; compare it with the chaff, and the grains are few.
The same persons, considered in themselves, are many; in comparison with the bad, they are few.
How do we prove that in themselves they are many?
“Many will come from the east and from the west.”
Where will they come to?
To that feast into which both good and bad enter.
But speaking of another feast, He added, “and will sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.”
That is the feast which the bad will not approach.
Let the feast which now is be received worthily, that we may attain to the other.
The same, then, are many who are also few: in themselves many, in comparison with the bad few.
Therefore what does the Lord say?
He found one, and said, “Let the many be cast out, let the few remain.”
For to say, “many are called, but few chosen,” is nothing else than to show plainly who in this present feast are counted such as to be brought to that other feast, where no bad men will come.
5. What is it, then?
I would not have all of you who approach the Lord’s Table, which is in this life, be with the many who are to be shut out, but with the few who are to be kept.
And how will you be able to attain to this?
Take “the wedding garment.”
You will say, “Explain this ‘wedding garment’ to us.”

Without a doubt, that is the garment which none have but the good, who are to be left at the feast, kept for that other feast to which no bad man approaches, who are to be brought safely there by the grace of the Lord; these have “the wedding garment.”
Let us then, my brethren, seek among the faithful for those who have something which bad men do not have, and this will be “the wedding garment.”
If we speak of sacraments, you see how these are common to the bad and the good.
Is it Baptism? Without Baptism, it is true, no one attains to God; but not everyone who has Baptism attains to Him.
I cannot therefore understand Baptism—the Sacrament itself, that is—to be “the wedding garment”; for this garment I see in the good, I see in the bad.
Perhaps it is the Altar, or That which is received at the Altar.
But no; we see that many eat, and “eat and drink judgment to themselves.”
What is it then?
Is it fasting? The wicked fast also.
Is it running together to the church?
The wicked run there also.
Lastly, is it miracles?
Not only do both the good and the bad perform them, but sometimes the good do not perform them.
See, among the ancient people Pharaoh’s magicians worked miracles, the Israelites did not; among the Israelites, only Moses and Aaron worked them; the rest did not, but saw, and feared, and believed.
Were the magicians of Pharaoh who did miracles better men than the people of Israel who could not do them? And yet that people was the people of God.
In the Church itself, hear the Apostle: “Are all prophets?
Do all have the gifts of healing?
Do all speak with tongues?”
6. What then is that “wedding garment”?
This is the wedding garment: “Now the end of the commandment,” says the Apostle, “is love out of a pure heart, and of a good conscience, and of genuine faith.”
This is “the wedding garment.”
Not love of any kind whatever; for very often those who share together in an evil conscience seem to love one another.

Those who commit robberies together, who love together the harmful arts of sorcery and the theater, who join together in the shouting at the chariot race or the wild beast fight—these very often love one another; but in these there is no “love out of a pure heart, and of a good conscience, and of genuine faith.
The wedding garment” is love such as this.
“Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not love, I have become as sounding brass and a tinkling cymbal.”
Tongues have come in alone, and it is said to them, “How did you come in here without a wedding garment?”
“Though,” he said, “I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not love, I am nothing.”
See, these are the miracles of men who very often do not have “the wedding garment.”
“Though,” he says, “I have all these, and have not Christ, I am nothing.”
Is then “the gift of prophecy” nothing? Is then “the knowledge of mysteries” nothing?
It is not that these are nothing; but “I,” if I have them, “and have not love, am nothing.”
How many good things profit nothing without this one good thing!

If then I have not love, though I give alms freely to the poor, though I have come to the confession of Christ’s Name even to blood and fire, these things may be done even out of the love of glory, and so are empty.

Because, then, they may be done even out of the love of glory, and so be empty, and not through the rich love of a godly affection, he names them all expressly as well, and you must give ear to them: “Though I distribute all my goods for the use of the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and have not love, it profits me nothing.”
This then is “the wedding garment.”
Question yourselves; if you have it, you may be without fear at the Feast of the Lord.
In one and the same man there exist two things, love and desire.
Let love be born in you, if it is not yet born; and if it is born, let it be nourished, fostered, increased.

But as to that desire—though in this life it cannot be utterly extinguished, “for if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us,” and in so far as desire is in us, so far we are not without sin—let love increase and desire decrease, so that the one, that is, love, may one day be perfected, and desire be consumed.
Put on “the wedding garment”: I address you who do not yet have it.

You are already within, already you approach the Feast, and still you do not yet have the garment to do honor to the Bridegroom; “You are still seeking your own things, not the things which are Jesus Christ’s.”
For “the wedding garment” is put on in honor of the union—the union, that is, of the Bridegroom to the Bride.
You know the Bridegroom; it is Christ.
You know the Bride; it is the Church.
Pay honor to the Bride, pay honor to the Bridegroom.
If you pay due honor to them both, you will be their children.
Therefore make progress in this.
Love the Lord, and so learn to love yourselves; so that when by loving the Lord you have loved yourselves, you may safely love your neighbor as yourselves.
For when I find a man who does not love himself, how shall I entrust to him his neighbor, whom he should love as himself?
And who is there, you will say, who does not love himself?
Who is there? See, “He who loves iniquity hates his own soul.”
Does he love himself who loves his body and hates his soul, to his own hurt, to the hurt of both his body and soul?
And who loves his own soul?
He who loves God with all his heart and with all his mind.
To such a one I would at once entrust his neighbor.
“Love your neighbor as yourselves.”
7. Someone may say, “Who is my neighbor?”
Every man is your neighbor.
Did we not all have the same two parents?
Animals of every species are neighbors to one another—the dove to the dove, the leopard to the leopard, the asp to the asp, the sheep to the sheep—and is man not neighbor to man?
Call to mind the ordering of the creation.
God spoke; the waters brought forth swimming creatures, great whales, fish, birds, and suchlike things.
Did all the birds come from one bird?
Did all vultures come from one vulture?
Did all doves come from one dove?
Did all snakes come from one snake? Or all gilt-heads from one gilt-head? Or all sheep from one sheep?
No, the earth assuredly brought forth all these kinds together.
But when it came to man, the earth did not bring forth man.

One father was made for us—not even two, father and mother: one father, I say, was made for us, not even two, father and mother; but out of the one father came the one mother; the one father came from no one, but was made by God, and the one mother came out of him.
Note, then, the nature of our race: we flowed out of one fountain; and because that one was turned to bitterness, we all became, from a good olive tree, a wild olive tree.
And so grace came also.
One begot us to sin and death, yet as one race, yet as neighbors to one another, yet as not merely alike, but related to each other.
There came One against one: against the one who scattered, One who gathers.
So against the one who kills is the One who makes alive.
“For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.”
Now as whoever is born of the first dies, so whoever believes in Christ is made alive.
Provided, that is, that he has “the wedding garment,” and is invited as one who is to remain, and not to be cast out.
8. So then, my brethren, have love.
I have explained that this is the garment, this “wedding garment.”
Faith is praised—plainly it is praised; but what kind of faith this is, the Apostle distinguishes.
For certain people who boasted of faith and did not have a good way of life, the Apostle James rebukes, saying, “You believe there is one God, you do well; the devils also believe and tremble.”
Call to mind with me why Peter was praised, why he was called blessed.
Was it because he said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God”?
He who pronounced him blessed regarded not the sound of the words, but the affection of the heart.
For would you know that Peter’s blessedness did not lie in these words?
The devils also said the same.
“We know You, who You are, the Son of God.”
Peter confessed Him to be “the Son of God”; the devils confessed Him to be “the Son of God.”
“Distinguish, my lord, distinguish between the two.”
I do make a plain distinction.
Peter spoke in love, the devils from fear.
And again Peter says, “I am with You, even to death.”
The devils say, “What have we to do with You?”
So then, you who have come to the feast, do not glory in faith only.
Distinguish well the nature of this faith, and then “the wedding garment” is recognized in you.
Let the Apostle make the distinction, let him teach us: “neither circumcision avails anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith.”
Tell us, what faith? Do not even the devils believe and tremble?
I will tell you, he says, and listen, I will now draw the distinction: “But faith which works by love.”
What faith, then, and of what kind?
“That which works by love.”
