“Though I have all knowledge,” he says, “and all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not love, I am nothing.”
Have faith with love; for love without faith you cannot have.
This I warn, this I urge, this in the name of the Lord I teach you, beloved: that you have faith with love; for you may possibly have faith without love.
I do not urge you to have faith, but love.
For you cannot have love without faith—the love, I mean, of God and your neighbor; where can it come from without faith?
How does he love God who does not believe in God?
How does the fool love God, “who says in his heart, There is no God”?
It is possible that you may believe that Christ has come and not love Christ.
But it is not possible that you should love Christ and yet say that Christ has not come.
9. So then, have faith with love.
This is the “wedding garment.”
You who love Christ, love one another, love your friends, love your enemies.
Do not let this be hard for you.
What then do you lose by it, when you gain so much?
What? Do you ask of God, as some great favor, that your enemy may die?
This is not “the wedding garment.”
Turn your thoughts to the Bridegroom Himself, hanging on the Cross for you and praying to His Father for His enemies: “Father,” He says, “forgive them, for they do not know what they do.”
You have seen the Bridegroom speaking thus; see too the friend of the Bridegroom, a guest “with the wedding garment.”
Look at the blessed Stephen, how he rebukes the Jews as though in rage and resentment: “You stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you have resisted the Holy Spirit.
Which of the Prophets have your fathers not killed?”
You have heard how severe he is with his tongue.
And at once you are ready to speak against anyone; and I wish it were against him who offends God, and not him who offends you.
Someone offends God, and you do not rebuke him; he offends you, and you cry out. Where is that “wedding garment”?
You have heard, therefore, how Stephen was severe; now hear how he loved.
He offended those whom he was rebuking, and was stoned by them.
And as he was being overwhelmed and bruised to death on every side by the hands of his furious persecutors and the blows of the stones, he first said, “Lord Jesus Christ, receive my spirit.”

Then, after he had prayed for himself standing, he bent the knee for those who were stoning him, and said, “Lord, do not lay this sin to their charge; let me die in my body, but let not these die in their souls.
And when he had said this, he fell asleep.”
After these words he added no more; he spoke them and departed; his last prayer was for his enemies.
Learn from this to have “the wedding garment.”

So you too, bend the knee and strike your forehead against the ground, and as you are about to approach the Table of the Lord, the Feast of the Holy Scriptures, do not say, “Oh, that my enemy might die!
Lord, if I have deserved anything from You, slay my enemy.”
Because if you do say so, do you not fear that He may answer you, “If I chose to slay your enemy, I would first slay you.
What! Do you glory because you have now come here invited?
Just think what you were only a little while ago.
Did you not blaspheme Me? Did you not mock Me? Did you not wish to wipe out My Name from the earth?
Yet now you applaud yourself because you have come here invited!
If I had slain you when you were My enemy, how could I have made you My friend?
Why, by your wicked prayers do you teach Me to do what I did not do in your own case?”
No, rather God says to you, “Let Me teach you to imitate Me.
When I was hanging on the Cross, I said, ‘Forgive them, for they do not know what they do.’
This lesson I taught My brave soldier.
Be My recruit against the devil.
In no other way will you fight at all unconquerably, unless you pray for your enemies.
Yet by all means ask this—yes, ask this very thing—ask that you may persecute your enemy; but ask it with discernment; distinguish well what you are asking.
See, a man is your enemy; answer Me, what is it in him that is at enmity with you?
Is it in this, that he is a man, that he is at enmity with you?
No. What then? That he is evil.
In that he is a man, in that he is what I made him, he is not at enmity with you.”
He says to you, “I did not make man evil; he became evil by disobedience, he who obeyed the devil rather than God.
What he has made himself is at enmity with you; in that he is evil, he is your enemy, not in that he is a man.
For I hear the word ‘man’ and ‘evil’; the one is the name of nature, the other of sin; the sin I cure, and the nature I preserve.”

And so your God says to you, “See, I do avenge you, I do slay your enemy; I take away what makes him evil, I preserve what makes him a man. Now if I have made him a good man, have I not slain your enemy and made him your friend?”
So go on asking what you are asking—not that the men may perish, but that these enmities of theirs may perish.
For if you pray for this, that the man may die, it is the prayer of one wicked man against another; and when you say, “Slay the wicked one,” God answers you, “Which of you?”
10. Extend your love, then, and do not limit it to your wives and children.
Such love is found even in beasts and sparrows.

You know how the sparrows and the swallows love their mates, how together they hatch their eggs and nourish their young together, by a kind of free and natural kindliness, and with no thought of a return.
For the sparrow does not say, “I will nourish my young, so that when I have grown old, they may feed me.”
He has no such thought; he loves and feeds them for love of them; he shows the affection of a parent and looks for no return.
And so, I know, I am sure, you love your children.
“For the children ought not to lay up for the parents, but the parents for the children.”
Yes, it is on this plea that many of you excuse your covetousness: that you are acquiring for your children and laying up for them.
But I say, extend your love, let this love grow; for to love wives and children is not yet that “wedding garment.”
Have faith toward God.
First love God. Extend yourselves out to God; and whomever you are able, draw on to God.
There is your enemy: let him be drawn to God.
There is a son, a wife, a servant: let them all be drawn to God.
There is a stranger: let him be drawn to God.
There is an enemy: let him be drawn to God.
Draw, draw on your enemy; by being drawn on, he will cease to be your enemy.

So let love be advanced, so let it be nourished, that being nourished it may be perfected; so let “the wedding garment” be put on; so let the image of God, after which we were created, be engraved anew in us by this our advancing.
For by sin it was bruised and worn away.
How is it bruised? How worn away?
When it is rubbed against the earth?
And what is “When it is rubbed against the earth”?
When it is worn by earthly lusts.
For “though man walks in this image, yet he is disquieted in vain.”
Truth is looked for in God’s image, not vanity.
By the love of the truth, then, let that image after which we were created be engraved anew, and His own tribute be rendered to our Caesar.

For so you have heard from the Lord’s answer, when the Jews tempted Him, as He said, “Why do you tempt Me, you hypocrites? Show Me the tribute money,” that is, the impress and inscription of the image.
Show me what you pay, what you get ready, what is demanded of you.
And “they showed Him a denarius”; and “He asked whose image and inscription it had.”
They answered, “Caesar’s.” So Caesar looks for his own image.
It is not Caesar’s will that what he ordered to be made should be lost to him, and surely it is not God’s will that what He has made should be lost to Him.
Caesar, my brethren, did not make the money; the masters of the mint make it; the workmen have their orders; he issues his commands to his ministers.
His image was stamped on the money; on the money was Caesar’s image.
And yet he requires what others have stamped; he puts it in his treasuries; he will not have it refused him.
Christ’s coin is man.
In him is Christ’s image, in him Christ’s Name, Christ’s gifts, Christ’s rules of duty.

1. The blessed Apostle, to show that the times when all the nations would believe in Christ had been foretold by the Prophets, brought forward this testimony where it is written, “And it shall be that whoever calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved.”

For in former times the name of the Lord who made heaven and earth was called upon among the Israelites only; the rest of the nations called upon mute and deaf idols, by whom they were not heard, or upon devils, by whom they were heard to their harm.
“But when the fullness of time came,” that was fulfilled which had been foretold, “And it shall be that whoever calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.”

Moreover, because the Jews, even those who believed in Christ, begrudged the Gospel to the Gentiles, and said that the Gospel ought not to be preached to those who were not circumcised; because against these the Apostle Paul brought forward this testimony, “And it shall be that whoever calls upon the Name of the Lord shall be saved,” he immediately added, to convince those who were unwilling that the Gospel should be preached to the Gentiles, the words, “But how shall they call upon Him in whom they have not believed? Or how shall they believe in Him of whom they have not heard? Or how shall they hear without a preacher? Or how shall they preach unless they are sent?”

Because, then, he said, “How shall they call upon Him in whom they have not believed?” you have not first learned the Lord’s Prayer and after that the Creed, but first the Creed, where you might know what to believe, and afterwards the Prayer, where you might know whom to call upon.
The Creed, then, has to do with faith, the Lord’s Prayer with prayer; because it is the one who believes who is heard when he calls.
2. But many ask for what they ought not to ask, not knowing what is good for them.
Therefore the one who prays must beware of two things: that he not ask what he ought not, and that he not ask from whom he ought not.
From the devil, from idols, from evil spirits, nothing must be asked.

From the Lord our God Jesus Christ, God the Father of Prophets and Apostles and Martyrs, from the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from God who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all things in them, from Him we must ask whatever we have to ask.
But we must beware that we do not ask of Him what we ought not to ask.
If, because we ought to ask for life, you ask it of mute and deaf idols, what does it profit you?
So if from God the Father, who is in heaven, you wish for the death of your enemies, what does it profit you?
Have you not heard or read in the Psalm in which the damnable end of the traitor Judas is foretold, how the prophecy spoke of him, “Let his prayer be turned into sin”?
If, then, you rise up and pray for evil on your enemies, your “prayer will be turned into sin.”
3. You have read in the Holy Psalms how the one who speaks in them calls down, as it would seem, many curses upon his enemies.
And surely, one may say, the one who speaks in the Psalms is a righteous man; why then does he so wish evil upon his enemies?

He does not wish it, but he foresees it; it is the prophecy of one who is telling things to come, not a vow of cursing; for the prophets knew by the Spirit to whom evil was appointed to happen, and to whom good; and by prophecy they spoke as if they wished for what they foresaw.
But how can you know whether the one for whom you are asking evil today may not tomorrow be a better man than yourself?
But you will say, I know him to be a wicked man.
Well, you must know that you are wicked too.
Although it may be that you take it upon yourself to judge another’s heart, which you do not know; but as for your own self, you know that you are wicked.
Do you not hear the Apostle saying, “I who was formerly a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and insolent; but I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly in unbelief”?

Now when the Apostle Paul persecuted the Christians, binding them wherever he found them, and dragged them to the Chief Priests to be questioned and punished, what do you think, brethren, did the Church pray against him, or for him?

Surely the Church of God, which had learned instruction from her Lord, who said as He hung upon the Cross, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do,” prayed in this way for Paul (or rather, as yet, Saul), that what was worked in him might be worked.

For when he says, “But I was unknown by face to the churches of Judea which are in Christ; they only heard that he who persecuted us in times past now preaches the faith which he once destroyed; and they glorified God in me,” why did they glorify God, except because they asked this of God before it came to pass?
4. Our Lord, then, first of all cut off “much speaking,” so that you would not bring a multitude of words to God, as though by your many words you would teach Him.
Therefore, when you pray, you need piety, not wordiness.
“For your Father knows what you need before you ask Him.”
Be unwilling, then, to use many words, for He knows what you need.
But lest perhaps anyone should say here, If He knows what we need, why should we use even a few words? Why should we pray at all?
He knows Himself; let Him then give what He knows we need.
Yes, but it is His will that you should pray, so that He may give to your longings, so that His gifts may not be lightly esteemed; seeing that He Himself has formed this longing desire in us.
The words, therefore, which our Lord Jesus Christ has taught us in His prayer are the rule and standard of our desires.
You may not ask for anything but what is written there.
5. “Therefore say,” He says, “Our Father, who is in heaven.”
Here you see that you have begun to have God for your Father.
You will have Him when you are born anew.
Although even now, before you are born, you have been conceived of His seed, as being on the eve of being brought forth in the font, the womb, as it were, of the Church.
“Our Father, who is in heaven.”
Remember, then, that you have a Father in heaven.
Remember that you were born of your father Adam to death, and that you are to be born anew of God the Father to life.
And what you say, say in your hearts.
Only let there be the earnest affection of prayer, and there will be the effectual answer of Him who hears prayer.
“Hallowed be Your Name.”
Why do you ask that God’s Name may be hallowed?
It is holy. Why then do you ask for that which is already holy?
And then, when you ask that His Name may be hallowed, do you not, as it were, pray to Him for Him, and not for yourself?
No. Understand it rightly, and it is for your own self that you ask.
For this is what you ask: that what is always holy in itself may be hallowed in you.
What is “be hallowed”?
“Be regarded as holy,” not be despised.
So then you see that the good you wish, you wish for your own self.
For if you despise the Name of God, it will be bad for you, and not for God.
6. “Your kingdom come.”
To whom do we speak? And will God’s kingdom not come if we do not ask for it?
For we speak of that kingdom which will be after the end of the world.
For God always has a kingdom; nor is He ever without a kingdom, He whom the whole creation serves.
But what kingdom, then, do you wish for?
That of which it is written in the Gospel, “Come, you blessed of My Father, receive the kingdom which is prepared for you from the beginning of the world.”
See, here is the kingdom of which we say, “Your kingdom come.”
We pray that it may come in us; we pray that we may be found in it.
For come it certainly will; but what will it profit you if it finds you at the left hand?
Therefore, here again it is for your own self that you wish well; for yourself you pray.
This is what you long for; this is the desire in your prayer, that you may so live that you may have a part in the kingdom of God, which is to be given to all the saints.
Therefore, when you say, “Your kingdom come,” you pray for yourself, that you may live well.
Let us have part in Your kingdom: let that come even to us which is to come to Your saints and righteous ones.
7. “Your will be done.”
What! If you do not say this, will God not do His will?
Remember what you have repeated in the Creed, “I believe in God the Father Almighty.”
If He is Almighty, why do you pray that His will may be done?
What, then, is this, “Your will be done”?
May it be done in me, so that I may not resist Your will.
Therefore here again it is for yourself that you pray, and not for God.
For the will of God will be done in you, even if it is not done by you.

For both in those to whom He shall say, “Come, you blessed of My Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the beginning of the world,” shall the will of God be done, that the saints and righteous may receive the kingdom; and in those to whom He shall say, “Depart into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels,” shall the will of God be done, that the wicked may be condemned to everlasting fire.
That His will may be done by you is another thing.
It is not, then, without cause, but so that it may be well with you, that you pray that His will may be done in you.
But whether it be well or ill with you, it will still be done in you; but oh, that it may be done by you also!
Why, then, do I say, “Your will be done in heaven and on earth,” and do not say, “Your will be done by heaven and earth”?
Because what is done by you, He Himself does in you.
Never is anything done by you which He Himself does not do in you.
Sometimes, indeed, He does in you what is not done by you; but never is anything done by you if He does not do it in you.
8. But what is “in heaven and on earth,” or “as in heaven so on earth”?
The Angels do Your will; may we do it also.
“Your will be done as in heaven so on earth.”
The mind is heaven, the flesh is earth.
When you say (if indeed you do say it) with the Apostle, “With my mind I serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin,” the will of God is done in heaven, but not yet on earth.

But when the flesh shall be in harmony with the mind, and “death shall be swallowed up in victory,” so that no carnal desires shall remain for the mind to be in conflict with; when strife in the earth shall have passed away, the war of the heart be over, and that be gone of which it is said, “The flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; for these are contrary to one another, so that you cannot do the things that you would”; when this war, I say, shall be over, and all sinful desire shall have been changed into love, nothing shall remain in the body to oppose the spirit, nothing to be tamed, nothing to be bridled, nothing to be trodden down; but the whole shall go on through concord to righteousness, and the will of God will be done in heaven and on earth.
“Your will be done in heaven and on earth.”
We wish for perfection when we pray for this.
“Your will be done as in heaven so on earth.”
In the Church the spiritual are heaven, the carnal are earth.
So then, “Your will be done as in heaven so on earth”; that as the spiritual serve You, so the carnal, being reformed, may serve You also.
“Your will be done as in heaven so on earth.”
There is yet another very spiritual meaning of it.
For we are admonished to pray for our enemies.
The Church is heaven, the enemies of the Church are earth.
What, then, is “Your will be done as in heaven so on earth”?
May our enemies believe, as we also believe in You! May they become friends, and end their hostilities!
They are earth, and therefore they are against us; may they become heaven, and they will be with us.
9. “Give us this day our daily bread.”
Now here it is evident that it is for ourselves we pray.
When you say, “Hallowed be Your Name,” it requires explanation how it is that you pray for yourself, not for God.

When you say, “Your will be done,” here again there is need of explanation, lest you think that you are wishing well to God in this prayer, that His will may be done, and not rather that you are praying for yourself.
When you say, “Your kingdom come,” this again must be explained, lest you think that you are wishing well to God in this prayer, that He may reign.
But from this point onward to the end of the Prayer, it is plain that we are praying to God for our own selves.
When you say, “Give us this day our daily bread,” you profess yourself to be God’s beggar.
But do not be ashamed of this; however rich any man may be on earth, he is still God’s beggar.
The beggar takes his stand before the rich man’s house; but the rich man himself stands before the door of the great Rich One.
Petition is made to him, and he makes his own petition.
If he were not in need, he would not knock at the ears of God in prayer.
And what does the rich man need?
I dare to say, the rich man needs even daily bread.
For how is it that he has an abundance of all things? From where, except because God has given it to him?
What would he have if God withdrew His hand?
Have not many lain down to sleep in wealth, and risen up in beggary?
And that he is not in want is due to God’s mercy, not to his own power.

10. But this bread, dearly beloved, by which our body is filled, by which the flesh is restored day by day—this bread, I say, God gives not only to those who praise Him, but also to those who blaspheme Him; “Who causes His sun to rise upon the evil and upon the good, and sends rain upon the just and upon the unjust.”
You praise Him, and He feeds you; you blaspheme Him, and He feeds you.
He waits for you to repent; but if you will not change yourself, He will condemn you.

Because, then, both good and bad receive this bread from God, do you think there is no other bread for which the children ask, of which the Lord said in the Gospel, “It is not fitting to take the children’s bread and to cast it to dogs”?
Yes, surely there is.
What, then, is that bread? And why is it called daily?
Because this is necessary, as the other is; for without it we cannot live; without bread we cannot live.
It is shamelessness to ask God for wealth; it is no shamelessness to ask for daily bread.
That which serves pride is one thing; that which serves life is another.
Nevertheless, because this bread which can be seen and handled is given both to the good and to the bad, there is a daily bread for which the children pray.
That is the word of God, which is dealt out to us day by day.
Our bread is daily bread; and by it live not our bodies, but our souls.
It is necessary for us who are even now laborers in the vineyard—it is our food, not our wages.
For he who hires the laborer into the vineyard owes him two things: food, so that he does not faint, and his wages, with which he may rejoice.
Our daily food, then, on this earth is the word of God, which is always dealt out in the Churches; our wages after labor are called eternal life.

Again, if by this our daily bread you understand what the faithful receive, what you shall receive when you have been baptized, it is with good reason that we ask and say, “Give us this day our daily bread,” that we may live in such a way that we are not separated from the Holy Altar.
11. “And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.”
Concerning this petition, again, we need no explanation to show that it is for ourselves that we pray.
For we beg that our debts may be forgiven us.
For we are debtors, not in money, but in sins.
Perhaps you are saying at this moment, And you too.
We answer, Yes, we too.
What, you holy Bishops, are you debtors?
Yes, we are debtors too.
What, you! My Lord.
Far be it from you; do not do yourself this wrong.
I do myself no wrong, but I speak the truth; we are debtors: “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”
We have been baptized, and yet we are debtors.
Not that anything then remained which was not remitted to us in Baptism, but because in our lives we are constantly contracting what needs daily forgiveness.
Those who are baptized and immediately depart out of this life come up from the font without any debt; without any debt they leave the world.
But those who are baptized and are still kept in this life contract defilements by reason of their mortal frailty, by which, though the ship is not sunk, they still need to have recourse to the pump.
For otherwise, little by little, that will enter in by which the whole ship will be sunk.
And to offer this prayer is to have recourse to the pump.
But we ought not only to pray, but also to give alms, because when the pump is used to keep the ship from sinking, both the voices and the hands are at work.
Now we are at work with our voices when we say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”
And we are at work with our hands when we do this: “Break your bread to the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house.
Shut up alms in the heart of a poor man, and it shall intercede for you with the Lord.”
12. Although, therefore, all our sins were forgiven in the “washing of regeneration,” we would be driven into great straits if we were not given the daily cleansing of the Holy Prayer.

Alms and prayers purge away sins; only let such sins not be committed for which we must necessarily be separated from our daily Bread; let us avoid all such debts to which a severe and certain condemnation is due.
Do not call yourselves righteous, as though you had no cause to say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

Though you abstain from idolatry, from the consolations of astrologers, from the cures of enchanters; though you abstain from the seductions of heretics, from the divisions of schismatics; though you abstain from murders, from adulteries and fornications, from thefts and plunderings, from false witness, and from all such other sins which I do not name, which have ruinous consequences, for which it is necessary that the sinner be cut off from the altar, and be so bound on earth as to be bound in heaven, to his great and deadly danger, unless he is again so loosed on earth as to be loosed in heaven—yet after all these are excepted, there is still no lack of occasions by which a man may sin.
A man sins in seeing with pleasure what he ought not to see.
Yet who can hold in the quickness of the eye?
For from this the eye is said to have received its very name, from its quickness.
Who can restrain the ear or the eye?

The eyes may be shut when you wish, and are shut in a moment; but the ears you can close only with an effort: you must raise the hand and reach them, and if anyone holds your hand, they are kept open, and you cannot close them against reviling, impure, or flattering and seductive words.
And when you hear anything you ought not to hear, even though you do not do it, do you not sin with the ear? For do you not hear something that is bad with pleasure?
How great are the sins that the deadly tongue commits!
Yes, sometimes sins of such a nature that a man is separated from the altar for them.
To the tongue belongs the whole matter of blasphemies, and again many idle words are spoken which are not fitting.

But let the hand do nothing wrong, let the feet not run to any evil, nor the eye be directed to immodesty; let not the ear be open with pleasure to filthy talk, nor the tongue move to indecent speech; yet tell me, who can restrain the thoughts?
How often we pray, my brethren, and our thoughts are elsewhere, as though we forgot before whom we are standing, or before whom we are prostrating ourselves!
If all these things are collected together against us, will they therefore fail to overwhelm us because they are small faults?
What does it matter whether lead or sand overwhelms us?
The lead is all one mass, the sand is small grains, but by their great number they overwhelm you.
So your sins are small.
Do you not see how the rivers are filled and the lands are laid waste by small drops?
They are small, but they are many.
13. Let us therefore say every day—and say it in sincerity of heart, and do what we say—“Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”
It is an engagement, a covenant, an agreement that we make with God.
The Lord your God says to you, Forgive, and I will forgive.

You have not forgiven; it is you who retain your sins against yourself, not I. I beg you, my dearly beloved children, since I know what is good for you in the Lord’s Prayer, and most of all in that sentence of it, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors”—hear me.
You are about to be baptized: forgive everything; whatever anyone has in his heart against anyone else, let him forgive it from his heart.

So enter in, and be sure that all your sins which you have contracted—whether from your birth of your parents after Adam with original sin, for the sake of which sins you run with infants to the Savior’s grace, or whatever sins you have contracted afterwards in your lives, by word, or deed, or thought—all are forgiven; and you will go out of the water as from the presence of your Lord, with the sure discharge of all debts.

14. Now because, by reason of those daily sins of which I have spoken, it is necessary for you to say in that daily prayer of cleansing, as it were, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors,” what will you do?
You have enemies. For who can live on this earth without them?
Take heed to yourselves: love them.
In no way can your enemy hurt you by his violence as much as you hurt yourself if you do not love him.
For he may injure your estate, or flocks, or house, or your manservant, or your maidservant, or your son, or your wife; or at most, if such power is given him, your body.
But can he injure your soul, as you can yourself?
Reach forward, dearly beloved, I beg you, to this perfection.
But have I given you this power?
He alone has given it to whom you say, “Your will be done as in heaven so on earth.”
Yet do not let it seem impossible to you.
I know, I have known by experience, that there are Christian men who do love their enemies.
If it seems impossible to you, you will not do it.
Believe, then, first that it can be done, and pray that the will of God may be done in you.
For what good can your neighbor’s evil do you?
If he had no evil, he would not even be your enemy.
Wish him well, then, that he may end his evil, and he will be your enemy no longer.
For it is not the human nature in him that is at enmity with you, but his sin.
Is he therefore your enemy because he has a soul and a body?
In this he is as you are: you have a soul, and so has he; you have a body, and so has he.
He is of the same substance as you are; you were both made out of the same earth, and given life by the same Lord.
In all this he is as you are. Acknowledge in him, then, your brother.
The first pair, Adam and Eve, were our parents—the one our father, the other our mother; and therefore we are brethren.
But let us leave aside the consideration of our first origin.
God is our Father, the Church our Mother, and therefore we are brethren.
But you will say, My enemy is a heathen, a Jew, a heretic, of whom I spoke some time ago on the words, “Your will be done as in heaven so on earth.”
O Church, your enemy is the heathen, the Jew, the heretic; he is the earth.
If you are heaven, call on your Father who is in heaven, and pray for your enemies; for so Saul was an enemy of the Church; thus prayer was made for him, and he became her friend.
He not only ceased to be her persecutor, but he labored to be her helper.
And yet, to tell the truth, prayer was made against him—but against his malice, not against his nature.
So let your prayer be against the malice of your enemy, that it may die and he may live.
For if your enemy were dead, you would have lost, it might seem, an enemy, yet you would not have found a friend.
But if his malice dies, you have at once lost an enemy and found a friend.
15. But still you are saying, Who can do this? Who has ever done it?
May God bring it about in your hearts!
I know as well as you that there are but few who do it; great and spiritual men are they who do so.
Are all the faithful in the Church who approach the altar and take the Body and Blood of Christ—are they all such?
And yet they all say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”
What if God should answer them, “Why do you ask Me to do what I have promised, when you do not do what I have commanded?”
What have I promised?
“To forgive your debts.”
What have I commanded?
“That you also forgive your debtors.”
How can you do this if you do not love your enemies?
What then must we do, brethren?
Is the flock of Christ reduced to such a scanty number?
If only those who love their enemies ought to say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors,” I do not know what to do, I do not know what to say.
For must I say to you, If you do not love your enemies, do not pray? I dare not say so; rather, pray that you may love them.
But must I say to you, If you do not love your enemies, do not say in the Lord’s Prayer, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors”?
Suppose that I were to say, Do not use these words.
If you do not, your debts are not forgiven; and if you do use them and do not act accordingly, they are not forgiven.
In order, therefore, that they may be forgiven, you must both use the prayer and act accordingly.
16. I see some ground on which I may comfort not only a few, but the multitude of Christians; and I know that you are longing to hear it.
Christ has said, “Forgive, that you may be forgiven.”
And what do you say in the Prayer which we have now been discussing?
“Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”
So, Lord, forgive, as we forgive.
This is what you say: “O Father, who is in heaven, so forgive our debts as we also forgive our debtors.”
For this you ought to do, and if you do not do it, you will perish.
When your enemy asks pardon, forgive him at once.
And is this much for you to do?
Though it were much for you to love your enemy when he is violent against you, is it much to love a man who is a suppliant before you?
What do you have to say?
He was violent before, and then you hated him.

I would rather you had not hated him even then; I would rather that then, when you were suffering from his violence, you had remembered the Lord saying, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do.”
I would have wished very much that even at that time when your enemy was violent against you, you had paid regard to the Lord your God speaking thus.
But perhaps you will say, He did it, but He did it as being the Lord, as the Christ, as the Son of God, as the Only-Begotten, as the Word made flesh.
But what can I, a weak and sinful man, do?
If your Lord is too high an example for you, turn your thoughts to your fellow servant.
The holy Stephen was being stoned, and as they stoned him, on bended knees he prayed for his enemies and said, “Lord, do not lay this sin to their charge.”
They were casting stones, not asking pardon, yet he prayed for them.
I wish you were like him; reach forward.
Why are you forever trailing your heart along the earth?
Hear, “Lift up your heart”; reach forward, love your enemies.
If you cannot love him in his violence, love him at least when he asks pardon.
Love the man who says to you, “Brother, I have sinned, forgive me.”
If you do not forgive him then, I say not merely that you blot this prayer out of your heart, but that you yourself shall be blotted out of the book of God.
17. But if you then at least forgive him, or let go of hatred from your heart—it is hatred from the heart that I bid you give up, and not proper discipline.
What if one who asks my pardon is one who ought to be chastised by me!
Do what you will, for I suppose that you love your child even when you chastise him.
You do not regard his cries under the rod, because you are reserving his inheritance for him.
This, then, is what I say: that you give up all hatred from your heart when your enemy asks pardon of you.
But perhaps you will say, “He is playing false, he is pretending.”
O you judge of another’s heart, tell me your own father’s thoughts; tell me your own thoughts yesterday.
He asks and petitions for pardon; forgive, by all means forgive him.
If you will not forgive him, it is yourself you hurt, not him, for he knows what he has to do.
You are not willing to forgive your own fellow servant; he will go, then, to your Lord and say to Him, “Lord, I have begged my fellow servant to forgive me, and he would not; do You forgive me.”
Has not the Lord power to release His servant’s debts?
So he, having obtained pardon from his Lord, returns released, while you remain bound.

How bound? The time of prayer will come, the time must come for you to say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors”; and the Lord will answer you, You wicked servant, when you owed Me so great a debt, you asked Me, and I forgave you; “ought you not also to have had compassion on your fellow servant, even as I had pity on you?”
These words are from the Gospel, not from my own heart.
But if, on being asked, you forgive him who begs for pardon, then you can say this prayer.
And if you do not yet have the strength to love him in his violence, you may still offer this prayer, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”
Let us pass on to the rest.
18. “And lead us not into temptation.
Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors,” we say because of past sins, which we cannot undo so that they should not have been done.
You can labor not to do what you have done before, but how can you bring it about that what you have done should not have been done?
As regards those things which have been done already, that sentence of the prayer is your help, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”
As regards those into which you may fall, what will you do?
“Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.”
“Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil”—that is, from temptation itself.

19. Now these three first petitions, “Hallowed be Your Name, Your kingdom come, Your will be done as in heaven so on earth”—these three concern the life eternal; for God’s Name ought to be hallowed in us always, we ought to be in His kingdom always, we ought to do His will always.
This will be to all eternity.
But “daily bread” is necessary now.
All the rest that we pray for from this petition onward concerns the necessities of the present life.
Daily bread is necessary in this life; the forgiveness of our debts is necessary in this life.
For when we arrive at the other life, there will be an end of all debts.
In this life there is temptation; in this life the sailing is dangerous; in this life something is always stealing its way in through the chinks of our frailties, which must be pumped out.
But when we are made equal to the Angels of God, there will be no more need to say and pray to God to forgive us our debts, when there will be none.

Here, then, is the “daily bread”; here the prayer that our “debts may be forgiven”; here that we “enter not into temptation,” for in that life temptation does not enter; here that we may be “delivered from evil,” for in that life there will be no evil, but eternal and abiding good.
1. Yesterday the holy Gospel warned us not to neglect the sins of our brothers: “But if your brother sins against you, rebuke him between him and you alone.
If he hears you, you have gained your brother.
But if he refuses to hear you, take with you two or three more, so that every word may be established in the mouth of two or three witnesses.
And if he neglects to hear them too, tell it to the Church.
But if he neglects to hear the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector.”
Today also the passage that follows, which we heard when it was read, relates to the same subject.
For when the Lord Jesus had said this to Peter, he went on to ask his Master how often he should forgive a brother who had sinned against him; and he asked whether seven times would be enough.
“The Lord answered him: Not only seven times, but seventy times seven.”
Then He added a parable very full of terror: that “the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who settled accounts with his servants; among them he found one who owed ten thousand talents.
And when he commanded that all he had, and all his family, and he himself be sold, and the debt be paid, he fell down at his lord’s feet,” and begged for time, and obtained complete remission.
For as we have heard, “His lord was moved with compassion, and forgave him all the debt.”

Then that man, free from his debt but a slave of wickedness, after he had gone out from the presence of his lord, found in his turn a debtor of his own, who owed him not ten thousand talents, the sum that had been forgiven him, but a hundred denarii; and “he began to drag him by the throat, saying, Pay me what you owe.”
Then he pleaded with his fellow servant as he had done with his lord; but he did not find his fellow servant to be such a man as the other had found his lord to be.
He not only would not forgive him the debt; he did not even grant him time.
He hurried him along with great violence to make him pay, he who had only just been set free from his debt to his lord.

His fellow servants were displeased, and “went and told their lord what had been done”; and the lord summoned his servant into his presence and said to him, “You wicked servant, when you owed me so great a debt, out of pity for you I forgave you all.
Ought you not also to have had compassion on your fellow servant, even as I had pity on you?”
And he commanded that all he had forgiven him should be paid.
2. It is, then, for our instruction that He put forth this parable, and by this warning He would save us from perishing.
“So,” He said, “will My heavenly Father also do to you, if from your hearts you do not each forgive your brother his trespasses.”
Look, brothers, the matter is plain, the warning is useful, and a wholesome obedience is by all means due, so that what has been commanded may be fulfilled.
For every man is at once God’s debtor, and also has some brother who is a debtor to himself.
For who is there who is not God’s debtor, except the one in whom no sin can be found?
And who is there who does not have a brother as his debtor, except the one against whom no one has sinned?
Do you think anyone among mankind can be found who is not himself bound to his brother by some sin?
So then every man is a debtor, yet he also has debtors of his own.
The righteous God therefore sets a rule for you toward your debtor, which He also will observe with His.
For there are two works of mercy that set us free, which the Lord Himself has briefly laid down in the Gospel: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven; give, and it shall be given to you.”
“Forgive, and you shall be forgiven” relates to pardoning.
“Give, and it shall be given to you” relates to doing kindnesses.
As to what He says about pardoning: you both want your sin to be pardoned, and you have another whom you may pardon.
Again, as to doing kindnesses: a beggar asks of you, and you are God’s beggar.

For when we pray we are all God’s beggars; we stand, or rather we fall prostrate, before the door of the Great Householder; we groan in supplication, wishing to receive something; and this something is God Himself.
What does the beggar ask of you?
Bread. And what do you ask of God, but Christ, who says, “I am the living Bread which came down from heaven”?
Do you want to be forgiven?
Forgive. “Forgive, and it shall be forgiven you.”
Do you want to receive? “Give, and it shall be given to you.”
3. But now hear what difficulty I may raise in so plain a precept.
In this question of forgiveness, when pardon is asked and it is due from the one who should grant it, it may be a difficulty to us as it was to Peter.
“How often ought I to forgive?
Is up to seven times enough?”
“It is not enough,” says the Lord; “I do not say to you, until seven times, but until seventy times seven.”
Now count up how often your brother has sinned against you.
If you can reach the seventy-eighth fault, so as to get beyond the seventy times seven, then set about revenge.

Is this then what He really means, and is it really so: that if he sins “seventy times seven,” you should forgive him, but if he sins seventy-eight times, it would then be lawful for you not to forgive?
No, I dare to say that even if he should sin seventy-eight times, you must forgive.
Yes, as I have said, if he sins seventy-eight times, forgive.
And if he sins a hundred times, forgive.
And why need I name this number or that?
In one word, as often as he sins, forgive him.
Have I then taken it upon myself to go beyond the measure of my Lord?
He fixed the limit of forgiveness at the number seventy-seven; shall I presume to leap over this limit?
It is not so; I have not presumed to go beyond it at all.
I have heard the Lord Himself speaking in His Apostle, where no measure or number is fixed.
For He says, “Forgiving one another, if anyone has a quarrel against anyone, just as God in Christ has forgiven you.”
Here you have the rule.

If Christ has forgiven you your sins only “seventy times and seven,” if He has pardoned up to this point and refused to pardon beyond it, then you also fix this limit and be unwilling to forgive beyond it.
But if Christ has found thousands of sins upon sins and has still forgiven all, then do not withdraw your mercy, but ask forgiveness for that great number.
For it was not without meaning that the Lord said “seventy times seven,” since there is no trespass whatever that you ought not to forgive.
See this servant in the parable, who, being a debtor, was found to have a debtor: he owed ten thousand talents.
And I suppose that ten thousand talents are at least ten thousand sins.
For I will not say how even one talent may include all sins.
But how much did the other servant owe him?
He owed a hundred denarii.
Now is this not more than “seventy and seven”?
And yet the Lord was angry, because he did not forgive him.
For not only is a hundred more than “seventy-seven,” but a hundred denarii are perhaps a thousand “asses.”
But what was this compared to ten thousand talents?
4. And so let us be ready to forgive all the trespasses that are committed against us, if we desire to be forgiven.

For if we consider our sins, and count up what we do in deed, what by the eye, what by the ear, what by thought, what by countless movements, I do not know whether we so much as sleep without a talent.
And therefore we beg daily, daily knock at the ears of God by prayer, daily prostrate ourselves and say, “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.”
What debts of yours?
All, or a certain part?
You will answer, All.
So then do the same with your debtor.
This, then, is the rule you lay down, this the condition you speak of; this the covenant and agreement you mention when you pray, saying, “Forgive us, as we forgive our debtors.”
5. What then, brothers, is the meaning of “seventy times seven”?
Listen, for it is a great mystery, a wonderful sacrament.

When the Lord was baptized, the Evangelist St. Luke recorded in that place His generations in the regular order, series, and line in which they had come down to that generation in which Christ was born.
Matthew begins at Abraham and comes down to Joseph in descending order; but Luke begins to count in ascending order.
Why does the one count in descending order, and the other in ascending order?
Because Matthew set forth the generation of Christ by which He came down to us; and so he began to count from when Christ was born, in descending order.

But because Luke begins to count from when Christ was baptized, and in this is the beginning of ascent, he begins to count in ascending order, and in his count he has completed seventy-seven generations.
With whom did he begin his count?
Notice with whom. He began to count from Christ up to Adam himself, who was the first sinner, and who begot us with the bond of sin.
He counted up to Adam, and so seventy-seven generations are counted; that is, from Christ up to Adam and from Adam up to Christ are the aforementioned seventy-seven generations.
So then, if no generation was omitted, no trespass is exempted from those which ought to be forgiven.

For this is why he counted up his seventy-seven generations, the number the Lord mentioned concerning the forgiveness of sins: since he begins to count from the baptism, in which all sins are remitted.
6. And, brothers, observe in this a still greater mystery.
In the number seventy-seven is a mystery of the remission of sins.
That many generations are found from Christ to Adam.
Now then, ask with somewhat more careful diligence for the secret meaning of this number, and inquire into its hidden meaning; knock with more careful diligence, that it may be opened to you.
Righteousness consists in keeping the Law of God: true.
For the Law is set forth in ten commandments.
That is why the servant in the parable “owed ten thousand talents.”
This is that memorable Decalogue written by the finger of God, and delivered to the people by Moses, the servant of God.
He “owed,” then, “ten thousand talents,” which signifies all sins, with reference to the number of the Law.
And the other “owed a hundred denarii,” derived equally from the same number.
For a hundred times a hundred make ten thousand, and ten times ten make a hundred.
And the one “owed ten thousand talents,” and the other ten times ten denarii.
For there was no departure from the number of the law, and in both numbers you will find every kind of sin included.
Both are debtors, and both implore and beg for pardon; but the wicked, ungrateful servant would not repay what he had received, would not grant the mercy that had been shown him undeservedly.

7. Consider then, brothers: every man begins from Baptism; he goes out free, the “ten thousand talents” are forgiven him; and when he goes out, he will soon find some fellow servant who is his debtor.
Let him note, then, what sin itself is; for the number eleven is the transgression of the law.
For the law is ten, sin eleven.
For the law is denoted by ten, sin by eleven.
Why is sin denoted by eleven?
Because to get to eleven, there is the transgression of the ten.
But the due limit is fixed in the law; and the transgression of it is sin.
Now when you have passed beyond the ten, you come to eleven.
This high mystery was prefigured when the tabernacle was commanded to be built.
Many things are mentioned there by number, which are a great mystery.
Among the rest, curtains of haircloth were ordered to be made, not ten, but eleven; because haircloth signifies the confession of sins.
Now what more do you require?
Would you know how all sins are contained in this number “seventy-seven”?
Seven, then, is usually put for a whole; because in seven days the cycle of time is completed, and when the seventh is ended, it returns to the first again, so that the same cycle may be continued.
In such cycles whole ages pass away; yet there is no departure from the number seven.
For He spoke of all sins when He said “seventy times seven”; for multiply that eleven seven times, and it makes seventy-seven.
Therefore He would have all sins forgiven, for He marked them out by the number “seventy-seven.”
Let no one, then, retain anything to his own harm by refusing to forgive, lest it be retained against him when he prays.
For God says, “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven.”
For I have forgiven you first; you at least forgive after that.
For if you will not forgive, I will call you back and lay on you again all that I had forgiven you.
For the Truth does not speak falsely; Christ neither deceives nor is deceived, and He has said at the close of the parable, “So likewise will your Father who is in heaven do to you.”
You find a Father; imitate your Father.
For if you will not imitate Him, you are contriving to be disinherited.
“So likewise,” then, “will My heavenly Father also do to you, if from your hearts you do not each forgive your brother his trespasses.”
Do not say with the tongue, “I forgive,” while putting off forgiving in the heart; for by His threat of vengeance God shows you your punishment.
God knows from where you speak.
Man can hear your voice; God looks into your conscience.
If you say, I forgive, then forgive.
It is better that you should be violent in words and forgive in the heart, than be soft in words and relentless in the heart.
8. Now then, unruly boys will beg, and take it hard to be beaten, taking exception against us in this way when we want to punish them.
“I have sinned, but forgive me.”
Well, I have forgiven, and he sins again.
“Forgive me,” he cries, and I have forgiven him.
He sins a third time.
“Forgive me,” he cries, and a third time I have forgiven him.
Now then, the fourth time let him be beaten.
And he will say, “What! Have I worn you out up to seventy-seven times?”
Now if by such objections the severity of discipline falls asleep, then once discipline is suppressed, wickedness will rage unpunished.
What then is to be done?
Let us rebuke with words, and if need be with the lash; but let us at the same time forgive the sin, and cast the memory of it out of the heart.
For this is why the Lord added, “from your hearts”: that though discipline be exercised out of love, gentleness might not depart from the heart.
For what is so kind and gentle as the surgeon with his knife?
The one who is to be cut cries out, yet he is cut; the one who is to be cauterized cries out, yet he is cauterized.
This is not cruelty; on no account let that surgeon’s treatment be called cruelty.
He is cruel to the wounded part so that the patient may be cured; for if the wound is treated softly, the man is lost.

So this is my advice, my brothers: that we love our brothers, however they may have sinned against us; that we do not let affection toward them depart from our hearts; and that when there is need, we exercise discipline toward them; lest through the relaxing of discipline wickedness increase, and we begin to be accused on God’s behalf, for it has been read to us, “Rebuke those who sin in the presence of all, that others also may fear.”
Certainly, if one distinguishes the times, which is the only true way, and so solves the question, all is true.
If the sin is in secret, rebuke it in secret.
If the sin is public and open, rebuke it publicly, that the sinner may be reformed, and “that others also may fear.”
1. The holy Gospel, which we heard just now as it was being read, has admonished us concerning the remission of sins.
And on this subject you must now be admonished by my sermon.
For we are ministers of the word, not our own word, but the word of our God and Lord, whom no one serves without glory, whom no one despises without punishment.

He, then, the Lord our God, who, abiding with the Father, made us, and, having been made for us, re-made us, He, the Lord our God, Jesus Christ Himself, says to us what we have heard just now in the Gospel.
“If,” He says, “your brother sins against you, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him; and if he sins against you seven times in a day, and comes and says, I repent, forgive him.”
He would not have “seven times in a day” understood otherwise than “as often as may be,” lest perhaps he sin eight times, and you be unwilling to forgive.
What then is “seven times”?
Always, as often as he sins and repents.
For this, “Seven times in a day I will praise You,” is the same as what another Psalm says, “His praise shall always be in my mouth.”
And there is the strongest reason why seven times should be put for that which is always: for the whole course of time revolves in a circle of seven days that come and return.
2. Whoever you are, then, who have your thoughts on Christ and desire to receive what He has promised, do not be slow to do what He has commanded.
Now what has He promised?
“Eternal life.” And what has He commanded?
That pardon be given to your brother.
As if He had said to you, “You, O man, give pardon to a man, so that I, who am God, may come to you.”

But to pass over, or rather to pass by for a while, those more exalted divine promises in which our Creator pledges to make us equal to His angels, so that we may live without end with Him, and in Him, and by Him; not to speak of this just now, do you not wish to receive from your God this very thing which you are commanded to give your brother?
This very thing, I say, which you are commanded to give your brother, do you not wish to receive from your Lord?
Tell me if you do not wish it; and then do not give it.
What is this, but that you should forgive the one who asks you, if you need to be forgiven?
But if you have nothing to be forgiven, I dare to say, be unwilling to forgive.
Though I ought not even to say this.
Even if you have nothing to be forgiven, forgive.
3. You are just on the point of saying to me, “But I am not God; I am a man, a sinner.”
Thank God that you confess that you have sins.
Forgive, then, so that they may be forgiven you.
Yet the Lord our God Himself exhorts us to imitate Him.

In the first place God Himself, Christ, exhorts us, of whom the Apostle Peter said, “Christ has suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow His steps, who did no sin, nor was deceit found in His mouth.”
He, then, truly had no sin, and yet He died for our sins, and shed His Blood for the remission of sins.
For our sakes He took upon Himself what was not His due, so that He might deliver us from what was due to us.
Death was not due to Him, nor life to us.
Why? Because we were sinners.
Death was not due to Him, nor life to us; He received what was not due to Him, He gave what was not due to us.

But since we are speaking of the remission of sins, lest you should think it too high a thing to imitate Christ, hear the Apostle saying, “Forgiving one another, even as God in Christ has forgiven you.”
“Therefore be imitators of God.”
These are the Apostle’s words, not mine.
Is it really a proud thing to imitate God?
Hear the Apostle: “Be imitators of God as dearly beloved children.”
You are called a child: if you refuse to imitate Him, why do you seek His inheritance?
4. I would say this even if you had no sin which you might desire to have forgiven.
But as it is, whoever you are, you are a man; though you are righteous, you are a man; whether you are a layman, or a monk, or a cleric, or a bishop, or an apostle, you are a man.
Hear the Apostle’s voice: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves.”
He, that famous John, and an Evangelist, he whom the Lord Christ loved beyond all the rest, who lay on His breast, he says, “If we say.”
He did not say, “If you say that you have no sin,” but “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”
He joined himself in the guilt, so that he might be joined in the pardon also.
“If we say.”
Consider who it is that says, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
But if we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all iniquity.”
How does He cleanse?
By forgiving; not as though He found nothing to punish, but as finding something to forgive.
So then, brothers, if we have sins, let us forgive those who ask us.
Let us not retain enmities in our heart against another.
For retaining enmities corrupts this heart of ours more than anything.
5. I want you, then, to forgive, since I find you asking for forgiveness.

You are asked: forgive. You are asked, and you yourself will ask; you are asked: forgive; you will ask to be forgiven; for, look, the time of prayer will come: I hold you fast by the words you will have to speak.
You will say, “Our Father, who is in heaven.”
For you will not be among the number of children if you do not say, “Our Father.”
So then you will say, “Our Father, who is in heaven.”
Go on: “Hallowed be Your Name.”
Say on: “Your kingdom come.”
Go on still: “Your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.”
See what you add next: “Give us this day our daily bread.”
Where are your riches?
So you are a beggar.
Nevertheless, in the meantime (it is the point I am speaking of), say what comes next after “Give us this day our daily bread.”
Say what follows this: “Forgive us our debts.”
Now you have come to my words: “Forgive us our debts.”
By what right? By what covenant? On what condition? On what express stipulation?
“As we also forgive our debtors.”
It is only a small thing that you do not forgive; indeed you do more: you lie to God.
The condition is laid down, the law fixed.
“Forgive as I forgive.”
Therefore He does not forgive unless you forgive.
“Forgive as I forgive.”
You wish to be forgiven when you ask; forgive the one who asks of you.
He who is skilled in heaven’s laws has dictated these prayers: He does not deceive you; ask according to the wording of His heavenly voice: say, “Forgive us, as we also forgive,” and do what you say.
He who lies in his prayers loses the benefit he seeks; he who lies in his prayers both loses his case and finds his punishment.
And if anyone lies to the emperor, he is convicted of his lie at his coming; but when you lie in prayer, you are convicted by your very prayer.
For God does not look for a witness concerning you in order to convict you.
He who dictated the prayers to you is your Advocate; if you lie, He is a witness against you; if you do not amend yourself, He will be your Judge.
So then, both say it and do it.
For if you do not say it, you will not obtain what you ask, since you make your requests contrary to the law; but if you say it and do not do it, you will be guilty of lying as well.
There is no way of evading that verse except by fulfilling what we say.
Can we blot this verse out of our prayer?
Would you have that clause, “Forgive us our debts,” remain there, and have us blot out what follows, “As we also forgive our debtors”?
You shall not blot it out, lest you yourself be blotted out first.
So then in this prayer you say, “Give,” and you say, “Forgive,” so that you may receive what you do not have, and be forgiven what you have done wrong.
So then, you wish to receive: give; you wish to be forgiven: forgive.
It is a brief summary.
Hear Christ Himself in another place: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven.”
What will you forgive?
What others have sinned against you.
What will you be forgiven?
What you yourselves have sinned.
“Forgive.” “Give, and there shall be given you what you desire”: eternal life.
Support the temporal life of the poor man, sustain the poor man’s present life, and for this so small and earthly seed you shall receive as your harvest life eternal. Amen.

1. The divine readings, which we have just heard as they were being read, warn us to gather a store of virtues, to fortify a Christian heart against the offenses which were predicted to come, and this from the mercy of the Lord.
“For what is man,” says Scripture, “except that You are mindful of him?”
“Woe to the world because of offenses,” says the Lord; the Truth says so; He alarms and warns us, He would not have us be off our guard; for surely He would not make us despair.

Against this “woe,” that is, against this evil which is to be feared, and dreaded, and guarded against, Scripture counsels, and exhorts, and instructs us in that place where it is said, “Great peace have they who love Your law, and nothing is an offense to them.”
He has shown us an enemy to be guarded against, but He has not failed to show us also a wall of defense.
You were thinking, as you heard, “Woe to the world because of offenses,” where you might go beyond the world, so that you might not be exposed to offenses.
Therefore, to avoid offenses, where will you go beyond the world, unless you flee to Him who made the world?
And how shall we be able to flee to Him who made the world, unless we give ear to His law, which is preached everywhere?
And to give ear to it is but a small matter, unless we love it.
For divine Scripture, in making you secure against offenses, does not say, “Great peace have they who hear Your law.”
For it is not the hearers of the law who are just before God.
But because “the doers of the law shall be justified,” and “faith works by love,” it says, “Great peace have they who love Your law, and nothing is an offense to them.”
With this sentiment the passage which we have sung in its turn also agrees: “But the meek shall inherit the earth, and shall delight themselves in the abundance of peace.”
Because “great peace have they who love Your law.”
For these “meek” ones are those who “love the law of God.”
For, “Blessed is the man whom You chasten, O Lord, and teach out of Your law, that You may give him rest from the days of adversity, until the pit is dug for the sinner.”

How different those words of Scripture seem, yet they so flow and meet together into one meaning that, whatever you can hear out of that most rich fountain, so that you rest in it and are in loving harmony with the truth, you will at once be filled with peace, glowing with love, and fortified against offenses.
2. It is our part, then, to see, or seek, or learn how we must be “meek”; and we are guided by what I have just brought forward out of the Scriptures to find what we are seeking.
Be attentive, then, Beloved, for a little while; it is a weighty matter that is at hand, that we may be meek; a necessary thing in the adversities of life.
But it is not the adverse circumstances of this life that are called offenses; but note what “offenses” are.
A man, for instance, under some hard necessity, is weighed down by a pressure of trouble.
That he is weighed down by a pressure of trouble is no offense.
By such pressure even the Martyrs were pressed, but not oppressed.
Beware of an offense, but of a pressure of trouble not so much.
The latter presses you; an offense oppresses you.
What, then, is the difference between the two?
In the pressure of trouble you made ready to maintain patience, to hold fast to constancy, not to abandon faith, not to consent to sin.

If you maintain this, or shall have maintained it, the trouble that presses you shall not be your fall; but that pressure of trouble shall serve the same end as in the oil press: not to destroy the olive, but to extract the oil.
In a word, if in this trouble that presses you, you give praise to God, how useful the press will be to you, by which such oil is pressed out!
Under such a press the Apostles sat in chains, and in that press they sang a hymn to God.
What precious oil was this that was pressed and forced out!

Beneath a heavy press Job sat on the dunghill, without resources, without help, without substance, without children; full, but of worms only, as far, that is, as concerned the outward man; but because he too was full of God within, he praised God, and that press was no “offense” to him.
Where, then, was the “offense”?
When his wife came to him and said, “Speak a word against God, and die.”
When all had been taken from him by the devil, an Eve was kept back for the tried sufferer, not to console but to tempt her husband.
See, then, where the offense was.
She exaggerated his miseries, and her own miseries too along with his, and began to persuade him to blaspheme.

But he who was “meek,” because “God had taught him out of His law, and given him rest from the days of adversity,” had “great peace” in his heart, as one “loving the law of God, and nothing was an offense to him.”
She was an offense, but not to him.
In a word, behold the meek man, behold one taught in the law of God, the eternal law of God, I mean.

For that law on tablets was not yet given to the Jews in the time of Job, but in the hearts of the godly there still remained the eternal law, from which the law that was given to the people was copied.
Because, then, by the law of God he had “rest given him from the days of adversity,” and “had great peace as loving the law of God,” see how “meek” he is, and what he answers.
Learn from this what I propose to inquire into: who the meek are.
“You speak,” he says, “as one of the foolish women speaks.
If we have received good from the hand of the Lord, shall we not bear the evil?”
3. We have heard by an example who the meek are; let us, if we can, define them in words.
The meek are those to whom, in all their good deeds, in all the things they do well, nothing is pleasing but God; to whom, in all the evils they suffer, God is not displeasing.
Now, Brethren, pay attention to this rule, to this pattern; let us stretch ourselves out toward it, let us seek to grow, that we may fill it.
For what does it profit that we plant and water, unless God gives the increase?
“For neither is he who plants anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase.”

Give ear, whoever you are who would be “meek,” who would have “rest from the days of adversity, who love the law of God,” that there may be “no offense to you,” and that you may “have great peace,” that you may “possess the earth, and delight in the multitude of peace”; give ear, whoever you are who would be “meek.”
Whatever good you do, do not be pleased with yourself.
“For God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”
So then, whatever good you do, let nothing but God be pleasing to you; whatever evil you suffer, let not God be displeasing to you.
What more do you need?
Do this, and you shall live.
The days of adversity shall not overwhelm you; you shall escape what is said, “Woe to the world because of offenses.”
For to what world is there woe because of offenses, but to that of which it is said, “And the world did not know Him”?
Not to that world of which it is said, “God was in Christ reconciling the world to Himself.”
There is an evil world, and there is a good world; the evil world is all the evil men in this world, and the good world is all the good in this world.
As we frequently observe with a field.
This field is full: of what?
Of wheat. Yet we also say, and say truly too, This field is full of chaff.
So with a tree: it is full of fruit.
Another says it is full of leaves.
And both he who says it is full of fruit speaks truly, and he who says it is full of leaves speaks truly.
Neither has the full display of leaves taken away the room for the fruit, nor has the full display of fruit driven off the abundance of leaves.
It is full of both; but the one the wind searches out, the other the farmer gathers in.
So therefore, when you hear, “Woe to the world because of offenses,” do not be afraid; “love the law of God, and nothing shall be an offense to you.”
4. But your wife comes to you advising you to some evil thing.
You love her as a wife should be loved; she is one of your members.
“But if your eye offends you, if your hand offends you, if your foot offends you,” you have just heard the Gospel, “cut them off, and cast them from you.”

Whoever he is that is dear to you, whoever he is that is held in high esteem by you, let him be held in high esteem by you only so long, and be your beloved member only so long, as he does not begin to offend you, that is, to advise you to any evil.
Hear now that this is the meaning of “offense.”
I have brought forward the example of Job and his wife; but there the word “offense” did not occur.
Hear the Gospel: when the Lord prophesied of His Passion, Peter began to persuade Him not to suffer.
“Get behind Me, Satan, you are an offense to Me.”
Here undoubtedly the Lord, who has given you an example of life, has taught you both what an “offense” is and how an offense is to be avoided.
Him to whom He had a little while before said, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah,” He had shown to be His member.
But when he begins to be an offense, He cuts off the member; only He restored the member, and put it back into its place again.
He, then, will be an “offense” to you who begins to persuade you to any evil thing.
And here, Beloved, take heed; this happens for the most part not through any evil will, but through a mistaken good will.
Your friend who loves you and is loved by you in return, your father, your brother, your child, your wife, sees you in an evil plight, and would have you do what is evil.
What do I mean by “sees you in an evil plight”?
Sees you in some pressure of trouble.
Perhaps you are suffering this pressure for righteousness’ sake; you are suffering it because you will not give false witness.
I would speak merely by way of illustration.
Examples abound; for “woe to the world because of offenses.”
See, for instance, some powerful person, to cover up his robbery and plunder, asks of you the service of a false witness.
You refuse: refuse the false oath, lest you should deny Him who is true.

Not to dwell long on this: he is angry, he is powerful, he oppresses you; a friend comes who would not have you in this pressure of trouble, in this evil plight: “I beg you, do what you are told; what great matter is it?”
And then perhaps, as Satan did with the Lord: “It is written of You, He shall give His Angels charge concerning You, so that You do not dash Your foot against a stone.”
Perhaps too this friend of yours, because he sees that you are a Christian, wishes to persuade you out of the Law to do what he thinks you ought to do.
“Do what the other tells you.”
“What? Do what the other wishes.”
“But it is a lie, it is false.”
“Well, have you not read, ‘All men are liars’?”
Now he is an “offense.”
He is a friend; what will you do?
He is an eye, he is a hand: “Cut it off, and cast it from you.”
What is “cut it off, and cast it from you”?
Do not consent to him.
For the members in our body make up a unity by consent; by consent they live, by consent they are joined together one with another.
Where there is dissent, there is disease, or a sore.
He is, then, one of your members; you will love him.
But he is an offense to you: “Cut him off, and cast him from you.”
Do not consent to him; drive him away from your ears; it may be he will return corrected.
5. And how will you do this that I say, “Cut him off, and cast him from you,” and so, it may be, correct him? Answer me: how are you going to do it?
He wished to persuade you out of the Law to tell a lie.
For he said, “Speak.”
And perhaps he did not dare to say, “Speak a lie”; but rather, “Speak what the other wishes.”
You say, “But it is a lie.”
And he, to excuse it, says, “All men are liars.”
Then you, my brother, say against this, “The mouth that lies slays the soul.”
Note, it is no light thing you have heard: “The mouth that lies slays the soul.”
What can that powerful enemy who oppresses me do to me, that you pity me and my condition, and would not have me be in this evil plight, while you would have me be evil?
What can that powerful man do to me, and what can he oppress?
The flesh. He can oppress your body, you will say: I grant he may oppress it even to destruction.
Still, how much more mildly he deals with me than I would deal with myself if I were to lie!
He kills my flesh; I kill my soul.
He, in his power and anger, slays the body; “the mouth that lies slays the soul.”
He slays the body; and die it must, even if it were not slain; but the soul which iniquity does not slay, the truth receives forever.
Preserve, then, what you can preserve; and let that perish which must perish sometime or other.
You have given an answer, then, but you have not resolved the “All men are liars.”
Answer him on this too, so that he may not imagine he has said anything to persuade you to lie by bringing a testimony out of the Law, thus urging you out of the Law against the Law.
For it is written in the Law, “You shall not bear false witness”; and it is written in the Law, “All men are liars.”
Go back, then, to what I suggested just now, when I defined in words, as best I could, the “meek” man.
He is “meek” to whom, in all things that he does well, nothing but God is pleasing, and in all the evils which he suffers, God is not displeasing.
Answer him, then, who says, Lie, for it is written, “All men are liars”: I will not lie, for it is written, “The mouth that lies slays the soul.”
I will not lie, because it is written, “You shall destroy those who speak lies.”
I will not lie, because it is written, “You shall not bear false witness.”
Though he whom I displease by the truth harass my body with oppressions, I will give ear to my Lord: “Do not fear those who kill the body.”
6. “How, then, are all men liars?
What! You are not a man, I suppose?”
Answer quickly and truly.
“And oh, that I may not be a man, so that I may not be a liar.”
For see: “God looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see if there were any who understood and sought after God.
They have all gone out of the way, they have all together become unprofitable; there is none who does good, no, not even one.”
Why? Because they wished to be sons of men.
But in order that He might deliver them from these iniquities, and cure, heal, and change the sons of men, “He gave them power to become the sons of God.”
What marvel, then! You were men, if we were the sons of men; you were all men, and were liars, for “All men are liars.”
The grace of God came to you, and “gave you power to become the sons of God.”
Hear the voice of My Father saying, “I have said, You are gods, and you are all children of the Most High.”
Since, then, they are men, and the sons of men, if they are not the children of the Most High, they are liars, for “all men are liars.”

If they are the sons of God, if they have been redeemed by the Savior’s grace, if purchased with His precious Blood, if born again of water and of the Spirit, if predestined to the inheritance of heaven, then indeed they are children of God.
And so, by this, they are gods.
What, then, would a lie have to do with you?
For Adam was a mere man; Christ, man and God; God, the Creator of all creation.
Adam a mere man; the Man Christ, the Mediator with God, the Only Son of the Father, the God-man.
Look, you, O man, are far from God, and God is far above man; between them the God-man placed Himself.
Acknowledge Christ, and through Him as Man ascend up to God.
7. Being now, then, reformed, and, if my words have been so blessed, “meek,” let us “hold fast our profession without wavering.”
Let us love the law of God, that we may escape what is written, “Woe to the world because of offenses.”
Now I would say a few words about “offenses,” of which the world is full, and how it is that offenses thicken and pressing troubles abound.
The world is laid waste; the winepress is trodden.

Ah, Christians, heavenly shoot, you strangers on the earth, who seek a city in heaven, who long to be joined with the holy Angels; understand that you have come here on this condition only, that you should soon depart.
You are passing on through the world, striving to reach Him who created it.
Let not the lovers of the world, who wish to remain in the world and yet, whether they will or not, are compelled to move from it—let them not disturb you, let them not deceive or seduce you.
These pressing troubles are not offenses.
Be righteous, and they will be only exercises.
Tribulation comes; it will be as you choose it, either an exercise or a condemnation.
Such as it finds you to be, such will it be.
Tribulation is a fire; does it find you gold? It takes away the filth. Does it find you chaff? It turns it into ashes.
The pressing troubles, then, which abound are not “offenses.”
But what are “offenses”?
Those expressions, those words in which we are addressed like this:
“See what Christian times bring about”; look, these are the true offenses.
For this is said to you to this end: that, if you love the world, you may blaspheme Christ.
And the one who says this to you is your friend and counselor; and so he is “your eye.”
